before.question_text: The cumulative frequency curve below shows the time taken by 80 students in School A to complete a 1.6 km run.

parts.text: Use the graph to estimate
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the median,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: The median is the time at a cumulative frequency of 40: about $7.35$ min.

subparts.text: the interquartile range,
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Lower quartile (CF 20) $\approx 6.45$ min; upper quartile (CF 60) $\approx 8.25$ min.
IQR $= 8.25 - 6.45 = 1.8$ min.

subparts.text: Find the 90th percentile.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution: The 90th percentile is the time at a cumulative frequency of $0.9 \times 80 = 72$: about $9$ min.

parts.text: The box-and-whisker plot shows the distribution of time taken by another group of 80 students in School B to complete a 1.6 km run.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Which school had the faster time on average? Give a reason for your answer.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: School A. School A has a median time ($7.35$ min) which is lower than School B's median ($8.8$ min).

subparts.text: Which school had the less variation in time compared to the other? Give a reason for your answer.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: School A. School A has a smaller interquartile range ($1.8$ min) compared to School B (about $3.6$ min), so School A has less variation.

before.question_text: A conical paper cup of radius 4 cm has a capacity of $64\pi\text{ cm}^{3}$. It is filled with water to a depth of $\dfrac{3}{4}$ the height of the cone.

parts.text: Find, in terms of $\pi$, the volume of the water in the cup.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Method 1: Volume of water in cup $= \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{3} \times 64\pi = 27\pi\text{ cm}^{3}$

Method 2: Let the height of the cup be $h$. $\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(4)^{2}h = 64\pi$, so $h = 12$ cm.
Height of water $= \dfrac{3}{4} \times 12 = 9$ cm.
$\dfrac{9}{12} = \dfrac{\text{radius of water}}{4}$, so radius of water $= \dfrac{9}{12} \times 4 = 3$ cm.
$\therefore$ Volume of water in cup $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(3)^{2}(9) = 27\pi\text{ cm}^{3}$

parts.text: The water in the cup is emptied. The cup is cut along its slant height from $MN$ to $O$ to form a sector $OMN$ of a circle with centre $O$. Calculate angle $MON$ in radians.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let $h$ be the height of the cone. $\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(4)^{2}h = 64\pi$, so $h = 12$ cm.
$OM = \sqrt{4^{2} + 12^{2}} = \sqrt{160}$ cm (slant height)
Circumference of base of cone $= 2\pi(4) = 8\pi$ cm (this is the arc length of the sector)
$\angle MON = \dfrac{8\pi}{\sqrt{160}} \approx 1.98691 = 1.99$ radians (3 s.f.)

before.question_text: The equation of the line $l_{1}$ is $x + 4y = 20$. The line cuts the $x$-axis at point $A$ and the $y$-axis at point $B$.

parts.text: Find the length of $AB$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: A point $C$ lies on the line $l_{1}$ such that it is equidistant from the coordinate axes. Show that the coordinates of point $C$ is $(4,4)$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$C$ is equidistant from both axes, so in the first quadrant $y = x$.
Substituting into $x + 4y = 20$: $x + 4x = 20$, $5x = 20$, $x = 4$.
Then $y = 4$, so $C(4, 4)$ (shown).

parts.text: Another line $l_{2}$, which is perpendicular to $l_{1}$, passes through the origin $O$ and intersects $l_{1}$ at $P$. The product (gradient of $AB$) $\times$ (gradient of $OP$) $= -1$. Use this information to find the equation of the line $OP$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Gradient of $l_1$ (the gradient of $AB$) $= -\dfrac{1}{4}$.
Since (gradient of $AB$) $\times$ (gradient of $OP$) $= -1$, gradient of $OP = 4$.
As $OP$ passes through the origin, its equation is $y = 4x$.

parts.text: Hence find the coordinates of $P$.
parts.label: d

parts.text: State a pair of similar triangles from the diagram.
parts.label: e
parts.answer: $\triangle AOP$ and $\triangle APO$ (or $\triangle BOA$ and $\triangle BPO$, or $\triangle BPO$ and $\triangle OPA$)
parts.solution:
Since $OP \perp AB$, triangles $BOA$, $APO$ and $OPB$ are all right-angled and equiangular.
A pair of similar triangles is $\triangle APO$ and $\triangle OPB$ (both similar to $\triangle BOA$).

before.question_text: The speeds of $600$ vehicles travelling on an expressway in January are recorded. The cumulative frequency curve below shows the distribution of the speeds.

parts.text:
(i) Complete the frequency table for the speed of the vehicles.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Speed } (v\text{ km/h}) & 40 \leq v < 60 & 60 \leq v < 80 & 80 \leq v < 100 & 100 \leq v < 120 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 40 & \; & \; & 130 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
(ii) Calculate an estimate of the mean speed of the vehicles.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
**(i)** The cumulative frequency (CF) at a speed is the number of vehicles travelling at or below that speed, so read the curve at the upper end of each class:
CF$(60) = 40$, CF$(80) = 170$, CF$(100) = 470$, CF$(120) = 600$
Frequency of a class $=$ CF at its upper end $-$ CF at its lower end:
$60 \leq v < 80$: $170 - 40 = 130$
$80 \leq v < 100$: $470 - 170 = 300$
Check: $40 + 130 + 300 + 130 = 600$, which is the total number of vehicles.

**(ii)** Use the mid-value of each class ($50$, $70$, $90$, $110$):
Mean $= \dfrac{50(40) + 70(130) + 90(300) + 110(130)}{600}$
$= \dfrac{2000 + 9100 + 27\,000 + 14\,300}{600}$
$= \dfrac{52\,400}{600}$
$= 87.33\ldots$
Mean $= 87.3\text{ km/h}$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: Use the curve to estimate (i) the median speed. (ii) the interquartile range of the speeds.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: (i) Median $\approx 88\text{ km/h}$  (ii) IQR $= Q_{3} - Q_{1} \approx 98 - 78 = 20\text{ km/h}$
parts.solution:
There are $600$ vehicles altogether.

**(i)** The median is the $\dfrac{600}{2} = 300$th value.
Read across from CF $= 300$ to the curve, then down to the speed axis:
Median $\approx 88\text{ km/h}$

**(ii)** $Q_{1}$ is the $\dfrac{600}{4} = 150$th value and $Q_{3}$ is the $\dfrac{3 \times 600}{4} = 450$th value.
From CF $= 150$: $Q_{1} \approx 78\text{ km/h}$
From CF $= 450$: $Q_{3} \approx 98\text{ km/h}$
Interquartile range $= Q_{3} - Q_{1} = 98 - 78$
$= 20\text{ km/h}$

parts.text: The speed limit on the road is $90\text{ km/h}$. Estimate the percentage of cars that exceeded the speed limit.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Read the cumulative frequency at $v = 90$: CF$(90) \approx 335$.
That is the number of vehicles travelling at $90\text{ km/h}$ or less, so the number that exceeded the speed limit is
$600 - 335 = 265$
Percentage $= \dfrac{265}{600} \times 100\%$
$= 44.16\ldots\%$
$\approx 44\%$

parts.text: The speeds of $600$ cars travelling on the same expressway in March are recorded. The box-and-whisker plot shows the distribution of the speeds. Make two comments comparing the speeds of the vehicles in January and in March.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: 1) The median speed in March ($72\text{ km/h}$) is lower than in January ($88\text{ km/h}$), so vehicles generally travelled more slowly in March. 2) The interquartile range in March ($88 - 63 = 25\text{ km/h}$) is larger than in January ($20\text{ km/h}$), so the March speeds are more spread out / less consistent.
parts.solution:
Read the five values off the March box-and-whisker plot:
minimum $= 42$, $Q_{1} = 63$, median $= 72$, $Q_{3} = 88$, maximum $= 94$ (all km/h)
From part (b), January has median $88\text{ km/h}$ and IQR $20\text{ km/h}$.

**Comment 1 — average.** The median speed in March is $72\text{ km/h}$, which is lower than January's $88\text{ km/h}$, so on average the vehicles travelled more slowly in March than in January.

**Comment 2 — spread.** March: IQR $= Q_{3} - Q_{1} = 88 - 63 = 25\text{ km/h}$. January: IQR $= 20\text{ km/h}$.
Since $25 > 20$, the middle $50\%$ of the speeds are more spread out in March, so the March speeds are less consistent than the January speeds.

before.question_text: According to the United States Golf Association (USGA) Rules of Golf, the diameter of the ball shall not be less than 42.67 mm (1.680 inches). The majority of manufacturers follow this guideline when producing golf balls.

parts.text: A golf ball has a volume of $42$ cm$^3$. Showing your working clearly, determine if this golf ball meets the USGA standards.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Yes. Diameter $\approx 4.31$ cm $> 4.267$ cm, so the ball meets the USGA standards.

parts.text: Esther has three golf balls, each of radius 2.14 cm. She wants to make a container for the three balls. Diagram I shows two possible designs for the containers that she can make with clear plastic sheet. The first design is a closed cylindrical container and the second one is a closed triangular container. Assume that the 3 golf balls fit tightly in each container. The top view of the triangular container can be modelled by an equilateral triangle $ABC$ with a circle, centre $O$, inscribed in it, as shown in Diagram II. By finding the length of $BM$, show that the length of $BC$ is 7.4132 cm, correct to 5 significant figures.

parts.text: Esther claims that the amount of plastic sheet used to make one triangular container is enough for making two cylindrical containers. Showing your working clearly, determine whether Esther's claim is correct.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Surface area of 2 cylindrical containers $\approx 402$ cm$^2$ $> 333$ cm$^2$ (triangular container). The plastic sheet used for 1 triangular container is not enough for 2 cylindrical containers, so Esther's claim is incorrect.

before.question_text: Question $10$ has multiple parts based on tourism data.

parts.text: The graph below shows the number of tourists who visited Singapore from $2018$ to $2022$. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, there was a restriction on travelling from $2020$. The travel restriction was lifted in $2022$. The graph is titled "Tourist Boom After 2021". What feature of the graph makes the claim "Tourist Boom After 2021" appear true?
parts.label: a
parts.answer: The steep gradient makes the increase look huge.
parts.solution: The steep gradient makes the increase look huge.

parts.text: The pie chart shows the different countries tourists who visited Singapore in $2022$ were from. Korean and Chinese tourists make up half of the total amount of tourists. Korea is $60^\circ$, Malaysia and Canada form a right angle. There are $19\,200\,000$ tourists who visited Singapore in $2022$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Calculate the number of tourists from China.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Give your answer in $\textbf{part (i)}$ in standard form.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: The entrance ticket to Flower Dome and Cloud Forest at Gardens by the Bay is listed below: Adults $\$53 / \yen 5300$; Child $\$42 / \yen 4200$; Senior $\$40 / \yen 4000$; Family of 4 (2 Adult + 2 Children) $\$188 / \yen 18800$; Family of 4 (2 Adult + 2 Senior) $\$185 / \yen 18500$. Exchange rate: SGD $\$1$ = $\yen 99$. A family of 4 from Japan (a couple and their 2 children) would like to purchase $4$ entrance tickets. Should they purchase tickets on the spot or on the website and which currency should they pay in, to get the best deal out of this entrance ticket? Show your workings.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Family of 4 package online = SGD $\$189.90$ (cheapest). Buy online.
parts.solution:
2 adult tickets $+$ 2 children in SGD $= (53 \times 2) + (42 \times 2) = \$190$
2 adult tickets in Yen $= [(5300 \times 2) + (4200 \times 2)] \div 99 = \$191.91$
Family-for-4 package $= 18800 \div 99 = \$189.90$
Buy online a family of 4, as it is cheaper than buying individual tickets online or buying family-of-4 tickets on the spot.

The travel restriction was lifted in $2022$. The graph is titled "Tourist Boom After 2021". What feature of the graph makes the claim "Tourist Boom After 2021" appear true?
parts.label: a
parts.answer: The steep gradient makes the increase look huge.
parts.solution: The steep gradient makes the increase look huge.

parts.text: The pie chart shows the different countries tourists who visited Singapore in $2022$ were from. Korean and Chinese tourists make up half of the total amount of tourists. Korea is $60^\circ$, Malaysia and Canada form a right angle. There are $19\,200\,000$ tourists who visited Singapore in $2022$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Calculate the number of tourists from China.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Give your answer in $\textbf{part (i)}$ in standard form.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: The entrance ticket to Flower Dome and Cloud Forest at Gardens by the Bay is listed below: Adults $\$53 / \yen 5300$; Child $\$42 / \yen 4200$; Senior $\$40 / \yen 4000$; Family of 4 (2 Adult + 2 Children) $\$188 / \yen 18800$; Family of 4 (2 Adult + 2 Senior) $\$185 / \yen 18500$. Exchange rate: SGD $\$1$ = $\yen 99$. A family of 4 from Japan (a couple and their 2 children) would like to purchase $4$ entrance tickets. Should they purchase tickets on the spot or on the website and which currency should they pay in, to get the best deal out of this entrance ticket? Show your workings.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Family of 4 package online = SGD $\$189.90$ (cheapest). Buy online.
parts.solution:
2 adult tickets $+$ 2 children in SGD $= (53 \times 2) + (42 \times 2) = \$190$
2 adult tickets in Yen $= [(5300 \times 2) + (4200 \times 2)] \div 99 = \$191.91$
Family-for-4 package $= 18800 \div 99 = \$189.90$
Buy online a family of 4, as it is cheaper than buying individual tickets online or buying family-of-4 tickets on the spot.

before.question_text: The cumulative frequency curve shows the distribution of the lengths (cm) of $800$ lobsters caught in May during a lobster fishing trip.

parts.text: Use the graph to estimate
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the median length,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Middle position (median) $= \dfrac{800}{2} = 400$th.
Reading from the cumulative frequency curve, median length $\approx 10.6$ cm.

subparts.text: the interquartile range.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$Q_1$ position $= 200$th, $Q_3$ position $= 600$th.
$Q_1 \approx 9.95$ cm, $Q_3 \approx 11.25$ cm.
Interquartile range $= 11.25 - 9.95 = 1.3$ cm.

parts.text: To ensure sustainability of the lobster population, it is illegal to catch lobsters shorter than $8.3$ cm or longer than $12.7$ cm. Estimate the percentage of lobsters that needs to be released.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Number of lobsters shorter than $8.3$ cm: read off the cumulative frequency curve $\approx 15$.
Number of lobsters longer than $12.7$ cm: read off $\approx 800 - 775 = 25$.
Percentage to be released $= \dfrac{15 + 25}{800} \times 100\% = 5\%$ (or $\dfrac{20 + 25}{800} \times 100\% \approx 5.625\%$ depending on reading).

parts.text: The lengths of another $800$ lobsters caught in June are recorded. The box-and-whisker plot shows the distribution of the lengths. Make two comments comparing the lengths of the lobsters caught in May and June. Use figures to support your answers.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Lobsters caught in June are shorter: median $9.3$ cm (June) vs $10.6$ cm (May). Lengths in June are more spread out: IQR $3.7$ cm (June) vs $1.3$ cm (May).
parts.solution:
(1) Lobsters caught in June are shorter on average: median $\approx 9.3$ cm (June) compared with $10.6$ cm (May).
(2) The lengths of lobsters caught in June are more widely spread: IQR $= 3.7$ cm (June) compared with $1.3$ cm (May).

parts.text: Jill makes a claim that "fishermen are able to keep a larger percentage of their lobsters in June as compared to May". Do you agree?
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Disagree. In June, $25\%$ of lobsters are below $8.3$ cm and must be released, which is higher than the $\approx 5.625\%$ released in May; hence a larger proportion must be released in June, not kept.
parts.solution: Disagree. In June, $25\%$ of lobsters are shorter than $8.3$ cm (below $Q_1$ on the box-plot), so at least $25\%$ must be released. In May, only about $5.625\%$ needed to be released. Therefore a larger percentage must be released in June, so a smaller percentage can be kept, contradicting Jill's claim.

before.question_text: A skateboard park has a mould that is $h$ metres high at the point where the horizontal distance, from a fixed point $A$, is $x$ metres. The height of the mould can be modelled by $h = -x^2 + 6x - 3$ for $1 < x < 5$.

parts.text: By only completing the square, find the height of the mould at its highest point.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: $-(x - 3)^2 + 6$, so the height at the highest point is 6 m
parts.solution:
$h = -x^2 + 6x - 3$
$= -(x^2 - 6x + 3)$
$= -\left[\left(x - 3\right)^2 - 9 + 3\right]$
$= -(x - 3)^2 + 6$
Therefore the height of the mould at its highest point is $6$ m.

parts.text: A ramp built up the side of the mould is a tangent to the mould. The ramp can be modelled by the function $h = 2.5x + c$. Find the vertical distance where the ramp will meet the mould. (Ignore the thickness of the ramp.)
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Gradient of ramp $= 2.5$.
$\dfrac{dh}{dx} = -2x + 6$
Set $-2x + 6 = 2.5$:
$x = \dfrac{7}{4}$
Sub into $h$: $h = -\left(\dfrac{7}{4}\right)^2 + 6\left(\dfrac{7}{4}\right) - 3 = -\dfrac{49}{16} + \dfrac{42}{4} - 3 = 4.4375$
Therefore the vertical distance is $4.4375$ m.

parts.text: The height $h$ metres of a skateboard path at a horizontal distance $r$ metres from another point $B$, can be modelled by the function $h = \frac{2}{3}r^3 - 4r^2 + 6r$, $0 < r < 4$. For the safety of the skaters, there is a height regulation that requires no part of the skateboard path to be 3 metres above the ground. Fully describe this curve, including its turning points, the horizontal distance $r$ metres from point $B$, and state whether the skateboard path complies with the height regulations.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Maximum stationary point of $h = \frac{8}{3}$ m at $r = 1$ and minimum stationary point of $h = 0$ m at $r = 3$. The skateboard path complies with the height regulation.
parts.solution:
$h = \dfrac{2}{3}r^3 - 4r^2 + 6r$
$\dfrac{dh}{dr} = 2r^2 - 8r + 6$
Set $\dfrac{dh}{dr} = 0$:
$2(r - 1)(r - 3) = 0$
$r = 1$ or $r = 3$.
At $r = 1$: $h = \dfrac{2}{3} - 4 + 6 = \dfrac{8}{3}$ m.
At $r = 3$: $h = 18 - 36 + 18 = 0$ m.
$\dfrac{d^2h}{dr^2} = 4r - 8$
At $r = 1$: $\dfrac{d^2h}{dr^2} = -4 < 0$, so maximum point.
At $r = 3$: $\dfrac{d^2h}{dr^2} = 4 > 0$, so minimum point.
At $r = 4$ (endpoint): $h = \dfrac{128}{3} - 64 + 24 = \dfrac{8}{3}$ m.
The curve has a maximum stationary point at $\left(1, \dfrac{8}{3}\right)$ and a minimum stationary point at $(3, 0)$, with height $\dfrac{8}{3}$ m at $r = 4$.
Maximum height of path is $\dfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67$ m, which is less than $3$ m.
Therefore the skateboard path complies with the height regulations.

before.question_text: The diagram below shows the major segment $XZY$, of circle centre $O$, which is the cross-section of a $250$ m long tunnel and track. It is given that $OX = OY = 5$ m and the perimeter of $OXZYO$ is $32$ m.

parts.text: Show that the reflex angle $XOY$ is $4.4$ radians.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Shown: arc $XZY = 32 - 5 - 5 = 22$ m. Reflex $\angle XOY = \dfrac{22}{5} = 4.4$ rad.
parts.solution:
Perimeter $= 32 = 5 + 5 + 5\theta$
$\theta = \dfrac{32 - 10}{5} = 4.4$ rad  (shown)

parts.text: Find the total internal surface area of the tunnel and its track.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The major segment of circle $XYZ$ can also be represented as the uniform cross-section of a circular container, not filled with sand sediment, as shown. The container is $8$ m long. Calculate the volume of the container which is not filled with sand sediment.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Cross-sectional area $= \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 5 \times \sin(2\pi - 4.4)\right) + \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 5 \times 4.4\right)$
$= 66.8950$ m$^2$
Volume not filled with sand $= 66.8950 \times 8 = 535.16$ m$^3 \approx 535$ m$^3$ (3 s.f.)

before.question_text:
Sarah owns a plot of land on which she wishes to build a house.
This plot of land consists of a trapezium $ABCE$ and a semicircle $CDE$ with diameter $EC$.

parts.text: Find the perimeter of the entire region.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
The perimeter is $AB + BC + AE$ together with the semicircular arc $CDE$.
Arc $CDE = \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 43 = 67.544\text{ m}$
Perimeter $= 22 + 36.6 + 30 + 67.544 = 156.144 \approx 156\text{ m}$

parts.text: Find the area of the entire region.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Area of trapezium $ABCE = \frac{1}{2}(22 + 43)(30) = 975\text{ m}^{2}$
Area of semicircle $= \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 21.5^{2} = 726.15\text{ m}^{2}$
Total area $= 975 + 726.15 = 1701.15 \approx 1701\text{ m}^{2}$

parts.text:
Sarah now looks to two suppliers to line the perimeter of the land with fences, and to lay tiles covering the entire area of the plot of land.
The details of the two suppliers and her considerations are presented in the table below.
Sarah wants the same supplier to do both the fencing and woodwork.
Assuming the quality of the materials of both suppliers are the same, which supplier should she choose? Justify your answer with a reason, and show your calculations clearly.
You may use your answers from parts (a) and (b).
parts.label: c
parts.answer: WELLMART $= \$53322$, GOODBUY $= \$51048$. GOODBUY is cheaper, so Sarah should choose GOODBUY.
parts.solution:
Using perimeter $= 156\text{ m}$ and area $= 1701\text{ m}^{2}$.
WELLMART: fencing $= 12 \times 156 = \$1872$; tiling $= 30 \times 1701 = \$51030$; transport $= \$420$

before.question_text: The table below shows the cost of Corrugated Cardboard Sheets in British pounds, $\pounds$.

parts.text: Using an exchange rate of $S\$1 = \pounds 0.55$, calculate the cost of one sheet of cardboard in Singapore dollars (S$\$$).
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
From the table, 15 units (sheets) cost $\pounds 10.80$.
Cost of one sheet $= \pounds 10.80 \div 15 = \pounds 0.72$
Since $S\$1 = \pounds 0.55$, cost $= \frac{0.72}{0.55} = 1.3090...$
Cost of one sheet $= S\$1.31$ (to the nearest cent).

parts.text: Ali was to make an open recycle bin with cardboard in the shape of a prism with a square base. The uniform cross-section of the prism is a trapezium $WXYZ$ with height $70$ cm, $XY = 30$ cm, $WZ = 50$ cm and $WX = 70.71$ cm. Calculate the total area of cardboard to be used for this bin.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The base $XY$ is a square of side $30$ cm, so the prism is $30$ cm long.
Two trapezium faces: $2 \times \frac{1}{2}(30 + 50)(70) = 2 \times 2800 = 5600$ cm$^{2}$
Square base: $30 \times 30 = 900$ cm$^{2}$
Two slanting rectangular faces: $2 \times (70.71 \times 30) = 4242.6$ cm$^{2}$
The bin is open, so no top is needed.
Total area of cardboard $= 5600 + 900 + 4242.6 = 10742.6$ cm$^{2}$

parts.text: If Ali had used one sheet of the cardboard mentioned in (a) to make the bin, calculate the percentage of wasted cardboard.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
One sheet is $1000$ mm by $1200$ mm, i.e. $100$ cm by $120$ cm.
Area of one sheet $= 100 \times 120 = 12000$ cm$^{2}$
Cardboard wasted $= 12000 - 10742.6 = 1257.4$ cm$^{2}$
Percentage wasted $= \frac{1257.4}{12000} \times 100\% = 10.478...\% = 10.5\%$ (to 3 significant figures).

before.question_text: The figure shows Soda Can A, which can be modelled as a cylinder of height $12\text{ cm}$ and radius $3\text{ cm}$.

parts.text: Using the model, show that the volume of the Soda Can A is $108\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Volume $= \pi r^2 h = \pi(3)^2(12) = \pi \times 9 \times 12 = 108\pi\text{ cm}^3$ (shown)

parts.text: Using the model, estimate the total surface area of the Soda Can A, in $\text{cm}^2$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total surface area $= 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h$
$= 2\pi(3)^2 + 2\pi(3)(12)$
$= 18\pi + 72\pi = 90\pi$
$= 282.74\ldots = 283\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text:
The figure shows another Soda Can B, which can be modelled as a cylinder of height $17.28\text{ cm}$ and radius $2.5\text{ cm}$.
The volume of the Soda Can B is $108\pi\text{ cm}^3$ and its total surface area is $98.9\pi\text{ cm}^2$.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: As a manufacturer of drink cans, which design will you use? Justify your answer.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Soda Can A, as it has a smaller total surface area and hence will be cheaper to manufacture
subparts.solution:
Both cans hold the same volume of $108\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
Can A: total surface area $= 90\pi\text{ cm}^2$
Can B: total surface area $= 98.9\pi\text{ cm}^2$

$90\pi < 98.9\pi$, so Can A uses less material for the same volume and is cheaper to manufacture.
Choose Soda Can A.

subparts.text:
The smaller the volume to surface-area ratio, the faster the soda drink can will cool down in the freezer.
Determine which Soda Can will cool down faster in the freezer. Show your working clearly.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Soda Can B will cool down faster.
subparts.solution:
Can A: $\frac{\text{volume}}{\text{surface area}} = \frac{108\pi}{90\pi} = 1.2$

Can B: $\frac{\text{volume}}{\text{surface area}} = \frac{108\pi}{98.9\pi} = 1.0919\ldots$

$1.0919\ldots < 1.2$, so Can B has the smaller volume to surface-area ratio.
Soda Can B will cool down faster.

before.question_text: Jynn wants to make 35 strawberry cookies.

parts.text: How many grams of baking soda will she use?
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
The recipe makes 14 cookies using 5 grams of baking soda.
Number of batches $= \frac{35}{14} = 2.5$
Baking soda needed $= 5 \times 2.5 = 12.5$ grams

parts.text: Each box of strawberry costs $\$8$. How much will Jynn spend on buying strawberries?
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Strawberries needed $= 1 \times 2.5 = 2.5$ boxes, so she must buy 3 whole boxes.
Cost $= 3 \times \$8 = \$24$

parts.text: Each cookie has a diameter of approximately 5 cm. She packed the cookies into a box with a rectangular base of dimension 17 cm by 28 cm. She used cardboards as partitions to separate layers of cookies. How many cardboards will she need to use as partitions to stack up the cookies?
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Along the 28 cm side: $28 \div 5 = 5$ cookies (whole cookies only).
Along the 17 cm side: $17 \div 5 = 3$ rows.
Cookies per layer $= 5 \times 3 = 15$
Layers needed $= 15 + 15 + 5$, i.e. 3 layers for 35 cookies.
Partitions between 3 layers $= 3 - 1 = 2$ cardboards

before.question_text: Sketch a straight line graph for the given scenarios, clearly labelling the vertical axis values when the horizontal axis values are 0 and 6 respectively.

parts.text:
The flag down fare of a taxi is $\$3$.
Passengers have to pay $\$0.50$ for each km.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: A straight line from $(0,\ 3)$ to $(6,\ 6)$: vertical axis value $\$3$ at 0 km and $\$6$ at 6 km.
parts.solution:
Fare $= 3 + 0.5d$, where $d$ is the distance in km.
When $d = 0$: fare $= \$3$
When $d = 6$: fare $= 3 + 0.5(6) = \$6$
Draw the straight line joining $(0,\ 3)$ to $(6,\ 6)$.

parts.text:
Carpark A charges: free 20 minutes of parking $+\ \$0.05$ per minute thereafter.
Carpark B charges: single entry charge of $\$12$.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Carpark A: from $(0,\ 0)$ to $(6,\ 17)$. Carpark B: horizontal line at $\$12$, from $(0,\ 12)$ to $(6,\ 12)$.
parts.solution:
Carpark A: the first 20 minutes are free, then $\$0.05$ per minute.
At 0 hours the charge is $\$0$.
6 hours $= 360$ minutes, of which $360 - 20 = 340$ minutes are charged:
charge $= 340 \times 0.05 = \$17$
So A rises from $(0,\ 0)$ to $(6,\ 17)$.
Carpark B: a flat $\$12$ however long the stay, so B is the horizontal line
from $(0,\ 12)$ to $(6,\ 12)$.

before.question_text: Diagram 1 shows a car porch. The roof of the car porch can be modelled as a square pyramid as shown in Diagram 2.

parts.text: $VA = 5$ m, $AB = 6$ m and $VM$ perpendicular to $AB$. Calculate the surface area of the rooftop.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $AM = 3$ m.
In $\triangle VAM$, right-angled at $M$:
$VM = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ m
Area of $\triangle VAB = \frac{1}{2} \times AB \times VM = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 = 12$ m$^2$
The rooftop is made up of 4 identical triangular faces.
Surface area $= 4 \times 12 = 48$ m$^2$

parts.text: The entire rooftop will be reroofed with rectangular tiles. Some information about one tile used is given below. Given that density $= \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$ and taking the breadth of each tile as $x$ cm,
parts.label: b

subparts.text: form an equation for the volume and show that it reduces to $x^{2} + 10x - 600 = 0$,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Volume of one tile $= \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{density}} = \frac{3120}{2.6} = 1200$ cm$^3$
The breadth is $x$ cm and the breadth is $10$ cm less than the length, so the length is $(x + 10)$ cm. The thickness is $2$ cm.
Volume $=$ length $\times$ breadth $\times$ thickness:
$(x + 10)(x)(2) = 1200$
$x(x + 10) = 600$
$x^2 + 10x = 600$
$x^2 + 10x - 600 = 0$ (shown)

subparts.text: hence, calculate the dimensions of each tile.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$x^2 + 10x - 600 = 0$
$(x + 30)(x - 20) = 0$
$x = -30$ or $x = 20$
A length cannot be negative, so $x = 20$.
Breadth $= 20$ cm and length $= 20 + 10 = 30$ cm.
Each tile measures $30$ cm by $20$ cm by $2$ cm.

before.question_text: **In this question, you should state the parameters of any distributions you use.**

parts.text:
The number of hours worked per week by employees of Company $A$ follow a normal distribution with mean 40 hours and standard deviation $\alpha$ hours, while the number of hours worked per week by employees of Company $B$ follow a normal distribution with mean 40 hours and standard deviation $\beta$ hours, where $\alpha > \beta$.
The diagram shows the probability density function of $X$, where $X$ is the random variable denoting the number of hours worked per week by a randomly chosen employee of Company $A$.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: On the copy of the diagram in the **Printed Answer Booklet**, sketch on the same diagram the probability density function of $Y$, where $Y$ is the random variable denoting the number of hours worked per week by a randomly chosen employee of Company $B$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: [See solution diagram - normal distribution curve centered at 40, with $X$ and $Y$ axes labeled]

subparts.text:
The probability that a randomly chosen employee of Company $A$ works less than $t$ hours per week is represented by the shaded area of the standard normal curve in the diagram below.

Write down an equation involving $t$ and $\alpha$.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Two employees of company $A$ are randomly chosen. Find the probability that both employees work more than $t$ hours per week.
subparts.label: iii

subparts.text: Given that the probability that a randomly chosen employee of Company $B$ works more than 42 hours per week is at least 0.25 , find the range of values of $\beta$.
subparts.label: iv
subparts.solution:
$Y \sim N(40, \beta^2)$
$P(Y > 42) \geq 0.25$
$P\left(\frac{Y-40}{\beta} > \frac{2}{\beta}\right) \geq 0.25$
$P\left(Z > \frac{2}{\beta}\right) \geq 0.25$
$\frac{2}{\beta} \leq 0.67449$
$\beta \geq 2.9652 = 2.97$

parts.text: A shop sells small and large bags of rice. The masses of small bags of rice are normally distributed with mean 1 kg and standard deviation 0.16 kg . The masses of large bags of rice have mean 5 kg and standard deviation 0.5 kg . The masses of the small and large bags of rice are independent of one another.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: In a random sample of 300 small bags of rice, find the expected number of bags that have a mass greater than 1.25 kg .
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let $S$ be the mass, in kg, of a small bag of rice.
$S \sim N(1, 0.16^2)$
$P(S > 1.25) = 0.059085$
Let $W$ be the number of small bags with mass greater than 1.25 kg out of 300 bags.
$W \sim B(300, 0.059085)$
$E(W) = 300 \times 0.059085 = 17.7$
Expected number of small bags of rice with a mass greater than 1.25 kg is 17.7.

subparts.text: Find the probability that the total mass of 5 randomly chosen small bags of rice exceed the mean mass of 30 randomly chosen large bags of rice by more than 0.25 kg .
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Let $L$ be the mass, in kg, of a big bag of rice.
Since $n = 30$ is large enough, by Central Limit Theorem,
$\bar{L} \sim N\left(5, \frac{0.5^2}{30}\right)$ approximately.
Let $W = S_1 + S_2 + \cdots + S_5 - \bar{L}$.
$E(W) = 5E(S) - E(\bar{L}) = 5(1) - 5 = 0$

parts.text: A shop sells small and large bags of rice. The masses of small bags of rice are normally distributed with mean 1 kg and standard deviation 0.16 kg . The masses of large bags of rice have mean 5 kg and standard deviation 0.5 kg . The masses of the small and large bags of rice are independent of one another.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: In a random sample of 300 small bags of rice, find the expected number of bags that have a mass greater than 1.25 kg .
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let $S$ be the mass, in kg, of a small bag of rice.
$S \sim N(1, 0.16^2)$
$P(S > 1.25) = 0.059085$
Let $W$ be the number of small bags with mass greater than 1.25 kg out of 300 bags.
$W \sim B(300, 0.059085)$
$E(W) = 300 \times 0.059085 = 17.7$
Expected number of small bags of rice with a mass greater than 1.25 kg is 17.7.

subparts.text: Find the probability that the total mass of 5 randomly chosen small bags of rice exceed the mean mass of 30 randomly chosen large bags of rice by more than 0.25 kg .
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Let $L$ be the mass, in kg, of a big bag of rice.
Since $n = 30$ is large enough, by Central Limit Theorem,
$\bar{L} \sim N\left(5, \frac{0.5^2}{30}\right)$ approximately.
Let $W = S_1 + S_2 + \cdots + S_5 - \bar{L}$.
$E(W) = 5E(S) - E(\bar{L}) = 5(1) - 5 = 0$
$\text{Var}(W) = 5\text{Var}(S) + \text{Var}(\bar{L}) = 5(0.16^2) + \frac{0.5^2}{30} = \frac{409}{3000}$
$\therefore W \sim N\left(0, \frac{409}{3000}\right)$ approximately.
Required Prob. $= P(W > 0.25) = 0.249$ (3 s.f.)

before.question_text: A vase that is 17 cm tall can be modelled by a frustum, $A$, on top of an egg-shaped container, $B$. A sketch of the vase is shown in Figure 1. Figure 2 shows the cone that the frustum $A$ is a part of. The diameter $QRS$ of the top of the frustum is $8$ cm and the diameter $PVT$ of the bottom is $7$ cm. The height of the frustum, $RV$, is $8$ cm. $R$ and $V$ are the midpoints of $QS$ and $PT$ respectively.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the frustum, $A$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $UV = x$ cm. Triangles $UPT$ and $UQS$ are similar.
$\dfrac{x}{7} = \dfrac{x + 8}{8}$
$8x = 7x + 56$
$x = 56$
$UR = 56 + 8 = 64$ cm
Volume of $A = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{8}{2}\right)^{2}(64) - \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^{2}(56)$
$= 353.9528$
$\approx 354\ \text{cm}^{3}\ (3\text{ s.f.})$

parts.text: The volume of $B$ is about $650\ \text{cm}^{3}$ and its height is $9$ cm. Water is poured into the vase at the rate of $10\ \text{cm}^{3}$ per second until it is full. Sketch the height of the water in the vase with respect to time.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Curve starting at origin, concave (steep then slower) for egg-shaped portion from $t = 0$ to about $t = 65$ s reaching height $9$ cm, then increasing more gently (widening frustum) up to $17$ cm at about $t = 100$ s.
parts.solution:
Time to fill $B$: $\dfrac{650}{10} = 65$ s, with water reaching height $9$ cm.
Time to fill $A$: $\dfrac{354}{10} \approx 35.4$ s additional, total $\approx 100.4$ s.
Total height $= 17$ cm.
Sketch: $(0, 0)$ rising rapidly initially through the egg shape (concave shape due to widening then narrowing of the egg), passes through approximately $(65, 9)$, then continues to rise more gradually through the widening frustum, ending at approximately $(100.4, 17)$.

parts.text:
After meeting Mary, Sally needs to run multiple errands to different parts of Singapore. She decides to rent a car from 8am to 12pm for that day. The tables showing the cost of car rental from two companies, GetCar and FindCar, are given in the diagram above. The table below shows the price per litre of different grades of petrol from three different petrol companies, Company Messo, Company Shore and Company SCP. Each litre of petrol allows $12.5$ km of travel.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Petrol Grade} & \text{Company Messo} & \text{Company Shore} & \text{Company SCP} \\ \hline  & \text{Price per litre (discounted price with ABC Bank credit card)} & & \\ \hline 92 & \$2.70 \text{ (NA)} & - & \$2.70 \text{ (NA)} \\ \hline 95 & \$2.75 \text{ (NA)} & \$2.79 \text{ (\$2.20)} & \$2.74 \text{ (NA)} \\ \hline 98 & \$3.22 \text{ (NA)} & \$3.28 \text{ (\$2.59)} & \$3.22 \text{ (NA)} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
Sally estimates that she needs to travel $67$ km that day. She carries an ABC Bank credit card. She wants to minimise her costs in the rental. Suggest the company from which Sally should rent the car. Justify any decisions you make and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: b
parts.answer:
Sally should rent from GetCar.
GetCar: rental $= \$7 \times 4 = \$28$; mileage $= \$0.39 \times 67 = \$26.13$; total $= \$54.13$.
FindCar: rental $= \$3 + \$5 \times 3 = \$18$; mileage $= \$0.39 \times 67 = \$26.13$; petrol needed $= 67/12.5 = 5.36$ L at \$2.20 per litre $= \$11.79$; total $= \$18 + \$26.13 + \$11.79 = \$55.92$.
Since $\$54.13 < \$55.92$, Sally should rent from GetCar.
parts.solution:
Renting from GetCar:
Car rental & mileage charges $= (\$7 \times 4) + (\$0.39 \times 67)$
$= \$54.13$

Renting from FindCar:
Car rental & mileage charges $= (\$3 \times 1 + \$5 \times 3) + (\$0.39 \times 67)$
$= \$44.13$

Amount of petrol needed $= \dfrac{67}{12.5} = 5.36$ litres

Fuel charges $= \$2.20 \times 5.36 = \$11.792$

Total charges (FindCar) $= 44.13 + 11.792 = \$55.92 > \$54.13$

Since it costs less to rent from GetCar, Sally should rent from Company GetCar.

parts.label: a

subparts.text: the $15^{\text{th}}$ percentile,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: From the graph, $15^{\text{th}}$ percentile $= 60$ minutes.

subparts.text: the median time,
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: From the graph, median time $= 72$ minutes.

subparts.text: the interquartile range.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution: Interquartile range $= 76 - 66 = 10$ minutes.

parts.text: $12.5\%$ of the boys took more than $n$ minutes. Find $n$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$12.5\% \times 200 = 25$ boys
From the graph, $n = 80$.

parts.text: With practice, each boy uses $5$ less minutes to complete the same task in June. Describe how the cumulative frequency curve would have been different.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: The cumulative frequency curve would be shifted to the left by $5$ minutes.
parts.solution: The cumulative frequency curve would be shifted to the left by $5$ minutes.

parts.text: The box-and-whiskers plot below shows the time taken by $200$ Secondary One girls to complete the same task in January. Make two comments comparing the times taken by the boys and girls to complete the task.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Girls' median ($62$ min) is less than boys' median ($72$ min), so the girls took a shorter time on average. Girls' interquartile range ($7$ min) is less than boys' interquartile range ($10$ min), so the girls' times were more consistent.
parts.solution:
Secondary 1 Girls: Median $= 62$ minutes; Interquartile range $= 7$ minutes.

1. The girls took a shorter time to complete the task as compared to the boys because the girls' median at $62$ minutes is shorter than the boys' median at $72$ minutes.

2. The time taken by the girls to complete the task is more consistent because the interquartile range for the girls at $7$ minutes is shorter than the boys' at $10$ minutes.

before.question_text: The diagram shows the positions of four checkpoints $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ in a jungle reserve area. The checkpoints are connected by the irregular tracks shown. $X$ is due north of $Y$ and is on a bearing of $077^{\circ}$ from $W$. Angle $XWY = 53^{\circ}$ and $WY$ is $60$ metres.

parts.text: Calculate the distance $XY$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Since $X$ is due north of $Y$, the bearing of $W$ from $X$ is $077^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 257^{\circ}$, and $XY$ points due south ($180^{\circ}$) from $X$.
$\angle WXY = 257^{\circ} - 180^{\circ} = 77^{\circ}$.
$\angle WYX = 180^{\circ} - 53^{\circ} - 77^{\circ} = 50^{\circ}$.
By the sine rule: $\dfrac{XY}{\sin \angle XWY} = \dfrac{WY}{\sin \angle WXY}$
$XY = \dfrac{60 \sin 53^{\circ}}{\sin 77^{\circ}} = 49.18$ m

parts.text: Given that the bearing of $Y$ from $Z$ is $152^{\circ}$, write down the bearing of $Z$ from $Y$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution: Bearing of $Z$ from $Y = $ bearing of $Y$ from $Z$ $+ 180^{\circ} = 152^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 332^{\circ}$.

parts.text: A hidden camera, $C$, is to be fixed at checkpoint $Y$ to capture animals that move from $W$ to $Y$ via $Z$, along the irregular track. The camera has a view angle of $50^{\circ}$ and can capture anything within this angle, as shown in the diagram below. By measurement, determine the minimum bearing where the line $CP$ must be pointed when the camera is fixed at point $Y$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The camera at $Y$ has a $50^{\circ}$ field of view that must cover the track from $W$ to $Y$ via $Z$.

after.question_text: The diagram shows the positions of four checkpoints $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ in a jungle reserve area. The checkpoints are connected by the irregular tracks shown. $X$ is due north of $Y$ and is on a bearing of $077^{\circ}$ from $W$. Angle $XWY = 53^{\circ}$ and $WY$ is $60$ metres.

parts.text: Calculate the distance $XY$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Since $X$ is due north of $Y$, the bearing of $W$ from $X$ is $077^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 257^{\circ}$, and $XY$ points due south ($180^{\circ}$) from $X$.
$\angle WXY = 257^{\circ} - 180^{\circ} = 77^{\circ}$.
$\angle WYX = 180^{\circ} - 53^{\circ} - 77^{\circ} = 50^{\circ}$.
By the sine rule: $\dfrac{XY}{\sin \angle XWY} = \dfrac{WY}{\sin \angle WXY}$
$XY = \dfrac{60 \sin 53^{\circ}}{\sin 77^{\circ}} = 49.18$ m

parts.text: Given that the bearing of $Y$ from $Z$ is $152^{\circ}$, write down the bearing of $Z$ from $Y$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution: Bearing of $Z$ from $Y = $ bearing of $Y$ from $Z$ $+ 180^{\circ} = 152^{\circ} + 180^{\circ} = 332^{\circ}$.

parts.text: A hidden camera, $C$, is to be fixed at checkpoint $Y$ to capture animals that move from $W$ to $Y$ via $Z$, along the irregular track. The camera at $Y$ has a $50^{\circ}$ field of view that must cover the track from $W$ to $Y$ via $Z$.

before.question_text: To prevent vehicles from speeding, speed humps are built on the roads to regulate the speed of cars. Diagram 1 shows the length, width and height of one speed hump. Each speed hump along a road has 4 identical speed humps joined together. Diagram 2 shows the cross-section of one speed hump. $BCD$ is part of sector $OBCD$ with centre $O$, radius 5.438 m and angle $BOD$ of 0.33 radians.

parts.text: Find the length of the arc $BCD$ of the speed hump as shown in Diagram 2.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Arc length $s = r\theta = 5.438 \times 0.33 = 1.79454 \approx 1.79$ m.

parts.text: Diagram 3 shows the top view of 4 identical speed humps joined together. The thickness of the rubber to cover the top of each speed hump is 0.5 cm and the total cost to cover four such speed humps is $\$240$. Using the information given in the table (density of rubber $= 1060$ kg/m$^3$, cost of rubber per kg $= \$20$), calculate the length of one speed hump.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let length of one hump be $x$ m.
Volume of rubber on 1 hump $= 0.005 \times \text{(arc length)} \times x = 0.005 \times 1.79454 \times x = 0.0089727x$ m$^{3}$.
Mass of rubber on 1 hump $= 1060 \times 0.0089727x = 9.511062x$ kg.
Cost of rubber for 1 hump $= \dfrac{\$240}{4} = \$60$.
$20 \times 9.511062x = 60$
$x = \dfrac{60}{20 \times 9.511062} = 0.3154$
$\approx 0.315$ m.

parts.text:
The engineers are to ensure that the height ($h$), width ($w$) and length ($l$) of each speed hump meet the safety criteria as shown in the table:
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline \text{Height of the hump } (h) & 0.0732 \text{ m} \leq h < 0.1016 \text{ m} \\ \hline \text{Width of the hump } (w) & 0.9144 \text{ m} \leq w < 1.8288 \text{ m} \\ \hline \text{Gradient of the hump } (g) & g < 0.1 \\ \hline \text{Length of one speed hump } (l) & 0.3048 \text{ m} \leq l \leq 0.9144 \text{ m} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
where $g$ is the ratio of the height of the hump to the horizontal length of $BX$ or $XD$. Show with clear working if the engineers should approve this speed hump.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Height: $h = 5.438 - 5.438\cos(0.165) = 0.0739$ m, which satisfies $0.0732 \leq h < 0.1016$. Width (chord $BD$): $w = 2 \times 5.438\sin(0.165) = 1.79$ m, which satisfies $0.9144 \leq w < 1.8288$. Gradient: $g = \frac{0.0739}{0.8932} = 0.0827 < 0.1$. Length: $0.315$ m satisfies $0.3048 \leq l \leq 0.9144$. All four criteria are met, so the engineers can approve this speed hump.
parts.solution:
Half angle $= 0.33 / 2 = 0.165$ rad $= 9.4538^{\circ}$.

**Height $h$:**
$\cos 9.4538^{\circ} = \dfrac{OX}{5.438} \Rightarrow OX = 5.438\cos 9.4538^{\circ} = 5.36414$
$h = 5.438 - 5.36414 = 0.0739$ m. ✓ ($0.0732 \leq 0.0739 < 0.1016$)

**Width (chord $BD$):**
$\sin 9.4538^{\circ} = \dfrac{BX}{5.438} \Rightarrow BX = 5.438\sin 9.4538^{\circ} = 0.893204$
$BD = 2 \times 0.893204 = 1.79$ m. ✓ ($0.9144 \leq 1.79 < 1.8288$)

**Gradient:**
$g = \dfrac{h}{BX} = \dfrac{0.073857}{0.893204} = 0.0827 < 0.1$. ✓

**Length:** $0.315$ m satisfies $0.3048 \leq 0.315 \leq 0.9144$. ✓

All four criteria are met, so the engineers **can approve** this speed hump.

before.question_text: Kelly has a box of spherical beads labelled with the 26 letters from A to Z, all of which have the same size. For each letter, there are exactly 3 beads of different colours, red, blue and gold.

parts.text: Find the number of ways the beads in the keychain can be arranged:
parts.label: a

subparts.text: 6 beads with distinct letters but are of the same colour.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Number of ways to arrange 6 distinct-letter beads of the same colour:
$= {}^{30}C_6 \times \frac{6!}{2} = {}^{30}C_6 \times 360 = 497\,296\,800$

subparts.text: 6 beads with 3 distinct letters.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Each letter has exactly one bead of each colour, so all $78$ beads in the box are different from one another. Once the $6$ beads have been chosen they are all distinct, so each selection can be arranged in $6! = 720$ ways.

Choosing the letters: ${}^{26}C_3 = 2600$ ways.

A letter can supply at most $3$ beads (one of each colour), and each of the $3$ chosen letters must appear at least once, so the $6$ beads split between the letters as $2+2+2$ or $3+2+1$.

Case 1: $2 + 2 + 2$

For each of the $3$ letters, choose $2$ of its $3$ colours: ${}^{3}C_2 = 3$ ways, so $3^3 = 27$ ways in all.

Number of selections $= 2600 \times 27 = 70\,200$

Number of arrangements $= 70\,200 \times 6! = 50\,544\,000$

Case 2: $3 + 2 + 1$

Decide which chosen letter supplies $3$ beads, which supplies $2$ and which supplies $1$: $3! = 6$ ways.

Choose the colours: ${}^{3}C_3 \times {}^{3}C_2 \times {}^{3}C_1 = 1 \times 3 \times 3 = 9$ ways.

Number of selections $= 2600 \times 6 \times 9 = 140\,400$

Number of arrangements $= 140\,400 \times 6! = 101\,088\,000$

Total number of ways $= 50\,544\,000 + 101\,088\,000 = 151\,632\,000$

parts.text: Kelly chooses two beads from a new box. The probability that both are star-shaped but neither is gold is $\frac{1}{66}$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Find $c$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let star-shaped beads be $S$. Given $P(\text{both star, neither gold}) = \frac{1}{66}$.
With $c$ added beads (per the question's parameterisation), drawing two beads without replacement:
$\frac{2 + c}{41 + c} \cdot \frac{1 + c}{40 + c} = \frac{1}{66}$
$66(2 + c)(1 + c) = (41 + c)(40 + c)$
$66(c^2 + 3c + 2) = c^2 + 81c + 1640$
$65 c^2 + 117c - 1508 = 0$
Solving: $c = 4$ (rejecting $c = -\frac{29}{5}$).

subparts.text: Find the probability that two randomly chosen beads include exactly one red bead and at least one flower-shaped bead.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Case 1: red flower and non-red flower: $\frac{6}{45} \times \frac{5}{44} \times 2 = \frac{1}{33}$
Case 2: red flower and non-red non-flower: $\frac{6}{45} \times \frac{23}{44} \times 2 = \frac{23}{165}$
Case 3: red non-flower and non-red flower: $\frac{11}{45} \times \frac{5}{44} \times 2 = \frac{1}{18}$
Required probability $= \frac{1}{33} + \frac{23}{165} + \frac{1}{18} = \frac{223}{990}$

before.question_text: The diagram below shows a cylindrical container used to store sand. The cylinder has a radius of $7$ cm and a height of $25$ cm.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the cylinder.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cylinder $= \pi r^{2} h = \pi \times 7^{2} \times 25 = 3848.451...$ cm$^{3}$
$\approx 3850$ cm$^{3}$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The diagram below shows an open prism whose cross-section is a trapezium $ABCD$. $AB = 30$ cm, $DC = 13$ cm, $DE = 20$ cm, $AD = BC = 22$ cm and $CF = 50$ cm. Calculate the volume of the prism.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Base area (trapezium) $= \dfrac{1}{2}(13 + 30) \times 20 = 430$ cm$^{2}$
Volume of prism $= 430 \times 50 = 21\,500$ cm$^{3}$

parts.text: Kris decided to fill the trapezoidal prism with sand. Calculate the number of cylindrical containers of sand that is needed.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Number of containers $= \dfrac{21\,500}{3848.451...} = 5.586...$
$\approx 6$ containers (round up since partial container is not enough)

parts.text: Kris decided to paint the outer surfaces of the trapezoidal prism. Calculate the total surface area that she needs to paint.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
The prism is open (no top), so surface area $=$ two trapezium ends $+$ two slant sides $+$ base:
$= 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2}(13 + 30) \times 20 + 2 \times 22 \times 50 + 13 \times 50$
$= 860 + 2200 + 650$
$= 3710$ cm$^{2}$

parts.text: Use the curve to estimate
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the median mark,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: From the cumulative frequency curve, the median mark $= 68$.

subparts.text: the interquartile range.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Upper quartile $= 78$, Lower quartile $= 57$.

parts.text: If distinction is $75$ marks and above, find the number of students who received a distinction.

before.question_text: The velocity-time graph above shows the first $20$ seconds of the journey of an object.

parts.text: Find
parts.label: a

subparts.text: its acceleration for the first $5$ seconds of the journey,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Acceleration $= \dfrac{10 - 0}{5 - 0} = 2$ m/s$^2$

subparts.text: the velocity of the object at $t = 14$ s,
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
From the graph, the object decelerates uniformly from $14$ m/s at $t = 12$ s to rest at $t = 20$ s.

before.question_text: The diagram shows a pyramid $AWXYZ$. The base of the pyramid is a square of side $18$ cm. $A$ is vertically above the centre of the square base. The vertical height of the pyramid is $24$ cm.

parts.text: Show that the height of the triangle in one of the lateral faces is $25.6$ cm, correct to three significant figures.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Slant height of the triangular face $= \sqrt{24^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{576 + 81} = \sqrt{657} = 25.632...$
$\approx 25.6$ cm (3 s.f.) [Shown]

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total surface area $= 18 \times 18 + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 25.632$
$= 324 + 922.752$
$= 1246.75$
$\approx 1250$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: A smaller, similar pyramid is removed from the top of the original pyramid. The diagram shows the solid remaining. The vertical height of the solid remaining is $6$ cm.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Show that $PQ = 13.5$ cm.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
The smaller pyramid removed from the top is similar to the original. Its height is $24 - 6 = 18$ cm.
By similar triangles: $\dfrac{PQ}{18} = \dfrac{18}{24}$
$PQ = 18 \times \dfrac{18}{24} = 13.5$ cm [Shown]

subparts.text: Hence, calculate the volume of the remaining solid.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Volume of remaining solid $=$ volume of full pyramid $-$ volume of small pyramid
$= \dfrac{1}{3}(18)^2(24) - \dfrac{1}{3}(13.5)^2(18)$
$= \dfrac{1}{3}(7776) - \dfrac{1}{3}(3280.5)$
$= 2592 - 1093.5$
$= 1498.5$ cm$^3$

before.question_text:
The diagram below shows a paint volume calculation formula.

For example, if the paint can cover $10$ m$^2$ of surface per litre per coat, to paint two coats on a wall of height 2.5 m and length 10 m, the calculation for the amount of paint required is as shown in the diagram.
(Source: Nippon Paint Singapore)

parts.text: Assume that all types of paint can cover $10$ m$^2$ of surface per litre per coat, estimate the number of 5-litre paint cans required to paint the four walls and the ceiling of an event hall measuring 8 m by 8 m with a height of 5 m with one coat of paint.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Surface area to paint $=$ 4 walls $+$ ceiling $= 4(8 \times 5) + (8 \times 8) = 160 + 64 = 224$ m$^2$.

Amount of paint required $= \dfrac{224}{10} \times 1$ (1 coat) $= 22.4$ litres.

Number of 5-litre cans $= \dfrac{22.4}{5} = 4.48 \approx 5$ cans (round up).

parts.text: Mr Samad lives in a 5-room HDB flat that comes with a balcony. The floorplan of his flat has dimensions in millimetres. The height of the walls is 2.6 m. Estimate the amount of paint required, in litres, to paint the walls of the Main Bedroom and Bedroom 2 in two coats of paint each. You may include the areas covered by the windows and doors in your calculation.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
From the floorplan, the rooms have approximate dimensions (in metres):

Main Bedroom: $4.85 \text{ m} \times 3.9 \text{ m}$ (or $4.85 \text{ m} \times 3.8 \text{ m}$).

Bedroom 2: $4.3 \text{ m} \times 4.0 \text{ m}$.

Wall height $= 2.6$ m. Wall area per room = perimeter $\times$ height.

Main Bedroom walls: $2(4.85)(2.6) + 2(3.9)(2.6) = 25.22 + 20.28 = 45.50$ m$^2$.

Bedroom 2 walls: $2(4.3)(2.6) + 2(4.0)(2.6) = 22.36 + 20.80 = 43.16$ m$^2$.

Total wall area $= 88.66$ m$^2$. For two coats: paint $= \dfrac{88.66 \times 2}{10} = 17.7$ litres (accept $17.6$ to $17.8$ litres).

parts.text:
Mr Samad has a budget of $\$4500$ for painting services of his entire flat. Based on his budget, requirements and house size, determine if Mr Samad is able to use Company X's services to paint his entire flat. Show your workings clearly.
Mr Samad's requirements:
- Removal of wallpaper from the living room
- Mould treatment for three bedrooms
- Odourless paint and sealer for the entire house
- Paint suitable for exterior of house to be used for the balcony
- Same colour for living room and kitchen, another colour for the bedrooms
- Painting of bathrooms pipes
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Total without GST: $\$300 + 3 \times \$280 + \$2150 + \$500 + \$50 + \$80 + 2 \times \$50 = \$4020$. Total with 9\% GST: $\$4020 \times \dfrac{109}{100} = \$4381.80$. Since $\$4381.80 < \$4500$, Mr Samad is able to use Company X's services.
parts.solution:
Costs from the table:

Wallpaper removal $= \$300$

Mould treatment ($3$ bedrooms) $= 3 \times \$280 = \$840$

Paint package for 5-rm HDB using Odourless Paint $= \$2150$

Water-based sealer for 5-rm HDB $= \$500$

Additional colour (kitchen + living vs bedrooms) $= \$50$

Outdoor paint for balcony $= \$80$

Bathroom pipes (2 bathrooms) $= 2 \times \$50 = \$100$

Total without GST $= 300 + 840 + 2150 + 500 + 50 + 80 + 100 = \$4020$.

Total with 9\% GST $= 4020 \times \dfrac{109}{100} = \$4381.80$.

Since $\$4381.80 < \$4500$, Mr Samad is able to use Company X's services to paint his entire flat.

before.question_text:
[The arc length $L$ of a sector of radius $a$ and angle $\theta$ is given by $L = \text{aθ}$;The volume $V$ of a cone of base radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h$ ]

A metal sheet is shaped as a circular sector with angle $\theta$ and fixed radius $a$, as shown in Figure 1. This sector is then formed into a right circular cone with slant height $a$ by joining the two radii $OA$ and $OB$ together as shown in Figure 2.

parts.text: If $\theta$ is measured in radians, state the base radius of the cone, $r$, in term of $a$ and $\theta$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Circumference of base = length of arc $AB$
$2\pi r = a\theta$
$r = \frac{a}{2\pi}\theta$

parts.text:
Show that the volume of the cone, $V$, is given by
$$V^{2} = \frac{a^{6}}{576\pi^{4}}\theta^{4}\left( 4\pi^{2} - \theta^{2} \right)$$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let $h$ = height of cone
$h^2 = a^2 - r^2 = a^2 - \frac{a^2}{4\pi^2}\theta^2 = \frac{a^2}{4\pi^2}(4\pi^2 - \theta^2)$
$V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
$V^2 = \frac{1}{9}\pi^2 r^4 h^2$
$= \frac{1}{9}\pi^2\left(\frac{a^4}{16\pi^4}\right)\cdot\frac{a^2}{4\pi^2}(4\pi^2 - \theta^2)$
$= \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\theta^4(4\pi^2 - \theta^2)$

parts.text: Using differentiation, find the exact value of $\theta$ that will maximise $V$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\frac{dV^2}{d\theta} = \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\frac{d}{d\theta}(4\pi^2\theta^4 - \theta^6)$
$= \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}(16\pi^2\theta^3 - 6\theta^5)$
$= \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\cdot 2\theta^3(8\pi^2 - 3\theta^2)$
$\frac{dV}{d\theta} = 0$ when $\theta^3(8\pi^2 - 3\theta^2) = 0$
$\theta^2 = \frac{8\pi^2}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$
$\frac{d^2 V^2}{d\theta^2} = \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}(48\pi^2\theta^2 - 30\theta^4)$
When $\theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$,
$\frac{d^2 V^2}{d\theta^2} = \frac{a^6}{576\pi^4}\left[48\pi^2\left(\frac{8\pi^2}{3}\right) - 30\left(\frac{64\pi^4}{9}\right)\right] = -\frac{4a^6}{27} < 0$
Therefore $V$ is max when $\theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$

parts.text:
Two identical cones, as described in part (c), are joined together tip-to-tip to form a new object, as shown in Figure 3. The upper cone is initially filled with water, which leaks out into the lower cone at a rate of $\frac{\pi}{15}{\ cm}^{3}{\ s}^{- 1}$. At time $t$ seconds, the height of the water in the upper cone is $y$.
Show that the volume of water in the cone, $W{\ cm}^{3}$, is given by $W = \frac{2\pi y^{3}}{3}$.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Note that $\theta = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$:
$r = \frac{a}{2\pi}\left(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right) = a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$
$h^2 = a^2 - \left(a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{3}a^2 \Rightarrow h = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}a$
$\frac{r}{h} = a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{a} = \sqrt{2} \Rightarrow r = \sqrt{2}h$
$W = \frac{1}{3}\pi r_w^2 h_w = \frac{1}{3}\pi(\sqrt{2}y)^2 y = \frac{2\pi y^3}{3}$

parts.text: Calculate the rate of change of $y$ when $y = 2$.
parts.label: e
parts.solution:
$\frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{dW}{dy}\times\frac{dy}{dt}$
$-\frac{\pi}{15} = 2\pi y^2\times\frac{dy}{dt}$
$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{1}{30y^2}$
When $y = 2$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{1}{120}$ cm s$^{-1}$
Rate of change of $y$ is $-\frac{1}{120}$ cm s$^{-1}$.

before.question_text: The diagram shows a crane which has lifted a load from the ground. Loads are lifted and lowered vertically. The length of the arm of the crane is $a$ metres and the angle the arm makes with the horizontal is $\theta^{\circ}$. The distance from the base of the cabin to the load when resting on the ground is $x$ metres.

parts.text: Given that the height of the cabin is $2.5$ m, $x = 15$ m and $a = 25$ m, find the height of the highest point of the crane from the ground.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Using Pythagoras' Theorem on the right triangle formed by the arm:
Vertical reach of arm $= \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} = \sqrt{25^{2} - 15^{2}} = \sqrt{625 - 225} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ m
Height of highest point above the ground $= 2.5 + 20 = 22.5$ m.

parts.text: The Safety Manual for the crane is given in the second diagram. Using the information from the Safety Manual, find the values of $a$ and $\theta$ for the crane to lift a load of $9000$ kg.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The maximum load the crane can lift is $9000$ kg, i.e. $100\%$ in the table.
From the table, $100\%$ is achieved only at $a = 15$ m and $\theta = 80^\circ$.
$\therefore a = 15$ m, $\theta = 80^\circ$.

parts.text: A load of $5850$ kg is transported by the crane, and the crane is set to reach the maximum height allowed. Given that workers are not allowed to stand directly under the arm of a crane, work out the minimum distance that workers can safely stand from the cabin.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Percentage of maximum load $= \dfrac{5850}{9000} \times 100\% = 65\%$

after.question_text: The diagram shows a crane which has lifted a load from the ground. Loads are lifted and lowered vertically. The length of the arm of the crane is $a$ metres and the angle the arm makes with the horizontal is $\theta^{\circ}$. parts.text: Given that the height of the cabin is $2.5$ m, $x = 15$ m and $a = 25$ m, find the height of the highest point of the crane from the ground.

parts.solution:
Using Pythagoras' Theorem on the right triangle formed by the arm:
Vertical reach of arm $= \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} = \sqrt{25^{2} - 15^{2}} = \sqrt{625 - 225} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ m
Height of highest point above the ground $= 2.5 + 20 = 22.5$ m.

before.question_text: Below is some information about a light bulb which consists of two parts: cover and holder. All the dimensions are given in centimetres. The frustum is created by removing a cone of height $h$ from the bigger cone as shown.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the holder.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume $= \pi \times \dfrac{1.6}{2} \times \dfrac{1.6}{2} \times 1.5$

parts.text: Show that $h$ is $3.6$ cm.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the cover of the light bulb, leaving your answer to 3 decimal places.

$= 2 \times \pi \times 1.2^2 + (\pi \times 1.2 \times 5.53 - \pi \times 0.8 \times 3.69)$
$= 6.564\pi\ \text{cm}^2$

before.question_text: The diagram shows two identical trapeziums placed together to form a hexagon $ABCDEF$ such that $AF = FE = BC = CE = 5$ cm, $AB = ED = 6$ cm, $FC = 12$ cm and $EG = 4$ cm.

parts.text: Find the area of the hexagon $ABCDEF$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Area of one trapezium $= \dfrac{1}{2}(6 + 12)(4) = 36$ cm$^2$
Area of hexagon $= 2 \times 36 = 72$ cm$^2$

parts.text: Hexagon $ABCDEF$ is the cross-section of a metallic prism. The height of the prism is $7$ cm. Calculate the volume of the prism.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume $= 72 \times 7$
$\quad\quad\quad = 504$ cm$^3$

parts.text: The metal prism is melted and recast into a cylinder with radius $5$ cm. Find the height of the cylinder.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$\pi \times 5^2 \times h = 504$
$h = \dfrac{504}{\pi \times 5^2}$
$\quad = 6.417$
$\quad = 6.42$ cm (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The external surface area of the cylinder is to be painted in black. The cost of black painting is $\$0.45$ per cm$^2$. Find the cost of painting the cylinder, giving your answer to the nearest dollar.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
External surface area $= 2\pi(5^2) + 2\pi(5)(6.417)$
$\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad = 358.6$ cm$^2$
Cost $= 358.6 \times 0.45$
$\quad\quad = \$161.37$
$\quad\quad = \$161$ (nearest dollar)

before.question_text: Trinity de Rale is a budding installation artist. Her latest mobile artwork comprises of two fixed rails placed at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to each other at $O$ (refer to diagram). A rod $PQ$ of fixed length $L$ cm is placed such that its ends $P$ and $Q$ glide freely along each rail. It is given that the length $OP$ is $x$ cm, and that the angle $OPQ$ is $\theta$.

parts.text: Show that $x = L\left(\cos\theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta\right)$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Using sine rule,
$\frac{x}{\sin(120^\circ - \theta)} = \frac{L}{\sin 60^\circ}$
$x = \frac{L}{\sin 60^\circ}[\sin(120^\circ - \theta)]$
$= \frac{L}{\sin 60^\circ}[\sin 120^\circ \cos \theta - \cos 120^\circ \sin \theta]$
$= \frac{L}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}\left[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos \theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin \theta\right]$
$x = L\left(\cos \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin \theta\right)$ (shown)

parts.text: A motor is placed at $P$ to move that end of the rod along the rail, allowing $\theta$ to vary between $30^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. The motor is controlled such that the point $P$ moves at a constant rate for 60 seconds, starting from the position where $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and ending at the position where $\theta = 30^{\circ}$. Find, in terms of $L$, the exact rate of change of $\theta$ at the moment when $\theta = 60^{\circ}$. State clearly the units for your answer.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let $t$ be time in seconds.
Since $x$ increases at a constant rate, $\frac{dx}{dt}$ is a constant and equals $\frac{(\text{final } x) - (\text{initial } x)}{\text{time taken}}$.
When $\theta = 90^\circ$, $x = L\left(\cos 90^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin 90^\circ\right) = \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}$.
When $\theta = 30^\circ$, $x = L\left(\cos 30^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin 30^\circ\right) = L\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\right) = \frac{2L}{\sqrt{3}}$.
So $\frac{dx}{dt} = \left(\frac{2L}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \div 60 = \frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}$.
Differentiating $x = L\left(\cos \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin \theta\right)$ with respect to $\theta$:
$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = L\left(-\sin \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos \theta\right)$.
Thus, by chain rule, $\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{dx}{d\theta} \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$:
$\frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}} = L\left(-\sin \theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos \theta\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
When $\theta = 60^\circ$:
$\frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}} = L\left(-\sin 60^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 60^\circ\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
$\frac{1}{60\sqrt{3}} = \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{1}{2}\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
$\frac{1}{60\sqrt{3}} = \left(\frac{-3 + 1}{2\sqrt{3}}\right) \times \frac{d\theta}{dt}$
$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\frac{1}{60}$ rad s$^{-1}$ (or s$^{-1}$)

parts.text: However, when installing the work, the exhibit curator Mick Schupp programmed the motor incorrectly, causing $\theta$ to decrease at a constant rate from $90^{\circ}$ to $30^{\circ}$ in 60 seconds. As a result, at time $t$ seconds after the motor is started, point $P$ is further along its rail by a distance of $D$ cm compared to its correct position (refer to diagram). Find an expression for $D$ in terms of $L$ and $t$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
For the correct motion, $x$ starts at $\frac{L}{\sqrt{3}}$ when $t = 0$, and increases at constant rate of $\frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}$ (found in part (b)). Hence
$x_{\text{correct}} = \frac{L}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}t$
For the incorrect motion, at time $t$, notice that $\theta = (90 - t)^\circ$ and hence
$x_{\text{incorrect}} = L\left(\cos(90 - t)^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin(90 - t)^\circ\right)$
$= L\left(\sin t^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos t^\circ\right)$
Thus,
$D = x_{\text{incorrect}} - x_{\text{correct}}$
$= L\left(\sin t^\circ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos t^\circ\right) - \left(\frac{L}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{L}{60\sqrt{3}}t\right)$
$= L\left(\sin t^\circ + \frac{\cos t^\circ - 1}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{t}{60\sqrt{3}}\right)$ or equivalent

parts.text: Find, to 4 decimal places, the maximum value of $\frac{D}{L}$ during the motion. (You need not justify that the value is maximum.)
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
$\frac{D}{L} = \sin t^\circ + \frac{\cos t^\circ - 1}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{t}{60\sqrt{3}}$
From GC, plotting $Y = \sin t^\circ + \frac{\cos t^\circ - 1}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{t}{60\sqrt{3}}$ in degree mode,
The maximum value is 0.1343.

before.question_text: The diagram below shows a candle in the shape of a prism. $PQRS$ is a parallelogram.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the prism.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Area of cross-section $= 7 \times 12 = 84$ cm$^2$
Volume of prism $= 84 \times 20 = 1680$ cm$^3$

parts.text: Another candle is made in the shape of a cylinder of radius $6$ cm. The volume of this candle is the same as the volume of the candle in part (a). Show that the height of the cylindrical candle, when given to the nearest cm, is $15$ cm.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let height $= h$ cm.
Volume of cylinder $=$ Volume of prism
$\pi \times 6^2 \times h = 1680$
$h = \dfrac{1680}{36\pi} \approx 14.8545$
$h \approx 15$ cm (shown)

parts.text: $6$ such cylindrical candles are packed into a box in the shape of a cuboid. The top view of the box is shown below. The candles fit exactly into the box. Calculate the volume of the empty space in the box.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Length of box $= 6 \times 6 = 36$ cm
Breadth of box $= 4 \times 6 = 24$ cm
Height of box $= 14.85446$ cm
Volume empty $= (36 \times 24 \times 14.85446) - 6 \times 1680$
$= 12834.25 - 10080 = 2754.25 \approx 2750$ cm$^3$ (to 3 s.f.)

before.question_text: Sam wishes to build a kite made with two wooden sticks placed perpendicular to each other, forming the diagonals of the kite $AC$ and $BD$. $BD$ is given to be $2x$ cm. The perimeter of the kite is to be made from four plastic straws, two of which have fixed lengths $a$ cm each and the other two have fixed lengths $b$ cm each as shown in the diagram.

subparts.text: Show that the surface area of one side of the kite, $K$ cm$^2$, is given by $K = x\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + x\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Let the diagonals of the kite meet at $M$. Then $AM = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ and $MC = \sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$.

Area of kite $ABCD$ = area of $\triangle ABD$ + area of $\triangle BDC$

$K = \frac{1}{2}(2x)\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{1}{2}(2x)\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$

$= x\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + x\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$ (shown).

subparts.text: The surface area of a kite is one of the key factors that affect the aerodynamic forces on the flight of kites. To catch as much wind as possible, Sam wishes to maximise the surface area of his kite. Using differentiation, find the value of $x$ in terms of $a$ and $b$, such that $K$ is maximised. You do not need to show that $K$ is maximum.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Hence find the length of the wooden stick $AC$ in terms of $a$ and $b$ when $K$ is maximum.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
$AC = AM + MC = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \sqrt{b^2 - x^2}$.

Substituting $x^2 = \frac{a^2 b^2}{a^2 + b^2}$:

$a^2 - x^2 = a^2 - \frac{a^2 b^2}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{a^4}{a^2 + b^2}$, so $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{a^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

Similarly $\sqrt{b^2 - x^2} = \frac{b^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

$AC = \frac{a^2 + b^2}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

subparts.text: Using the result in part (iii), deduce the angle between the two straws, $AB$ and $BC$, when $K$ is maximised.
subparts.label: iv
subparts.solution:
From (iii) $AC^2 = a^2 + b^2 = AB^2 + BC^2$.

By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, $\angle ABC = 90^\circ = \frac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

parts.text: Sam tests his kite at an open area, and he wants to fly his kite at a fixed vertical height of 30 m above the horizontal ground. The wind blows the kite horizontally from point $P$ to $Q$ with a speed of 2.4 m/s. The string attached to the kite is temporarily tied to the point $O$ on the horizontal ground. Find the rate at which the angle made between the string and the horizontal, $\theta$ measured in radians, is decreasing at the instant when Sam lets out $10\sqrt{10}$ m of his string.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the horizontal distance travelled by the kite from $O$ to its projection below the kite be $y$ m. Then $\tan\theta = \frac{30}{y}$, i.e. $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{30}{y}\right)$.

$\frac{d\theta}{dy} = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\frac{30}{y}\right)^2}\left(-\frac{30}{y^2}\right) = -\frac{30}{y^2 + 900}$.

When $OQ = 10\sqrt{10}$ m: $y = \sqrt{(10\sqrt{10})^2 - 30^2} = \sqrt{1000 - 900} = 10$ m. Given $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2.4$ m/s.

$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{d\theta}{dy} \cdot \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{30}{10^2 + 900}(2.4) = -\frac{30}{1000}(2.4) = -\frac{9}{125}$ rad/s.

The angle is decreasing at $\frac{9}{125}$ rad/s (or $0.072$ rad/s).

before.question_text: A paper cup is in the shape of an inverted cone. The diameter of the top of the cup is $8$ cm. The height of the cone is $6$ cm. The thickness of the paper is negligible.

parts.text: Calculate the curved surface area of the inside of the paper cup.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Radius $r = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$ cm, height $= 6$ cm.
Slant height $l = \sqrt{4^{2} + 6^{2}} = \sqrt{52} = 7.211$ cm.
Curved surface area $= \pi r l = \pi (4)(7.211) = 90.6$ cm$^{2}$ (to 3 s.f.).

parts.text: Farah pours water into the paper cup. The surface of the water is $3$ cm below the top of the paper cup.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Farah thinks that the paper cup is filled to $50\%$ of its total capacity. Explain why she is wrong.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: The volume of water in the cone is not directly proportional to the depth of water (volume scales with the cube of the linear dimensions in similar cones).
subparts.solution: The water forms a smaller cone similar to the cup. The volume of a cone is proportional to the cube of its depth, not to the depth itself, so a depth that is half the height does not give half the volume. Hence the cup is not filled to $50\%$.

subparts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total capacity of the cup that is filled.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
The water surface is $3$ cm below the top, so the water cone has height $6 - 3 = 3$ cm (measured from the apex).
Ratio of heights $= \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so ratio of volumes $= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.
Percentage filled $= \dfrac{1}{8} \times 100\% = 12.5\%$.

subparts.text: Farah pours the water from this conical cup and it fills a hemispherical bowl completely. Calculate the diameter of the hemispherical bowl.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Volume of cup $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (4)^{2}(6) = 32\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
Volume of water $= 12.5\% \times 32\pi = 4\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
This fills a hemisphere completely:
$\dfrac{2}{3}\pi R^{3} = 4\pi$
$R^{3} = 6 \Rightarrow R = 1.817$ cm
Diameter $= 3.63$ cm.

before.question_text: $f(x) = x^2 + 2$, $0 \leq x \leq 2$. $R$ is bounded by $x$-axis, curve, $x = 0$, $x = 2$. $n$ rectangles of width $2/n$ estimate area.

parts.text: Show total area of $n$ rectangles is $\frac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} + 4$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Total area $= \dfrac{2}{n}\left\{\left[\left(\dfrac{2}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] + \left[\left(\dfrac{4}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] + \ldots + \left[\left(\dfrac{2(n-1)}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] + \left[\left(\dfrac{2n}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right]\right\}$
$= \dfrac{2}{n}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\left(\dfrac{2i}{n}\right)^2 + 2\right] = \dfrac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{4}{n^2}i^2 + 2\right)$
$= \dfrac{2}{n}\left[\left(\dfrac{4}{n^2}\right)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\right] = \dfrac{2}{n}\left(\dfrac{4}{n^2}\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + 2n\right)$
$= \dfrac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} + 4 \quad$(shown)

parts.text: Least $n$ so rectangle area differs from $R$ by < 0.1.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Area of $R = \displaystyle\int_0^2 (x^2 + 2)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} + 2x\right]_0^2 = \dfrac{20}{3}$
Let $A_n$ denote the total area when $n$ rectangles are used.
So we need $A_n - R = \dfrac{4(n+1)(2n+1)}{3n^2} + 4 - \dfrac{20}{3} < 0.1$
From GC:
$n = 40$: $A_{40} - R = 0.1008$
$n = 41$: $A_{41} - R = 0.0984$
So least $n = 41$.

parts.text: Difference between 4 trapeziums and area of $R$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
[Note: area of a trapezium $= \dfrac{1}{2}(\text{sum of parallel sides}) \times \text{height}$.]
For $n$ trapeziums, width $= \dfrac{2}{n}$. So for $n = 4$, width $= \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Let $B_4$ denote the total area when 4 trapeziums are used.
$B_4 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f(0) + f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + f(1)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f(1) + f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left[f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + f(2)\right]\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}$
$= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[f(0) + 2f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2f(1) + 2f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + f(2)\right]$
$= 6.75$ units$^2$
$B_4 - R = 0.0833$

parts.text: Comment on trapeziums vs rectangles.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
In (ii), it takes 41 rectangles for the difference to be less than 0.1 units$^2$ of the actual area, whereas in (iii) it only takes 4 trapeziums to achieve that. So using trapeziums to estimate the area is more efficient.

[Possible way to organise the information from the two parts to help identify the more significant aspect to comment on:
Shape | $n$ | Difference
Rectangles | 41 | $< 0.1$
Trapeziums | 4 | $0.0833$
Comparison | $\sim 10$ times | $\sim$ equal]
