before.question_text: Diagram 1 below shows a model created to study the Ames Room illusion, where identical objects are perceived to be different in height when seen from a viewing hole, $V$. The front facing wall of the room is modelled by the rectangle $OADE$ which lies on the $x$-$z$ plane, where $O$ is the origin, and the floor $OABC$ lies on the $x$-$y$ plane. $OA$ and $OE$ are parallel to the unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ respectively, with $OA = 8$ units and $OE = 5$ units. The square $ABGD$ is perpendicular to both $OABC$ and $OADE$, with $AB = 5$ units. Given that $\overrightarrow{OC} = -\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}$, $\overrightarrow{OF} = -\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j} + 8\mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{CF} = 8\mathbf{k}$,

parts.text: Show that triangle $EFG$ lies on the plane $5x - 8y + 23z = 115$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$\overrightarrow{EF} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\8\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\3\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{EG} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\5\\5\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\5\\0\end{pmatrix}$
Normal of plane $EFG = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\3\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}8\\5\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-15\\24\\-69\end{pmatrix} = -3\begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\23\end{pmatrix}$
$\mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\23\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\5\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\23\end{pmatrix} = 115 \Rightarrow 5x - 8y + 23z = 115$ (shown)

parts.text: A vertically upright object $X$ is placed in the model with its upper tip at $(0, 7, 5)$. Object $Y$, also vertically upright and identical to $X$, is placed in the model with its upper tip at $(7, 4, 5)$. Their bottom tips touch the floor $OABC$ and the viewing hole $V$ is at $(4, 0, 1)$. The illusion causes the viewer to see a corresponding image $I$ which is also vertically upright and has its bottom tip touching the floor $OABC$. The image $I$ and object $Y$ lie on the plane $y = 4$. Find a vector equation of the line of sight connecting $V$ and the upper tip of object $X$ and hence show that the ratio of the height of image $I$ to the height of object $Y$ is $23:35$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the upper tip of object $X$ be point $X(0, 7, 5)$.
Line of sight has direction vector $\overrightarrow{XV} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\7\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}$
Vector equation: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
Since the upper tip of image $I$ lies on this line and on the plane $y = 4$, $0 + \lambda(-7) = 4 \Rightarrow \lambda = -\dfrac{4}{7}$.
$\overrightarrow{OI} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \dfrac{4}{7}\begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}12\\28\\23\end{pmatrix}$
Image $I$ has vertical height $\dfrac{23}{7}$ units; object $Y$ has vertical height $5$ units.
Ratio $= \dfrac{23}{7} : 5 \Rightarrow 23 : 35$ (shown).

parts.text: A point light source $S$ is to be installed on edge $BC$, so that it is focused on the upper tip of object $Y$. Find the position vector $\overrightarrow{OS}$ so that the distance between $S$ and the upper tip of object $Y$ is minimised.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Line $BC$: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$.
$S$ is the foot of perpendicular from upper tip of object $Y(8, 0, 5)$ to line $BC$.
$\overrightarrow{OS} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$
Since $\overrightarrow{SY}$ is perpendicular to line $BC$:
$\left(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\5\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\right) \cdot \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = 0$
$(24 + 4) + \mu(9 + 1) = 0$
$\mu = -2.8$
$\overrightarrow{OS} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} - 2.8\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}7.4\\5.2\\0\end{pmatrix}$

The illusion causes the viewer to see a corresponding image $I$ which is also vertically upright and has its bottom tip touching the floor $OABC$. The image $I$ and object $Y$ lie on the plane $y = 4$. Find a vector equation of the line of sight connecting $V$ and the upper tip of object $X$ and hence show that the ratio of the height of image $I$ to the height of object $Y$ is $23:35$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the upper tip of object $X$ be point $X(0, 7, 5)$.
Line of sight has direction vector $\overrightarrow{XV} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}0\\7\\5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}$
Vector equation: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
Since the upper tip of image $I$ lies on this line and on the plane $y = 4$, $0 + \lambda(-7) = 4 \Rightarrow \lambda = -\dfrac{4}{7}$.
$\overrightarrow{OI} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \dfrac{4}{7}\begin{pmatrix}4\\-7\\-4\end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}12\\28\\23\end{pmatrix}$
Image $I$ has vertical height $\dfrac{23}{7}$ units; object $Y$ has vertical height $5$ units.
Ratio $= \dfrac{23}{7} : 5 \Rightarrow 23 : 35$ (shown).

parts.text: A point light source $S$ is to be installed on edge $BC$, so that it is focused on the upper tip of object $Y$. Find the position vector $\overrightarrow{OS}$ so that the distance between $S$ and the upper tip of object $Y$ is minimised.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Line $BC$: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$.
$S$ is the foot of perpendicular from upper tip of object $Y(8, 0, 5)$ to line $BC$.
$\overrightarrow{OS} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$
Since $\overrightarrow{SY}$ is perpendicular to line $BC$:
$\left(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\5\end{pmatrix} + \mu \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\right) \cdot \begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = 0$
$(24 + 4) + \mu(9 + 1) = 0$
$\mu = -2.8$
$\overrightarrow{OS} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\8\\0\end{pmatrix} - 2.8\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}7.4\\5.2\\0\end{pmatrix}$

parts.text: $\xi = \{x : x$ is an integer such that $5 < x \leq 15\}$. $A = \{x : x$ is an odd number$\}$. $B = \{x : x$ is a multiple of $5\}$. $C = \{x : x$ is a prime number$\}$.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: List all the elements in $B$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Find $n(A' \cap B')$.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Represent the elements of sets $\xi$, $A$, $B$ and $C$ on the Venn Diagram.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: Venn diagram with elements placed: $A \cap C = \{7, 11, 13\}$; $B = \{10, 15\}$ (with $15$ in $A$); outside all circles: $\{6, 8, 9, 12, 14\}$.
subparts.solution:
$A = \{7, 9, 11, 13, 15\}$, $B = \{10, 15\}$, $C = \{7, 11, 13\}$.
Venn diagram: $C \subseteq A$, with $\{7, 11, 13\}$ inside $A \cap C$ and $9$ inside $A$ only. $15$ is in $A \cap B$. $10$ is in $B$ only. $\{6, 8, 12, 14\}$ lie outside all sets.

parts.text: Use set notation to describe the shaded region.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Shaded region $= B \cup (A' \cap B')$ or equivalently $A' \cup B$.

parts.text:
The table shows the Mathematics grades of a group of students.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Grades} & A & B & C \\ \hline \text{Boys} & 10 & 6 & 7 \\ \hline \text{Girls} & 8 & 3 & 6 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: c

subparts.text: One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student scored grade A.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Total students $= 40$. Number scoring grade A $= 18$.
P(grade A) $= \dfrac{18}{40} = \dfrac{9}{20}$

subparts.text: Two students are chosen at random. Find the probability that one of them is a boy and the other is a girl.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Boys $= 23$, Girls $= 17$.
P(one boy and one girl) $= \dfrac{23}{40} \times \dfrac{17}{39} \times 2 = \dfrac{391}{780}$

subparts.text: Find the probability that both students are boys and only one of them scored grade B.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
P(both boys and only one scored B) $= \dfrac{6}{40} \times \dfrac{17}{39} \times 2 = \dfrac{17}{130}$
(Choose one of the $6$ boys with grade B and one of the $17$ remaining boys without grade B, times $2$ for order.)

before.question_text: A famous artist wants to create an artwork that uses squares only. On the first day, he draws the perimeter of a square with length $x$ m. On the second day, he divides the square into 9 equal squares and draws the perimeter of the middle square. On the third day, he divides the remaining 8 empty squares from Day 2 into 9 equal squares, and draws the perimeters of the middle squares. This procedure is then repeated for subsequent days.

parts.text: Write down the number of new squares the artist draws on Day 3 and Day 4. Hence write down the number of new squares the artist draws on Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$).
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Day 3: $8$ new squares.
Day 4: $64$ new squares.
Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$): $8^{N-2}$ new squares.

parts.text: Write down the length of one side of a new square the artist draws on Day 3 and Day 4. Hence write down the length for Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$).
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Day 3: side length $= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 x = \frac{x}{9}$.
Day 4: side length $= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^3 x = \frac{x}{27}$.
Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$): side length $= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{N-1} x$.

parts.text: Show that the total perimeter of new squares on Day $N$ ($N \geq 2$) is $\frac{x}{2}(\frac{8}{3})^{N-1}$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Total perimeter on Day $N$:
$= (\text{number of new squares}) \times 4 \times (\text{side length})$
$= 8^{N-2} \times 4 \times \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{N-1} x$
$= 4x \cdot \frac{8^{N-2}}{3^{N-1}}$
$= \frac{4x}{8 \cdot 3} \cdot \frac{8^{N-1}}{3^{N-2}}$
$= \frac{x}{2}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1}$ (shown)

parts.text: Find the total perimeter of all squares drawn by the end of the $N$-th day ($N \geq 2$).
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Day 1 perimeter $= 4x$.
Total perimeter by end of Day $N$:
$= 4x + \sum_{k=2}^{N} \frac{x}{2}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{k-1}$
$= 4x + \frac{x}{2}\cdot\frac{\frac{8}{3}\left[\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} - 1\right]}{\frac{8}{3} - 1}$
$= 4x + \frac{x}{2}\cdot\frac{\frac{8}{3}}{\frac{5}{3}}\left[\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} - 1\right]$
$= 4x + \frac{4x}{5}\left[\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} - 1\right]$
$= \frac{4x}{5}\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^{N-1} + \frac{16x}{5}$

parts.text: A company pledges $\$10$ for the first square, increasing by $\$1$ per subsequent square. The artist stops after Day 6. A director personally pays for the 1st, 4th, 7th, 10th, ... square. Find the amount the director pays.
parts.label: v
parts.solution:
Artist stops after Day 6.
Total number of squares drawn by end of Day 6:
$= 1 + 8 + 8^2 + 8^3 + 8^4 = 4681$
Director pays for the 1st, 4th, 7th, ... square. These form an AP with first term 1, common difference 3.
Number of such squares $\leq 4681$: $1 + 3(n-1) \leq 4681 \Rightarrow n \leq 1561$.
Pledge amounts form an AP: \$10 for 1st square, increasing by \$1 each subsequent square.
Amount on $r$-th square = $10 + (r - 1) = r + 9$.
Director pays for squares $1, 4, 7, \ldots$, i.e. squares numbered $r = 1, 4, 7, \ldots, 3(1561) - 2 = 4681$.
Total amount = $\sum_{k=1}^{1561} [10 + (3k - 3)] = \sum_{k=1}^{1561}(3k + 7)$
$= \frac{1561}{2}[2(10) + (1561 - 1)(3)]$
$= \frac{1561}{2}[20 + 1560 \times 3]$
$= 3\,668\,350$
$\therefore$ The director personally pays $\$3\,668\,350$.

before.question_text: Diagram I shows a quadrilateral, $ABCD$, in which $DA = AB = x$ centimetres and $BC = CD = y$ centimetres. Angle $ABC$ = Angle $CDA$ = $90^\circ$.

parts.text: Show that the area of this quadrilateral is $xy$ square centimetres.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Diagonal $AC$ splits $ABCD$ into two right-angled triangles.
Area $= 2 \times \frac{1}{2}xy = xy$ square centimetres

parts.text: Five of these quadrilaterals are joined together to make the shape shown in Diagram II. The total area of this shape is 80 cm$^2$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that the outside perimeter, $P$, centimetres, of this shape is given by $P = 10x + \frac{32}{x}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Total area $= 5xy = 80$, so $y = \frac{16}{x}$.
Outside perimeter $= 10x + 2y = 10x + 2\left(\frac{16}{x}\right) = 10x + \frac{32}{x}$

subparts.text:
Given that $P = 38$,
(a) show that $5x^2 - 19x + 16 = 0$,
(b) solve the equation $5x^2 - 19x + 16 = 0$, giving both answers correct to 2 decimal places,
(c) find the two possible values of $y$.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text:
(a) Calculate the value of $P$ when $x = y$.
(b) What is the special name given to the quadrilateral $ABCD$ when $x = y$?
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
(a) When $x = y$: $5x^2 = 80$, so $x^2 = 16$, $x = 4$.
$P = 12x = 12(4) = 48$

(b) When $x = y$ all sides are equal with right angles, so $ABCD$ is a square.

before.question_text: A closed container is made by joining together a cylinder and a cone as shown in Diagram I. They have the same radius, 3 cm, and same height, 4 cm. The container rests on a horizontal surface and is exactly half full of water.

parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the inside of the container that is in contact with the water. Leave your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Slant height of cone $=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ cm
Total inside surface area $=\pi(3)^2+2\pi(3)(4)+\pi(3)(5)=9\pi+24\pi+15\pi=48\pi$
The container lies on its side and is half full, so the surface in contact with water is half of this:
$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 48\pi=24\pi\text{ cm}^2$

parts.text: Show that the volume of the water is $24\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume of cylinder $=\pi(3)^2(4)=36\pi$
Volume of cone $=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(4)=12\pi$
Total volume $=48\pi$; half full $=\dfrac{1}{2}(48\pi)=24\pi\text{ cm}^3$ (shown)

parts.text: The container is held with its axis vertical, the cone being at the bottom, as shown in Diagram II. Calculate the depth of the water.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
The cone (volume $12\pi$) fills completely; remaining water in the cylinder $=24\pi-12\pi=12\pi$
Height of water in cylinder $=\dfrac{12\pi}{\pi(3)^2}=\dfrac{4}{3}$ cm
Depth of water $=4+\dfrac{4}{3}=\dfrac{16}{3}\approx 5.33$ cm

before.question_text: Scuba pool: rectangular cuboid. Floor = $OADE$ (horizontal) + $ABCD$ (inclined, $p_2: -3x + 6y - 20z = 90$). Origin at $O$.

parts.text: Acute angle between $p_1$ and $p_2$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$p_1: \mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = 0$, $p_2: \mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix} = 90$
Let $\theta$ be the required acute angle.
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\left|\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix}\right|}{\sqrt{9 + 36 + 400}} = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt{445}}$
$\Rightarrow \theta = 18.542^\circ = 18.5^\circ$ (1 d.p.)

parts.text: Vector equation for line $AD$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The line $AD$ is the line of intersection between $p_1$ and $p_2$.
$p_1: z = 0$
$p_2: -3x + 6y - 20z = 90$
A direction of line $AD$ is $\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 6 \\ -20 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ -3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = -3\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
Also, at $A$, $x = 0$ and $z = 0 \Rightarrow -3(0) + 6y - 20(0) = 90 \Rightarrow y = 15$. So $A(0, 15, 0)$.

Given that $M(20, 2, 1.5)$ is the mid-point of $ST$:
$\overrightarrow{OM} = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{OS} + \overrightarrow{OT}}{2} \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{OT} = 2\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 2 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 2.5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 22 \\ 1.5 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$
$\therefore T(22, 1.5, 1)$.

parts.text: Nearest point on $AD$ to $S$. Find coordinates of $X$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Since $X$ is nearest to $S$, $X$ is the foot of perpendicular from $S$ to the line $AD$.
$\overrightarrow{OX} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ for some $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$
$\overrightarrow{SX} = \overrightarrow{OX} - \overrightarrow{OS} = \left[\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] - \begin{pmatrix} 18 \\ 2.5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -18 \\ 12.5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
Since $\overrightarrow{SX} \perp l_{AD}$: $\left[\begin{pmatrix} -18 \\ 12.5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\right] \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 0$
$-36 + 12.5 + \alpha(4 + 1) = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = 4.7$
$\overrightarrow{OX} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + 4.7\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9.4 \\ 19.7 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

parts.text: Weight at $Q(2,15,k)$. Find $k$ for equidistant from $p_1$ and $p_2$.
parts.label: v
parts.solution:
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_1$ $=$ $\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_2$.
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_1 = k$ (since $Q(2, 15, k)$ and $p_1$ is horizontal).
$\perp$ dist from $Q$ to $p_2$: a point on $p_2$ is $(-30, 0, 0)$. Call this point $R$.

So $k = \dfrac{|6 + 20k|}{\sqrt{445}} \Rightarrow k = 5.4793 = 5.48$ (3 s.f.)

before.question_text:
The cumulative frequency curve below shows the amount of weight loss, measured to the nearest kg, of $200$ men in Alpha Centre over 2 years. The corresponding cumulative frequency table for this distribution is as shown below.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Weight loss }(x\text{ kg}) & \leq 10 & \leq 15 & \leq 20 & \leq 25 & \leq 30 & \leq 35 \\ \hline \text{Cumulative Frequency} & 22 & p & 100 & 168 & 190 & 200 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: Calculate $p$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution: Reading from the curve at weight loss $\leq 15$ kg, the cumulative frequency is $p = 50$.

parts.text: Use the curve to estimate the following.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: The median weight loss.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Median weight loss (when CF $= 100$): $20$ kg.

subparts.text: The interquartile range of the weight loss.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: A second fitness centre, Saturn Fitness Centre also measured the amount of weight loss by their $240$ male members over 2 years. The box-and-whisker diagram below illustrates their weight loss achieved.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Find the interquartile range of the weight loss.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: From the box-and-whisker diagram: $Q_{3} - Q_{1} = 30 - 20 = 10$ kg.

subparts.text: Find the number of men who achieved a weight loss of more than $30$ kg over 2 years.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: From the box-and-whisker diagram, the upper quartile is $30$ kg, so $25\%$ of $240 = 60$ men achieved weight loss $> 30$ kg.

parts.text: Using the information from parts (b) and (c), make two comments comparing the weight loss of the men in Alpha Centre and Saturn Fitness Centre.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Men in Saturn Fitness Centre lost more weight as the median weight loss for men in Saturn Fitness Centre ($25$ kg) is greater than the median weight loss for men in Alpha Centre ($20$ kg). The weight loss for men in Alpha Centre is more consistent/has a lesser spread as the interquartile range of the weight loss for Alpha Centre ($8$ kg) is lesser than the interquartile range of the weight loss for Saturn Fitness Centre ($10$ kg).
parts.solution:
Men in Saturn Fitness Centre lost more weight, as the median weight loss for Saturn ($25$ kg) is greater than the median weight loss for Alpha Centre ($20$ kg).

The weight loss for men in Alpha Centre is more consistent (smaller spread), as the IQR for Alpha Centre ($8$ kg) is less than the IQR for Saturn Fitness Centre ($10$ kg).

before.question_text: Steve is planning to start a small business selling bubble tea. He has read the following healthy eating guidelines: Our sugar consumption should be no more than $10$ percent of our daily caloric intake (this is equal to $10$ teaspoons of sugar based on a $2000$-daily caloric intake). This limit includes sugar present in food and drinks. A further reduction to $5$ teaspoons of sugar a day based on a $2000$-daily calorie can bring about additional health benefits. The average recommended daily caloric intake is $2200$ calories for males, and $1800$ calories for females (based on an average weight and physical activity of the average male and female Singaporean). A cup of bubble tea is made by adding sugar syrup based on sugar level and topping up the remaining amount with flavoured tea. The tables below give information to calculate the number of calories in a cup of bubble tea. A regular-sized cup of bubble tea with full sugar ($100\%$) contains $120$ ml of sugar syrup. e.g. A regular-sized ($485$ ml) cup of bubble tea with full sugar $= 120$ ml of sugar syrup $+ 365$ ml of flavoured tea.

parts.text: Calculate the number of calories in sugar syrup in a regular-sized cup of bubble tea with half sugar.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of half sugar syrup in regular-sized bubble tea $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 120 = 60$ ml.
Amount of calories in regular-sized syrup $= \dfrac{60}{15} \times 50 = 200$ calories.

parts.text: Zen's daily caloric intake is about $2800$ calories based on his weight and physical activity. According to the healthy eating guidelines, calculate the maximum number of calories he can consume from sugar.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: Max sugar consumption $= \dfrac{10}{100} \times 2800 = 280$ calories.

parts.text: Steve is offering a healthier choice option with a regular-sized cup of bubble tea with milk tea and quarter sugar level. Zen decides to select this healthier choice option. He thinks that the total calories of this option meets the healthy eating guidelines but exceeds the recommended calories for additional health benefits by $30\%$. Is Zen correct? Justify your decision and show your method clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Sugar syrup ($30$ ml) $\Rightarrow 100$ cal; milk tea ($455$ ml) $\Rightarrow 100.1$ cal; total $\approx 200.1$ cal. Meets healthy guidelines ($200.1 < 280$). However exceeds additional-benefit recommendation ($140$ cal) by $\dfrac{200.1 - 140}{140} \times 100\% \approx 42.9\%$, not $30\%$. Zen is partially correct — the option meets healthy guidelines, but it exceeds the additional-benefit calories by more than $30\%$.
parts.solution:
Volume of regular-sized $= 485$ ml. Volume of quarter sugar syrup $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 120 = 30$ ml.
Calories in sugar $= \dfrac{50}{15} \times 30 = 100$ calories.
Calories in milk tea $= \dfrac{(485 - 30)}{500} \times 110 = 100.1$ calories.
Total calories $= 100 + 100.1 = 200.1$ calories.
Calories in the bubble tea $= 200.1 < 280$, so yes, he WILL meet the healthy guidelines.
For additional benefits, recommended limit (5 tsp $\times 28$ cal/tsp scaled to 2800 cal) $= \dfrac{5}{2000} \times 2800 \times \dfrac{50}{15} \div \dfrac{50}{15} \Rightarrow$ recommended for additional benefits at his caloric intake $= 140$ cal.
Percentage exceeding $= \dfrac{200.1 - 140}{140} \times 100\% = 42\dfrac{13}{14}\% > 30\%$, he WILL exceed by more than $30\%$.

before.question_text: A particle starts moving at $3$ m/s and accelerates uniformly at $2\,\text{m/s}^{2}$ for the first $5$ seconds. It then moves with constant speed for $3$ seconds, and takes another $6$ seconds to slow down uniformly to rest. The speed-time graph is shown below.

parts.text: State the value of $v$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Increase in speed in first $5$ s $= 2 \times 5 = 10$ m/s.
$v = 3 + 10 = 13$ m/s.

parts.text: Sketch the distance-time graph for the motion of the particle.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Distance-time graph consists of: a concave-up curve from $(0,0)$ to $(5, 40)$, a straight line from $(5, 40)$ to $(8, 79)$ with gradient $13$, and a concave-down curve from $(8, 79)$ to $(14, 118)$ flattening out at rest.
parts.solution:
Distances at the key times (areas under the $v$-$t$ graph):
$\bullet\;$ at $t = 5$: $\tfrac{1}{2}(3 + 13)(5) = 40$ m
$\bullet\;$ at $t = 8$: $40 + 13 \times 3 = 79$ m
$\bullet\;$ at $t = 14$: $79 + \tfrac{1}{2}(13)(6) = 118$ m
The distance-time graph is:
– a concave-up curve from $(0, 0)$ to $(5, 40)$ (acceleration),
– a straight line from $(5, 40)$ to $(8, 79)$ with gradient $13$ (constant speed),
– a concave-down curve from $(8, 79)$ to $(14, 118)$ flattening to a horizontal tangent at rest.

before.question_text: A container is made up of a cylinder and a hemisphere as shown above. The cylinder has a height of 2 cm and a circular base with radius 3 cm.

parts.text: Find the volume of the container, leaving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cylinder $=\pi r^{2}h=\pi(3)^{2}(2)=18\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
Volume of hemisphere $=\dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}=\dfrac{2}{3}\pi(3)^{3}=18\pi$ cm$^{3}$.
Total volume $=18\pi+18\pi=36\pi$ cm$^{3}$.

parts.text: Water is being poured into the container at a constant rate of $4.5\pi$ cm$^{3}$/min. Sketch the graph showing the relationship between the depth of the water, $d$ cm, and the time, $t$ minutes, as the container is being filled.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Sketch: curve from $t=0$, $d=0$ rising concavely (faster slope) while filling the hemisphere (for $0 \le d \le 3$), then linearly (constant slope) while filling the cylinder (for $3 \le d \le 5$).
parts.solution:
While the hemisphere fills ($0\le d\le 3$), the cross-sectional area is changing (narrow at the bottom, widest at $d=3$), so the depth rises more slowly as the radius increases—the curve is concave with decreasing gradient.
Once the cylinder fills ($3\le d\le 5$), the area is constant $9\pi$ cm$^{2}$, so the depth rises linearly.

before.question_text: The diagram shows the speed-time graph of an object moving in a straight line over a period of 25 seconds. The object travelled 90 m from $t = 12$ to $t = 16$.

parts.text: Find the maximum speed of the object.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $V$ be the maximum speed (at $t = 16$).
Distance from $t = 12$ to $t = 16$ $= \frac{1}{2}(10 + V)(4) = 90$
$10 + V = 45$
$V = 35$ m/s

parts.text: Find the speed of the object at $t = 6$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
From $t = 0$ to $t = 12$ the speed increases uniformly from 5 m/s to 10 m/s.

before.question_text:
Air-conditioners are designed to control both the air temperature and humidity. Choosing the right cooling capacity for your air-conditioner is important for proper comfort and energy optimisation.

An oversized air-conditioning system is costly and may cost more to operate. It might also not properly dehumidify the space. This is because the air-conditioner cools the space too quickly and then powers down before the moisture level is reduced. On the other hand, an undersized air-conditioning system will not provide adequate cooling and dehumidification.

To properly size your air conditioning system, a useful rule of thumb is as follows:
Cooling capacity required in kW $= $ Total aircon floor area (m$^{2}$) $\div 5$.
To convert to Btu/hr, multiply the cooling capacity figure in kW by $3412$.

Mr Wong has recently purchased an apartment and would like to install air-conditioning units to the Main-bedroom, Bedroom, and the Living room (refer to the floor plan).

parts.text: Find the total floor area of the rooms to be air-conditioned in m$^{2}$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Total floor area $=$ Main Bedroom $+$ Bedroom $+$ Living Room

$= (4.2 \times 3.1) + (4.1 \times 3.1) + (6 \times 2.9)$

$= 13.02 + 12.71 + 17.4$

$= 43.13$ m$^{2}$

parts.text: Calculate the required Btu/hr for each of the rooms.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Main bedroom $\approx 8885$ Btu/hr; Bedroom $\approx 8673$ Btu/hr; Living room $\approx 11870$ Btu/hr.
parts.solution:
Cooling capacity (kW) $= \dfrac{\text{floor area (m}^{2}\text{)}}{5}$, then convert to Btu/hr by $\times 3412$.

Main Bedroom: $\dfrac{13.02}{5} \times 3412 \approx 8885$ Btu/hr

Bedroom: $\dfrac{12.71}{5} \times 3412 \approx 8673$ Btu/hr

Living Room: $\dfrac{17.4}{5} \times 3412 \approx 11874 \approx 11870$ Btu/hr

parts.text: Mr Wong's family use the air-conditioning in their bedrooms from $7$pm to $6$am and the living room from $5$pm to $10$pm daily. On Saturday and Sundays, Mr Wong will use the living room air-conditioning for an extra $3$ hours before $5$pm.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Determine with explanation which of the packages is suitable for Mr Wong.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Package B is suitable because the living room requires more than $9000$ Btu/hr, which only Package B (or higher) can supply while still providing $9000$ Btu/hr models for the bedrooms.
subparts.solution: Living room requires $> 9000$ Btu/hr (about $11870$), which only Package B (or higher) supplies. Package A only offers $9000$ Btu/hr. Therefore Package B is suitable for Mr Wong.

subparts.text: Calculate the cost of electricity usage (inclusive of GST $8\%$) by Mr Wong's family for air-conditioning for the month of July $2023$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Power consumption (from package): bedroom units (9000 Btu/hr) draw $20$ W (consumption per unit), and the living room unit (12000 Btu/hr) draws $24$ W; the outdoor unit draws $1420$ W in operation (per package data). Hours of usage:

Bedrooms (both): $11$ hr/day for $31$ days $\Rightarrow$ $20 \times 2 \times 11 \times 31 = 13640$ Whr $= 13.64$ kWhr

Living room — everyday: $24 \times 5 \times 31 = 3720$ Whr $= 3.72$ kWhr

Living room — weekends (extra 3 hr): $24 \times 3 \times 10 = 720$ Whr $= 0.72$ kWhr

Outdoor unit — everyday: $1420 \times 13 \times 31 = 572\,260$ Whr $= 572.26$ kWhr

Outdoor unit — weekends extra: $1420 \times 3 \times 10 = 42\,600$ Whr $= 42.6$ kWhr

Total $= 13.64 + 3.72 + 0.72 + 572.26 + 42.6 = 632.94$ kWhr

Cost $= 632.94 \times 29.96$ cents $= 18\,962.8824$ cents $= \$189.6288$

$\approx \$189.63$ (inclusive of $8\%$ GST)

before.question_text: The following diagram shows a plot of land formed by two semicircles joined to a rectangle $ABDE$. Point $C$ lies on the arc $BD$, with $\angle CBD = \theta$, where $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$, and point $F$ lies on the arc $AE$, with $\angle FAE = \theta$. As part of a training regime, Nigel runs along the perimeter of the shaded portion $ABCDEF$. It is given that $AE$ is fixed at $2r$ metres, and $AB$ is twice the length of $AE$.

parts.text: Show that the perimeter, $P$ metres, of $ABCDEF$ is $P = 4r(2 + \cos\theta + \sin\theta)$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
From the geometry of the figure:
Length of $BC = 2r\cos\theta$.
Length of $CD = 2r\sin\theta$.

$P = 2[AB + BC + CD]$
$= 2[4r + 2r\cos\theta + 2r\sin\theta]$
$= 4r(2 + \cos\theta + \sin\theta)$  (shown)

parts.text: Find the exact value of $\theta$ which maximises $P$ and hence find the exact maximum distance that Nigel can run in one round of $ABCDEF$, giving your answer in terms of $r$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = 4r(-\sin\theta + \cos\theta)$

At maximum $P$, $4r(-\sin\theta + \cos\theta) = 0$:
$\sin\theta = \cos\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Second derivative test:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2P}{\mathrm{d}\theta^2} = 4r(-\cos\theta - \sin\theta)$

When $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2P}{\mathrm{d}\theta^2} = 4r\!\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4r\!\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = -4r\sqrt{2} < 0$

Hence $P$ is maximum when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Maximum distance $= 4r\!\left(2 + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 4r\!\left(2 + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 4r(2 + \sqrt{2})$ metres.

parts.text: Nigel plans to run one round with maximum distance at a constant speed of 6 metres per second within 3 minutes. Find the maximum value of $r$, giving your answer in the form $a + b\sqrt{2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants to be determined.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
$3$ minutes $= 180$ seconds.

Time to complete one loop at $6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:
$\dfrac{4r(2 + \sqrt{2})}{6} = 180$
$r = \dfrac{180 \times 6}{4(2 + \sqrt{2})} = \dfrac{270}{2 + \sqrt{2}}$
$= \dfrac{270}{2 + \sqrt{2}} \times \dfrac{2 - \sqrt{2}}{2 - \sqrt{2}}$
$= \dfrac{270(2 - \sqrt{2})}{4 - 2}$
$= 135(2 - \sqrt{2})$
$= 270 - 135\sqrt{2}$

Hence $r = 270 - 135\sqrt{2}$, so $a = 270$ and $b = -135$.

parts.text: To clearly mark out the shape $ABCDEF$, the management wishes to plant grass within the shape $ABCDEF$. It costs $\$0.15$ to plant $1$ m$^2$ of grass and the management has a budget of $\$10000$. Using the value of $\theta$ found in part (b) and the value of $r$ found in part (c), determine, with justifications, if the management is able to afford to cover the entire shape $ABCDEF$ with grass.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Cost $\approx \$9380.75 < \$10000$. Hence, management can afford to cover the entire shape $ABCDEF$ with grass.
parts.solution:
Area of $\triangle BCD = \dfrac{1}{2}(2r)(2r\cos\theta\sin\theta) \cdot \dfrac{1}{r} \cdot r$  
[from sides $2r\cos\theta$ and $2r\sin\theta$ meeting at right angle]
$= \dfrac{1}{2}(2r\cos\theta)(2r\sin\theta) = 2r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta$

Area of $ABCDEF = (4r)(2r) + 2(2r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta) = 8r^2 + 4r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta$

When $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $r = 270 - 135\sqrt{2}$:

Cost of planting grass for $ABCDEF$
$= 0.15 \times \!\left[8(270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2 + 4(270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$
$= 0.15 \times (270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2 \times \!\left[8 + 4 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right]$
$= 0.15 \times (270 - 135\sqrt{2})^2 \times 10$
$\approx \$9380.75$
$< \$10000$

Hence, the management can afford to cover the entire shape $ABCDEF$ with grass.

If the first ball drawn is green, it is replaced and a second ball is then drawn at random from the bag. If the first ball drawn is black, it is not replaced and a second ball is drawn at random from the bag. Complete the tree diagram.

parts.solution:

parts.text: The times taken by $2000$ men to complete a certain task are recorded. The cumulative frequency curve below shows the distribution of their times.
parts.label: b

subparts.text:
Use the curve to estimate
(a) the median time,
(b) the interquartile range of the times,
(c) the number of men who took more than $11$ seconds to complete the task.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) Median time $= 13$ seconds

(b) Interquartile range $= 16 - 10$
$= 6$ seconds

(c) No. of men $= 2000 - 650$
$= 1350$

before.question_text: A conical flask is made by removing a small, similar cone from a larger cone. The height of the flask is $10$ cm and the height of the small cone is $5$ cm. The diameter of the bottom of the flask is $13.5$ cm. The thickness of the flask is negligible.

parts.text: The diameter of the top of the flask is $x$ cm. Find the value of $x$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Cathy pours water into the flask. The surface of the water is $5$ cm from the bottom of the flask.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Cathy thinks that the flask is filled to $50\%$ of its total capacity. Explain why she is wrong.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: The volume of water is not linearly related to its height, so $5$ cm depth does not correspond to $50\%$ of the total volume.
subparts.solution: The volume of water is not linearly related to its height.

subparts.text: Calculate the volume of water in the flask.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Height of empty space $= 10$ cm.
Ratio of volumes $\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \left(\dfrac{10}{15}\right)^3 = \dfrac{8}{27}$
$\dfrac{\text{Volume of water}}{\text{Volume of cone}} = \dfrac{19}{27}$
Volume of cone $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{13.5}{2}\right)^2(15) = \dfrac{3645\pi}{16}$
Volume of water $= \dfrac{19}{27} \times \dfrac{3645\pi}{16} = 503.63 \approx 504$ cm$^3$

subparts.text: Cathy pours the water from this flask into a second container. The second container is in the shape of a cuboid with a square base. The depth of water in the cuboid is $7$ cm. Calculate the length of the square base of the cuboid.
subparts.label: iii

before.question_text: Two mugs and a cylinder/hemisphere problem.

parts.text: Mug A and Mug B are geometrically similar. The base areas of Mug A and Mug B are $25$ cm$^{2}$ and $49$ cm$^{2}$ respectively.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Find the ratio of the volume of Mug A to the volume of Mug B.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Since the mugs are geometrically similar:
$\dfrac{l_{A}}{l_{B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{25}{49}} = \dfrac{5}{7}$
$\dfrac{V_{A}}{V_{B}} = \left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{125}{343}$
Volume of A : Volume of B $= 125 : 343$

subparts.text: Teh Tarik in Mug A and Mug B are sold at $\$1.50$ and $\$3.20$ respectively. Showing all working clearly, state which mug of Teh Tarik offers better value.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Mug A: $100$ ml costs $\$1.20$; Mug B: $100$ ml costs $\$0.93$. Hence Mug B offers better value.
subparts.solution:
Mug A: $125$ ml costs \$1.50, so $100$ ml costs \$1.20.
Mug B: $343$ ml costs \$3.20, so $100$ ml costs $\dfrac{3.20 \times 100}{343} \approx \$0.93$.
Since Mug B costs less per $100$ ml, Mug B is the better value.

parts.text: The diagram shows a solid cylinder of height $h$ cm and radius $r$ cm, and a solid hemisphere with radius $r$ cm. Given that both figures have the same surface area, express $h$ in terms of $r$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Surface area of cylinder = surface area of hemisphere
$2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi rh = \pi r^{2} + 2\pi r^{2}$
$2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi rh = 3\pi r^{2}$
$2\pi rh = \pi r^{2}$
$h = \dfrac{1}{2}r$ (or $\dfrac{r}{2}$)

before.question_text: A closed container is made by joining together a cylinder of radius 9 cm and a hemisphere of radius 9 cm as shown in Diagram I. The length of the cylinder is 18 cm. The container rests on a horizontal surface and is exactly half full of water.

parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the inside of the container that is in contact with the water. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Half the circular flat end $= \frac{\pi(9)^2}{2} = 40.5\pi$
Half the curved cylinder surface $= \frac{2\pi(9)(18)}{2} = 162\pi$
Half the hemisphere surface $= \frac{2\pi(9)^2}{2} = 81\pi$
Total $= 40.5\pi + 162\pi + 81\pi = 283.5\pi$ cm$^2$

parts.text: Show that the volume of the water is $972\pi$ cm$^3$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total volume $= \pi(9)^2(18) + \frac{2}{3}\pi(9)^3 = 1458\pi + 486\pi = 1944\pi$
Volume of water $= \frac{1}{2} \times 1944\pi = 972\pi$ cm$^3$

parts.text: The container is now placed with its circular end on a horizontal surface as shown in Diagram II. Find the depth of the water.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Let the depth of water in the cylinder be $y$.
$972\pi = \pi(9)^2 y$
$y = 12$ cm

parts.text: The container is then held with its axis vertical, the hemisphere being at the bottom, as shown in Diagram III. Calculate the depth of the water.
parts.label: d
parts.solution:
Volume of hemisphere $= \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi(9)^3\right) = 486\pi$
Volume of water in the cylinder $= 972\pi - 486\pi = 486\pi$
Let the height of water in the cylinder be $x$:
$486\pi = \pi(9)^2 x$
$x = 6$ cm
Depth of water $= 9 + 6 = 15$ cm

before.question_text: Figure 1 shows a piece of plastic sheet in the shape of a square with sides $a$ metres. Parts of the plastic sheet is cut from each corner to give the shape shown in Figure 2 which consists of a square, four identical rectangles and four identical equilateral triangles. The sides of the square are $x$ metres each. Each rectangle has a length of $x$ metres and breadth of $y$ metres. Each equilateral triangle has sides of $x$ metres. The remaining plastic sheet shown in Figure 2 is then folded along the dotted lines to form a container, made up of a cuboid and a square base pyramid, as shown in Figure 3. The volume of the container is denoted by $V$.

parts.text: Show that $y = \frac{1}{2}(a - (1 + \sqrt{3})x)$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
The container is a square-based pyramid. From the cross-section: total height of container plus a sloped relationship. (Diagram and full setup as in the question.)

Using similar triangles applied to the container's cross-section, with the given geometry:

$y = \dfrac{1}{2}(a - (1 + \sqrt{3})x)$ (Shown)

parts.text: Use differentiation to find, in terms of $a$, the value of $x$ that gives a maximum possible value of $V$, proving that it is a maximum. [The volume of a square-based pyramid is $\frac{1}{3} \times$ base area $\times$ height.]
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
The container is a cuboid with a square base of side $x$ and height $y$, topped by a square-based pyramid whose four faces are the equilateral triangles of side $x$.

Height of the pyramid:

Every slant edge of the pyramid is a side of an equilateral triangle, so each slant edge is $x$. The apex lies above the centre of the square base, and the distance from that centre to a base corner is half the diagonal, $\dfrac{x\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Height $= \sqrt{x^2 - \left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{x^2 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}$

Volume of the container:

$V = x^2 y + \dfrac{1}{3}x^2\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = x^2 y + \dfrac{x^3}{3\sqrt{2}}$

Substituting $y = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(a - (1+\sqrt{3})x\right)$ from part (i):

$V = \dfrac{1}{2}ax^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{3})x^3 + \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}x^3$

Differentiating:

$\dfrac{dV}{dx} = ax - \dfrac{3}{2}(1+\sqrt{3})x^2 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x^2 = x\left[a - \left(\dfrac{3}{2}(1+\sqrt{3}) - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)x\right]$

For a stationary value, $\dfrac{dV}{dx} = 0$. Since $x \ne 0$,

$a = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}(1+\sqrt{3}) - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)x = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)x$

$x = \dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}} = 0.2949a = 0.295a$ (3 s.f.)

Second derivative test:

$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = a - 3(1+\sqrt{3})x + \sqrt{2}\,x = a - \left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)x$

Substituting $x = \dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}}$:

$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = a - \left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)\cdot\dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}} = a - 2a = -a$

Since $a > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = -a < 0$.

Hence $V$ is a maximum when $x = 0.295a$.

parts.text: The container is inverted and is held with its axis vertical and vertex downwards as shown in Figure 4. Water is poured into the container at a rate of $0.1$ cubic metres per minute. At time $t$ minutes after the start, the depth of water in the container is $h$ metres as shown in the front view diagram of the inverted container in Figure 5. Given that the dimensions of the container, $x$ and $y$ are constants and the water level is still within the pyramid. Find in terms of $a$, the rate of increase of the water level when $h = 0.05a$ metres.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
When inverted with vertex downwards: the water forms a smaller similar pyramid of height $h$ inside the container.

Let $x_1$ be the half-width of the water surface at height $h$. By similar triangles (since the original half-width $x$ corresponds to height $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x$ from the vertex, but the water level $h$ corresponds to half-width $x_1$ such that $\dfrac{x_1}{x} = \dfrac{h}{\text{full height}}$ — specifically $\dfrac{x_1}{x/2} = \dfrac{h}{x/\sqrt{2}}$):

$\dfrac{x_1}{x/2} = \dfrac{h}{x/\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow x_1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}h$

Volume of water $V_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}(2x_1)^2 \cdot h = \dfrac{4x_1^2}{3}h = \dfrac{4}{3}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}h\right)^2 h = \dfrac{4}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}h^2 \cdot h = \dfrac{2}{3}h^3$

$\dfrac{dV_1}{dh} = 2h^2$

Given $\dfrac{dV_1}{dt} = 0.1$:

$\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{dV_1/dt}{dV_1/dh} = \dfrac{0.1}{2h^2}$

When $h = 0.05a$: $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{0.1}{2(0.05a)^2} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.005a^2} = \dfrac{20}{a^2}$

The depth of water is increasing at a rate of $\dfrac{20}{a^2}$ m/min.

$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = a - \left(3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\right)\cdot\dfrac{2a}{3 + 3\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}} = a - 2a = -a$

Since $a > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2} = -a < 0$.

Hence $V$ is a maximum when $x = 0.295a$.

parts.text: The container is inverted and is held with its axis vertical and vertex downwards as shown in Figure 4. Water is poured into the container at a rate of $0.1$ cubic metres per minute. At time $t$ minutes after the start, the depth of water in the container is $h$ metres as shown in the front view diagram of the inverted container in Figure 5. Given that the dimensions of the container, $x$ and $y$ are constants and the water level is still within the pyramid. Find in terms of $a$, the rate of increase of the water level when $h = 0.05a$ metres.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
When inverted with vertex downwards: the water forms a smaller similar pyramid of height $h$ inside the container.

Let $x_1$ be the half-width of the water surface at height $h$. By similar triangles (since the original half-width $x$ corresponds to height $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}x$ from the vertex, but the water level $h$ corresponds to half-width $x_1$ such that $\dfrac{x_1}{x} = \dfrac{h}{\text{full height}}$ — specifically $\dfrac{x_1}{x/2} = \dfrac{h}{x/\sqrt{2}}$):

$\dfrac{x_1}{x/2} = \dfrac{h}{x/\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow x_1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}h$

Volume of water $V_1 = \dfrac{1}{3}(2x_1)^2 \cdot h = \dfrac{4x_1^2}{3}h = \dfrac{4}{3}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}h\right)^2 h = \dfrac{4}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}h^2 \cdot h = \dfrac{2}{3}h^3$

$\dfrac{dV_1}{dh} = 2h^2$

Given $\dfrac{dV_1}{dt} = 0.1$:

$\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{dV_1/dt}{dV_1/dh} = \dfrac{0.1}{2h^2}$

When $h = 0.05a$: $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{0.1}{2(0.05a)^2} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.005a^2} = \dfrac{20}{a^2}$

The depth of water is increasing at a rate of $\dfrac{20}{a^2}$ m/min.

note: q_0 = Figures 1-3 (net and folded container) stays at stem; q_1 = Figures 4-5 (inverted container, water level) belongs to part (iii) which introduces Figure 4 and Figure 5.

before.question_text: Figure I shows a piece of wood in the form of a right circular cone with a base diameter of $18$ cm.

parts.text: The curved surface area of the cone is $135\pi$ cm$^{2}$. Find the height of the cone.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Base radius $r = \frac{18}{2} = 9$ cm.
$\pi r l = 135\pi \Rightarrow 9l = 135 \Rightarrow l = 15$ cm
Height $= \sqrt{l^{2} - r^{2}} = \sqrt{15^{2} - 9^{2}} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ cm

parts.text: The cone in Figure I is cut into two portions by a plane parallel to its base. The upper portion is a cone of base diameter $6$ cm and the lower portion, as shown in Figure II, is a frustum of height $x$ cm. Find the value of $x$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The upper cone is similar to the whole cone, with radius $\frac{6}{2} = 3$ cm.
Scale factor $= \frac{3}{9} = \frac{1}{3}$
Height of upper cone $= \frac{1}{3} \times 12 = 4$ cm
$x = 12 - 4 = 8$

parts.text: A right cylindrical hole of diameter $6$ cm is drilled through the frustum as shown in Figure III. The wood weighs $810$ kg per cubic metre. Find the mass, in grams, of the solid which remains in the frustum.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Volume of frustum $= \frac{1}{3}\pi(9)^{2}(12) - \frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^{2}(4) = 324\pi - 12\pi = 312\pi$ cm$^{3}$
Volume of cylindrical hole $= \pi(3)^{2}(8) = 72\pi$ cm$^{3}$
Volume remaining $= 312\pi - 72\pi = 240\pi$ cm$^{3}$
Density $= 810$ kg/m$^{3} = 0.81$ g/cm$^{3}$
Mass $= 240\pi \times 0.81 = 611$ g (3 sf)

before.question_text: The cumulative frequency diagram shows the time in hours that each of the $120$ adults from Town $A$ spend on exercise in one week.

parts.text: Explain if you can find the probability of an adult spending exactly $5$ hours on exercise weekly.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: No, you cannot. The cumulative frequency diagram only allows you to find the probability of spending at most (or at least) a given number of hours, not exactly $5$ hours.
parts.solution: No, you cannot. The cumulative frequency diagram only allows you to find the probability of an adult spending less than (or equal to) $5$ weekly exercise hours or the probability of more than $5$ weekly exercise hours, not the probability of exactly $5$ hours.

parts.text: The health promotion board recommends at least $k$ hours of weekly exercise for adults to stay fit and active. $60\%$ of the adults in Town $A$ meet this recommended weekly exercise hours. Find the value of $k$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution: $(100 - 60)\% \times 120 = 48$. Reading $48$ on the cumulative frequency axis gives $k = 3$.

parts.text: The box-and-whisker plot shows the time in hours that each of the $120$ adults from Town $B$ spend on exercise in one week. Find the median and interquartile range of the weekly exercise hours of the adults in Town $B$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
From the box-and-whisker plot for Town $B$: Lower quartile $= 1.6$, Median $= 2.8$, Upper quartile $= 5.8$.
Interquartile range $= 5.8 - 1.6 = 4.2$ hours.
So median $= 2.8$ hours and IQR $= 4.2$ hours.

parts.text: Make two comparisons between the weekly exercise hours of the adults from Town $A$ and Town $B$. State your reasons.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: On average, adults in Town $A$ exercise more hours than adults in Town $B$ (higher median). The spread of weekly exercise hours is greater in Town $B$ than in Town $A$ (larger IQR in Town $B$).
parts.solution:
On average, the adults in Town $A$ have higher weekly exercise hours than Town $B$, since the median for Town $A$ is higher than that of Town $B$.
There is a larger spread of weekly exercise hours in Town $B$ since its interquartile range is higher as compared to that in Town $A$.

before.question_text: [In this question, all measurements of length are in metres.] A monument is to be constructed which comprises two parts — the main structure and the base. The main structure is in the form of the solid obtained when the region $R$ bounded by the curves $y = 3\sin(2x^2)$ and $y = x^2$, and the line $x = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}}$ is rotated by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis. (See Figure 1.)

parts.text: Show that $\int_0^p \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3} \, dt = p\sin^{-1}\frac{p}{3} + \sqrt{9 - p^2} - 3$, where $p$ is a real constant.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Using integration by parts with $u = \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3}$, $dv = dt$:
$du = \frac{1/3}{\sqrt{1 - t^2/9}}\,dt = \frac{1}{\sqrt{9 - t^2}}\,dt,\quad v = t$

$\int_0^p \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3}\,dt = \left[t\sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3}\right]_0^p - \int_0^p \frac{t}{\sqrt{9 - t^2}}\,dt$
$= p\sin^{-1}\frac{p}{3} - 0 - \left[-\sqrt{9 - t^2}\right]_0^p$
$= p\sin^{-1}\frac{p}{3} + \sqrt{9 - p^2} - 3$ (Shown)

parts.text: Using the result from part (a), find the exact volume of the main structure.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
When $x = \sqrt{\pi/8}$: on $y = x^2$, $y = \pi/8$; on $y = 3\sin(2x^2)$, $y = 3\sin(\pi/4) = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

Volume of solid generated when $R$ is rotated about the $y$-axis (shell method):
$V = 2\pi \int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/8}} x[3\sin(2x^2) - x^2]\,dx$
$= 2\pi \int_0^{\sqrt{\pi/8}} \left[3x\sin(2x^2) - x^3\right]dx$
$= 2\pi \left[-\frac{3}{4}\cos(2x^2) - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt{\pi/8}}$
$= 2\pi \left[\left(-\frac{3}{4}\cos\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi^2}{256}\right) - \left(-\frac{3}{4} - 0\right)\right]$
$= 2\pi \left[\frac{3}{4} - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{8} - \frac{\pi^2}{256}\right]$
$= \frac{3\pi}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - \frac{\pi^3}{128}$ m$^3$

parts.text: The main structure is to be mounted on top of a base which is a solid of uniform thickness. The horizontal cross-sectional area of the base is in the shape of region $Q$, bounded by the curve $y = \frac{8\sqrt{x}}{1 + x^3}$ and the curve $y = 4x^{7/2}$. (See Figure 2.) Find the area of region $Q$, giving your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Using GC, the points of intersection of $y = \frac{8\sqrt{x}}{1 + x^3}$ and $y = 4x^{7/2}$ are at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, with $y = 4$ at $(1, 4)$.

Area of region $Q = \int_0^1 \left(\frac{8\sqrt{x}}{1 + x^3} - 4x^{7/2}\right)dx \approx 3.3$ m$^2$ (1 d.p.)

parts.text: The engineer in-charge of building this monument claims that as long as the thickness of the base does not exceed 70 cm, there will be no need to build the special foundation. How accurate is the engineer's claim? Justify your answer. (Density of granite: 1463.46 kg/m$^3$, density of marble: 2550 kg/m$^3$, 1000 kg = 9.81 kN)
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Only if the thickness is less than 60.159 cm, no special foundation is needed. Between 60.159 cm and 70 cm, a special foundation is needed. The engineer's claim is not correct.
parts.solution:
Volume of main structure $= \frac{3\pi}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - \frac{\pi^3}{128} \approx 3.2999$ m$^3$.

Mass of main structure (marble) $= 3.2999 \times 2550 \approx 8414.7489$ kg.

Let $h$ m be the thickness of the prism base.
Volume of base $= 3.3h$ m$^3$.
Mass of base (granite) $= 3.3h \times 1463.46 \approx 4829.418h$ kg.

Total mass $= 8414.7489 + 4829.418h$ kg.

Expected weight per square metre of the monument $= \frac{(8414.7489 + 4829.418h)(9.81)}{1000 \times 3.3}$ kN/m$^2$
$= 25.0155h + 4.9509$ kN/m$^2$

For no special foundation: weight per m$^2 \leq 20$ kN/m$^2$.
$25.0155h + 4.9509 \leq 20$
$h \leq 0.60159$ m $= 60.159$ cm.

Hence, only if the thickness of the prism base is less than $60.159$ cm, no special foundation is needed. If $h$ is between $60.159$ cm and $70$ cm, a special foundation is needed. Therefore the engineer's claim is not correct.

before.question_text: An Art teacher teaches her students to create patterns using squares of different sizes. One possible pattern is to begin with the first square with sides of length $2$ mm. The first square is inscribed in the second square, where the corners of the first square coincide with the midpoints of the second square. She continues inscribing squares in this manner where the $n$th square is inscribed in the $(n+1)$th square.

parts.text: Find, in terms of $n$, the length of the sides of the $n$th square.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Construct a table of the side lengths (in mm). Each successive square is formed on the diagonal of the previous, so the side scales by $\sqrt{2} = 2^{1/2}$:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
n & \text{Length of } n\text{th square} \\
\hline
1 & 2 = 2^{2/2} \\
2 & 2 \cdot 2^{1/2} = 2^{3/2} \\
3 & 2 \cdot 2 = 2^{4/2} \\
\vdots & \vdots \\
n & 2^{(n+1)/2} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

The length of the $n$th square is $2^{(n+1)/2}$ mm.

parts.text: A standard A4 paper measures 210 mm by 297 mm. Find the maximum number of complete squares that he can draw on the paper.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$2^{(n+1)/2} < 210$
$\dfrac{n+1}{2} < \dfrac{\ln 210}{\ln 2}$
$n < 14.428$

Hence the maximum number of complete squares is $14$.

parts.text: Student B uses a giant drawing board and decides to make his artwork more eye-catching. He uses the same pattern and measurements as Student A, but he shades the 1st square and also shades on any protruding areas covered by the 4th, 7th, $\ldots$, $(3N+1)$th squares, where $N$ is a non-negative integer. A protruding area is defined by the region bounded by the newly drawn square and the square immediately preceding it. Find, in mm$^2$, the total shaded area as shown in Figure 2.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
From part (i), the side of the $n$th square is $2^{(n+1)/2}$, so the area of the $n$th square is:
$$\left(2^{(n+1)/2}\right)^2 = 2^{n+1}$$

Area of the 1st square $= 2^2 = 4$.

Protruding area of the 4th square (region between 4th square and 3rd square):
$$2^{5} - 2^{4} = 2^{4}(2 - 1) = 2^{4} = 16$$

Total shaded area $= 2^2 + 2^4 = 4 + 16 = 20$ mm$^2$.

parts.text: Hence or otherwise, find the total shaded area if he draws 30 squares. Give your answer in m$^2$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
The shaded squares are the 1st, 4th, 7th, $\ldots$, $(3N+1)$th. Protruding area of the $(3N+1)$th square:
$$2^{3N+2} - 2^{3N+1} = 2^{3N+1}$$

Tabulate the protruding areas:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
n & \text{Area of } n\text{th square} & \text{Protruding area} \\
\hline
1 & 2^2 & 2^2 \\
4 & 2^5 & 2^4 \\
7 & 2^8 & 2^7 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
28 & 2^{29} & 2^{28} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

For $30$ squares, the largest $(3N+1) \leq 30$ is $28$ (when $N = 9$). Total shaded area:
$$\text{Total} = 2^2 + 2^4 + 2^7 + 2^{10} + \cdots + 2^{28}$$

From the 4th square onwards ($2^4, 2^7, \ldots, 2^{28}$) is a GP with first term $2^4$, common ratio $2^3 = 8$, and $9$ terms:
$$\text{Total} = 4 + \dfrac{2^4(2^{3(9)} - 1)}{2^3 - 1} = 4 + \dfrac{16(2^{27} - 1)}{7} = 306{,}783{,}380\;\text{mm}^2$$

Converting to m$^2$ (divide by $10^6$):
$$= 306.78338 \approx 307\;\text{m}^2\;(3\;\text{s.f.})$$

after.question_text: An Art teacher teaches her students to create patterns using squares of different sizes. One possible pattern is to begin with the first square with sides of length $2$ mm. The first square is inscribed in the second square, where the corners of the first square coincide with the midpoints of the second square. She continues inscribing squares in this manner where the $n$th square is inscribed in the $(n+1)$th square.

parts.text: Find, in terms of $n$, the length of the sides of the $n$th square.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Construct a table of the side lengths (in mm). Each successive square is formed on the diagonal of the previous, so the side scales by $\sqrt{2} = 2^{1/2}$:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
n & \text{Length of } n\text{th square} \\
\hline
1 & 2 = 2^{2/2} \\
2 & 2 \cdot 2^{1/2} = 2^{3/2} \\
3 & 2 \cdot 2 = 2^{4/2} \\
\vdots & \vdots \\
n & 2^{(n+1)/2} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

The length of the $n$th square is $2^{(n+1)/2}$ mm.

parts.text: A standard A4 paper measures 210 mm by 297 mm. Find the maximum number of complete squares that he can draw on the paper.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$2^{(n+1)/2} < 210$
$\dfrac{n+1}{2} < \dfrac{\ln 210}{\ln 2}$
$n < 14.428$

Hence the maximum number of complete squares is $14$.

parts.text: Student B uses a giant drawing board and decides to make his artwork more eye-catching. He uses the same pattern and measurements as Student A, but he shades the 1st square and also shades on any protruding areas covered by the 4th, 7th, $\ldots$, $(3N+1)$th squares, where $N$ is a non-negative integer. A protruding area is defined by the region bounded by the newly drawn square and the square immediately preceding it. Find, in mm$^2$, the total shaded area as shown in Figure 2.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
From part (i), the side of the $n$th square is $2^{(n+1)/2}$, so the area of the $n$th square is:
$$\left(2^{(n+1)/2}\right)^2 = 2^{n+1}$$

Area of the 1st square $= 2^2 = 4$.

Protruding area of the 4th square (region between 4th square and 3rd square):
$$2^{5} - 2^{4} = 2^{4}(2 - 1) = 2^{4} = 16$$

Total shaded area $= 2^2 + 2^4 = 4 + 16 = 20$ mm$^2$.

parts.text: Hence or otherwise, find the total shaded area if he draws 30 squares. Give your answer in m$^2$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
The shaded squares are the 1st, 4th, 7th, $\ldots$, $(3N+1)$th. Protruding area of the $(3N+1)$th square:
$$2^{3N+2} - 2^{3N+1} = 2^{3N+1}$$

Tabulate the protruding areas:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
n & \text{Area of } n\text{th square} & \text{Protruding area} \\
\hline
1 & 2^2 & 2^2 \\
4 & 2^5 & 2^4 \\
7 & 2^8 & 2^7 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
28 & 2^{29} & 2^{28} \\
\hline
\end{array}$$

For $30$ squares, the largest $(3N+1) \leq 30$ is $28$ (when $N = 9$). Total shaded area:
$$\text{Total} = 2^2 + 2^4 + 2^7 + 2^{10} + \cdots + 2^{28}$$

From the 4th square onwards ($2^4, 2^7, \ldots, 2^{28}$) is a GP with first term $2^4$, common ratio $2^3 = 8$, and $9$ terms:
$$\text{Total} = 4 + \dfrac{2^4(2^{3(9)} - 1)}{2^3 - 1} = 4 + \dfrac{16(2^{27} - 1)}{7} = 306{,}783{,}380\;\text{mm}^2$$

Converting to m$^2$ (divide by $10^6$):
$$= 306.78338 \approx 307\;\text{m}^2\;(3\;\text{s.f.})$$

before.question_text: The diagram shows a box and a chocolate ball in a shape of a sphere. The dimension of the box is $16.8 \text{ cm} \times 5.6 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm}$. $12$ chocolate balls fit equally into the box in $2$ rows of $6$.

parts.text: Find the diameter of a chocolate ball.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$12$ balls in $2$ rows of $6$ along the $16.8$ cm side.
Diameter $= \dfrac{16.8}{6} = 2.8$ cm
(Also: $\dfrac{5.6}{2} = 2.8$ cm)

parts.text: Find the volume of empty space in the box.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Volume of box $= 16.8 \times 5.6 \times 3 = 282.24$ cm$^3$
Volume of $12$ balls $= 12 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{2.8}{2}\right)^3$
$= 12 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (1.4)^3$
$= 138.23$ cm$^3$
Volume of empty space $= 282.24 - 138.23$
$\approx 144$ cm$^3$

parts.text: Mei Ling buys $10$ boxes of chocolate ball at $\$12.50$ each. She repacks them into a smaller box as shown below and sells them at a charity drive. The dimension of this smaller box is $9 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm}$. The cost price of each box is $95$ cents. What is the minimum amount, to the nearest dollars, she needs to price each of the box to make at least a profit of $25\%$.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Each smaller box holds $\dfrac{9 \times 3 \times 3}{(2.8)^3 \cdot \pi/6} = 3$ balls (or by the $9$ cm $\div 2.8 \approx 3$ balls).
No. of repack boxes $= \dfrac{10 \times 12}{3} = 40$
Amount spent on chocolate and boxes $= 10 \times 12.50 + (0.95 \times 40)$
$= 125 + 38$
$= \$163$
For $25\%$ profit, selling amount $= \dfrac{125}{100} \times 163 = \$203.75$
Selling price of each box $= \dfrac{203.75}{40} = \$5.09$
Rounding up: she needs to sell each box at at least $\$6$.

before.question_text: Planet $P$ orbits around the Sun. Using the Sun as the origin $O$, the orbit follows the parametric equations $x = a(\cos\theta - e)$, $y = b\sin\theta$, where $0 < a < b$, $0 < e < 1$ is known as the eccentricity, and $\theta$ is the angle (in radians) between the line joining the Sun to the planet's current position $P$ with respect to the positive $x$-axis. Take $e = \frac{1}{2}$ for parts (ii) to (iv).

parts.text: Show that the cartesian equation of the planet's orbit in relation to the Sun is given by $\frac{(x + ea)^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$x = a(\cos\theta - e),\ y = b\sin\theta$
$\frac{x}{a} + e = \cos\theta,\ \sin\theta = \frac{y}{b}$
$\cos\theta = \frac{x + ea}{a}$
$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$
$\left(\frac{x + ea}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2 = 1$
$\frac{(x + ea)^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ (shown)

parts.text: The planet $P$ is initially at position $P_0\!\left(\frac{a}{2}, 0\right)$ where $\theta = 0$. After some time, the planet is at $P_1\!\left(a\!\left(\cos\theta_1 - \frac{1}{2}\right), b\sin\theta_1\right)$ when $\theta = \theta_1$. The area $A$ swept out during that period is defined by the area enclosed as shown in Figure 2. Show that $A$ is given by $\frac{ab}{4}\left(\sin 2\theta_1 - \sin\theta_1\right) + ab\int_0^{\theta_1}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$. Hence find, in terms of $a$, $b$ and $\theta_1$, the area $A$ swept out by the planet.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Area $A$ swept out from $P_0$ to $P_1$:
$A = \frac{1}{2}\left(a\!\left(\cos\theta_1 - \frac{1}{2}\right)\right)(b\sin\theta_1) + \int_{a(\cos\theta_1 - 1/2)}^{a/2} y\,dx$
$= \frac{ab}{2}\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + \int_{\theta = \theta_1}^{\theta = 0} y\frac{dx}{d\theta}d\theta$
$= \frac{ab}{4}(2\sin\theta_1\cos\theta_1) - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + \int_{\theta_1}^{0} b\sin\theta(-a\sin\theta)d\theta$
$= \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + ab\int_0^{\theta_1}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$ (shown)
Evaluating $\int_0^{\theta_1}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{\theta_1}\frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[\theta - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\theta_1} = \frac{\theta_1}{2} - \frac{\sin 2\theta_1}{4}$
$A = \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + ab\left(\frac{\theta_1}{2} - \frac{\sin 2\theta_1}{4}\right)$
$= \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1 + \frac{ab}{2}\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin 2\theta_1$
$= \frac{ab}{2}\theta_1 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_1$

parts.text: Using your result in part (ii), find the area swept out by the planet as it travels from $P_0$ (where $\theta = 0$) to $P_2$ (where $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$).
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Area swept out by the planet between $P_0$ and $P_2$ (where $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$):
$= \frac{ab}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{ab}{8}\pi - \frac{ab}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{ab}{8}\left(\pi - \sqrt{2}\right)$

parts.text: Kepler's Second Law states that the line joining the planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. Assume that the planet is at position $P_3$ (where $\theta = \theta_3$), $\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta_3 < \pi$, moving towards $P_4$ (where $\theta = \pi$). Using Kepler's Second Law, find the value of $\theta_3$ such that the planet takes an equal amount of time to travel from $P_3$ to $P_4$ as it takes to travel from $P_0$ to $P_2$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
Let $A_4$ be the area swept out by the planet from $P_3$ to $P_4$:
$A_4 = \frac{ab}{2}\pi - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\pi - \left(\frac{ab}{2}\theta_3 - \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_3\right)$
$= \frac{ab}{2}(\pi - \theta_3) + \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_3$
Since the areas swept out must be equal in the same amount of time (Kepler's Second Law):
$\frac{ab}{4}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \cdot 2 = \frac{ab}{2}(\pi - \theta_3) + \frac{ab}{4}\sin\theta_3$
$\frac{ab}{4}\left(\pi - \sqrt{2}\right)^{...}$
Equation: $\frac{ab}{4}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{ab}{4}(2\pi - 2\theta_3 + \sin\theta_3)$
$2\pi + \sin\theta_3 - 2\theta_3 = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\sin\theta_3 - 2\theta_3 = -\frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
From GC: $\theta_3 \approx 2.8523 \approx 2.85$

before.question_text: The diagram below shows an unsharpened pencil. It is cylindrical in shape. The diameter and length of the pencil are 0.7 cm and 16 cm respectively.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of the pencil, leaving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: A number of this pencil can fit exactly into a pencil case with dimensions as given in the diagram below.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Find the maximum number of pencils that can fit into the pencil case.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Max number of pencils per row $= 6 \div 0.7 = 8$ (rounded down)

Max number of rows $= 2 \div 0.7 = 2$ (rounded down)

Total number of pencils $= 8 \times 2 = 16$

subparts.text: Hence, find the percentage of empty space in the box.

Volume of 16 pencils $= 16 \times 1.96\pi = 31.36\pi$ cm$^3$

Required percentage $= \dfrac{(6 \times 16 \times 2) - 31.36\pi}{192} \times 100\% = 48.7\%$ (to 3 s.f.)

before.question_text: The marks scored by a group of $800$ students in a Science test are shown in the cumulative frequency curve below. The paper was marked out of $100$.

parts.text: Use the graph to estimate
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the median mark,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Median $\approx 72$

subparts.text: the interquartile range.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: Interquartile range $= 80 - 61 = 19$

parts.text: To get a distinction for the Science test, a student has to obtain more than $70$ marks. Find the probability that a student, selected at random, obtained a distinction. Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Number of students who scored less than $70$ marks $= 340$
Probability $= \dfrac{800 - 340}{800} = \dfrac{460}{800} = \dfrac{23}{40}$

parts.text: A student obtained $k$ marks or less in the Science test with probability $\dfrac{1}{5}$. Find the value of $k$.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Two students are chosen at random. Using the value of $k$ from part (c), find the probability that one of them obtained a distinction in the Science Test and the other obtained $k$ marks or less in the Science Test. Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
parts.label: d
parts.solution: $\left(\dfrac{460}{800} \times \dfrac{160}{799}\right) \times 2 = \dfrac{184}{799}$

parts.text: The same $800$ students also sat for an English test. The box and whisker diagram below illustrates the marks obtained. The maximum possible mark was also $100$. Compare the marks gained for the Science and English tests in two different ways.
parts.label: e
parts.answer: Science had a higher median than English; English had a larger IQR (less consistent).
parts.solution:
1) Median of Science test ($72$ marks) is higher than median of English test ($64$ marks). It shows that students scored higher in Science test than English test.

2) Interquartile range of English test $= 75 - 54 = 21$, which is higher than the interquartile range of Science test ($19$). The marks obtained from the students are more consistent in Science test.

before.question_text: The diagram shows the speed-time graph of a particle over a period of 90 seconds. The particle reaches a maximum speed of 15 m/s in $k$ seconds. The particle is travelling at a constant speed from time $= k$ seconds to time $= p$ seconds.

parts.text: The acceleration is $0.5$ m/s$^{2}$. Show that $k = 20$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Speed increases linearly from $5$ m/s to $15$ m/s during $0 \leq t \leq k$.
Acceleration $= \dfrac{15 - 5}{k} = \dfrac{10}{k} = 0.5$.
$k = \dfrac{10}{0.5} = 20$. Shown.

parts.text: The shaded area represents the distance travelled. The distance travelled is 800 m. Find the value of $p$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Total area under speed–time graph:
From $t=0$ to $t=20$: trapezium of parallel sides $5$ and $15$, height $20$: area $= \dfrac{1}{2}(5+15)(20) = 200$.
From $t=20$ to $t=90$: trapezium of parallel sides $(p-20)$ and $(90-0) = 70$ at speed $15$... 
Using $\dfrac{1}{2}\left[(p-20) + 70\right] \times 15 = 800 - 200 = 600$
$(p-20) + 70 = 80$
$p - 20 = 10$
$p = 30$.

parts.text: On the axes below, draw the distance-time graph for the 90 s of the particle's motion.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Curve from $(0,0)$ rising with increasing gradient to $(20, 150)$; straight line from $(20, 150)$ to $(30, 300)$; curve rising with decreasing gradient from $(30, 300)$ to $(90, 800)$.
parts.solution:
Distance is the integral of speed.
• From $t=0$ to $t=20$: speed increases linearly (acceleration), so distance is a curve with increasing gradient from $(0,0)$ to $(20,\ 200)$.
• From $t=20$ to $t=30$: constant speed $15$ m/s, so distance is a straight line from $(20,\ 200)$ to $(30,\ 350)$.
• From $t=30$ to $t=90$: speed decreases linearly to $0$, so distance is a curve with decreasing gradient from $(30,\ 350)$ to $(90,\ 800)$, with horizontal tangent at $(90,\ 800)$.

before.question_text:
Three friends, Tan, Mei and Jaya are planning for an $8$-day holiday trip to Japan in December $2023$. They plan to travel from Osaka to Tokyo and then back to Osaka. Below is the itinerary.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Day} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline \textbf{Location} & \text{Singapore to Osaka} & \text{Osaka to Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo} & \text{Tokyo to Osaka} & \text{Osaka to Singapore} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: Estimate, correct to the nearest km, the driving distance between Osaka and Tokyo.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Measured distance between Osaka and Tokyo on the map $\approx 12.4$ cm.
Scale $1 : 4\,050\,000$, so $1$ cm represents $40.5$ km.
Driving distance $= 12.4 \times 40.5 = 502$ km (nearest km).

parts.text: There are $2$ rest stops between Osaka and Tokyo. Jaya plans to drive for $2$ hours to the first rest stop at an average speed of $90$ km/h. Mei will drive to the second rest stop $200$ km away from the first rest stop at an average speed of $100$ km/h. Lastly, Tan will drive to Tokyo at an average speed of $110$ km/h. Tan, Mei and Jaya will take a $30$-minute break at each rest stop. Calculate the total amount of time taken to reach Tokyo. Give your answer to the nearest hour.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Osaka to rest stop $1$: distance $= 90 \times 2 = 180$ km (time = $2$ h).
Rest stop $1$ to rest stop $2$: time $= \dfrac{200}{100} = 2$ h.
Rest stop $2$ to Tokyo: time $= \dfrac{502 - 180 - 200}{110} \approx 1.11$ h.
Total time $= 2 + 2 + 1.11 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 6.11$ h $\approx 6$ hours (nearest hour).

parts.text: Tan, Mei and Jaya plan to rent a car that can fit $3$ luggage to drive to Tokyo and back to Osaka. Mei collated some information (shown above) that she found on the Internet and suggested to her other $2$ friends that taking the bullet train is a cheaper option than to drive. Do you agree with Mei? Justify your answer and show your working clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Yes, agree with Mei. Total cost for car (Large Car, fits $3$ luggage) including fuel, rental, parking and tolls $= \yen 161\,001$. Total cost for bullet train (Econ with luggage, $3$ persons, round trip, with $45\%$ increment after $1$ Oct $2023$) $= 1.45 \times \yen 18\,000 \times 2 \times 3 = \yen 156\,600$. Since $\yen 156\,600 < \yen 161\,001$, the bullet train is the cheaper option.
parts.solution:
Cost of driving (Large Car for $3$ luggage):
Fuel one way: $\dfrac{502}{100} \times 8.2 = 41.18$ litres; round trip $= 82.36$ litres.
Fuel cost $= 82.36 \times \yen 170 = \yen 14\,001$.
Parking: $\yen 6000 \times 5 = \yen 30\,000$.
Toll charges: $\yen 13\,500 \times 2 = \yen 27\,000$.
Car rental: $\yen 90\,000$.
Total car cost $= \yen 90\,000 + \yen 14\,001 + \yen 30\,000 + \yen 27\,000 = \yen 161\,001$.

Bullet train (Econ with luggage, $3$ persons, round trip, with $45\%$ increase after $1$ Oct $2023$):
$1.45 \times \yen 18\,000 \times 2 \times 3 = \yen 156\,600$.

Since $\yen 156\,600 < \yen 161\,001$, the bullet train is the cheaper option.
Yes, agree with Mei.

before.question_text: The figure shows a solid cone with height $VN = 12$ cm and radius $NB = 5$ cm. Find

parts.text: the volume of the cone,
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Volume of cone $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$
$= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (5)^2 (12)$
$= 100\pi$
$\approx 314$ cm$^3$

parts.text: the total surface area of the cone.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Slant height $l = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm
Total surface area $= \pi r^2 + \pi r l$
$= \pi(5)^2 + \pi(5)(13)$
$= 25\pi + 65\pi$
$= 90\pi$
$\approx 283$ cm$^2$

parts.text: A pyramid shown has a square base of sides $10$ cm and has the same volume as the cone. Find the height of the pyramid. Correct all answers to $3$ significant figures.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Volume of pyramid $=$ Volume of cone $= 100\pi$ cm$^3$
$\dfrac{1}{3} \times (10)^2 \times h = 100\pi$
$\dfrac{100h}{3} = 100\pi$
$h = 3\pi$
$\approx 9.42$ cm

before.question_text: Jack visited the Super Nintendo World in Japan and bought a night light in the shape of a star as shown in Diagram I. The star-shaped night light can be modelled as a prism with a cross-sectional area as shown in Diagram II. The star-shaped cross-sectional area is formed by a regular pentagon $ABCDE$ and five identical equilateral triangles. $O$ is the centre of the star. The thickness of the prism is $12$ cm and $AP = 10$ cm.

parts.text: Calculate the star-shaped cross-sectional area.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Cross-sectional area of the star $= $ area of pentagon $+ 5 \times$ area of equilateral triangle.
Using the given dimensions ($AP = 10$ cm; pentagon side worked out from the geometry):
Total area $= 388.555 \approx 389$ cm$^2$.

parts.text: Jack wants to build a wooden frame for the night light and mount it onto the wall using an adhesive tape. The night light fits exactly inside the wooden frames as shown in Design I and Design II. The adhesive tape is applied to one face of the cross surface area of the wooden frame before mounting onto the wall. In Design I, the wooden frame has a uniform width of $6$ cm. In Design II, the wooden frame is made up of five identical isosceles trapezium prisms with a height of $6$ cm. The thickness of the wooden frame is $12$ cm. Given density of wood $= 900$ kg/m$^3$, mass of the night light $= 600$ g, and maximum mass that the adhesive tape can hold $= 8$ kg. Which design should Jack choose to satisfy the condition of the maximum mass that the adhesive tape can hold? Justify your decision with calculations.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Design II (total mass $7932.17$ g, under the $8000$ g limit); Design I exceeds at $8149.46$ g.

before.question_text: The diagram shows a unit circle with centre $O$ and diameter $AB$. The point $C$ lies on the circumference of the circle. The position vectors of $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ respectively.

parts.text: By considering an appropriate scalar product, show that $AC$ and $BC$ are perpendicular.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC} = (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{b})$
$= (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{c}-(-\mathbf{a}))$ (since $\mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{a}$ as $O$ is the midpoint of diameter $AB$)
$= (\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a})$
$= \mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}$
$= |\mathbf{c}|^2 - |\mathbf{a}|^2$
$= 0$ (since $|\mathbf{c}| = |\mathbf{a}| = $ radius of circle)
Hence $AC$ and $BC$ are perpendicular.

parts.text: Give a geometrical interpretation of $\left|\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\right|$.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: It is the length of projection of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ onto $\overrightarrow{OA}$.
parts.solution: $\left|\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a})\right|$ is the length of projection of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ onto $\overrightarrow{OA}$.

parts.text: The point $D$ is such that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. The point $M$ is the mid-point of $AD$ and the point $R$ lies on $OA$ produced such that $OA : AR = 1 : 2$. By considering $\overrightarrow{CM} \times \overrightarrow{CR}$ or otherwise, show that the points $C$, $M$ and $R$ are collinear.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
By Ratio Theorem, $\overrightarrow{OM} = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{OD}+\overrightarrow{OA}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{c}+2\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{a}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}$
$\overrightarrow{CM}\times\overrightarrow{CR} = (\overrightarrow{OM}-\overrightarrow{OC})\times(\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OC})$
$= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}+\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c}\right]\times(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})$
$= \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}-\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}ight)\times(3\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{c})$
$= \dfrac{9}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{c}$
$= \mathbf{0} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{0}$
$= \mathbf{0}$
$\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{CM}$ and $\overrightarrow{CR}$ are parallel.
Since $\overrightarrow{CM}$ and $\overrightarrow{CR}$ are parallel and $C$ is a common point, the points $C$, $M$ and $R$ are collinear.
