The cumulative frequency curve shows the amount of weight loss, measured to the nearest kg, of $200$ men in Alpha Centre. The corresponding cumulative frequency table for this distribution is shown below.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Weight loss } (x\text{ kg}) & \leq 10 & \leq 15 & \leq 20 & \leq 25 & \leq 30 & \leq 35 \\ \hline \text{Cumulative Frequency} & 22 & p & 100 & 168 & 190 & 200 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

parts.text: Determine the value of $p$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Use the curve to estimate
parts.label: b

subparts.text: the median weight loss,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Median weight loss $= 20$ kg

subparts.text: the interquartile range of the weight loss,
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Lower quartile $= 15$ kg
Upper quartile $= 23$ kg
Interquartile range $= 23 - 15 = 8$ kg

subparts.text: the $44^{\text{th}}$ percentile weight loss.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution: $44^{\text{th}}$ percentile $= 19$ kg

parts.text: A second fitness centre, Genesis Centre, also measured the amount of weight loss by $200$ of their men. The box-and-whisker diagram shown illustrates their weight loss achieved.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Find the interquartile range of the weight loss.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: Interquartile range $= 30 - 20 = 10$ kg

subparts.text: How many men achieved a weight loss of more than $30$ kg?
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution: $\dfrac{1}{4} \times 200 = 50$ men

subparts.text: A physical instructor claimed that the weight loss programme at Alpha Centre is more effective than Genesis Centre. Explain if his statement is true.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: The claim is untrue. The median weight loss of Genesis Centre ($25$ kg) is higher than that of Alpha Centre ($20$ kg), so Genesis Centre is more effective at weight loss.

parts.text: Charles needs to take a certification test to become a physical instructor. He takes the test until he passes. Each time he takes the test, the probability that Charles passes is $0.8$. Find the probability that Charles
parts.label: d

subparts.text: passes only at the third attempt,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
P(Charles fails) $= 1 - 0.8 = 0.2$
P(Charles passes only at the third attempt) $= 0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.8 = 0.032$

subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:

before.question_text: The diagram shows a solid consisting of a right circular cone attached to a hemisphere with a common base which is a circle of radius $6$ cm. The volume of the cone is equal to twice the volume of the hemisphere.

parts.text: Show that the height of the cone is $24$ cm.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let the height of the cone be $h$.
Volume of cone $= 2 \times$ Volume of hemisphere
$\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2 h = 2 \times \dfrac{2}{3}\pi(6)^3$
$12h = 288$
$h = \dfrac{288}{12}$
$h = 24$ cm (shown)

parts.text: Find the total surface area of the solid.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Let the slant height of the cone be $l$.
By Pythagoras' Theorem,
$l^2 = 6^2 + 24^2$
$l = \sqrt{612}$
$l = 24.739$ (5 s.f.)
Total surface area of solid $= \pi(6)(24.739) + 2\pi(6)^2$
$= 692.51$ cm$^2$
$= 693$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

parts.text: The same solid is cut into two parts such that the upper part is a cone of base radius $x$ cm and height $y$ cm.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: Find the value of $\dfrac{x}{y}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{6}{24} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ (by similar triangles)

subparts.text: Find the value of $y$ such that the volume of the upper part is equal to the volume of the lower part.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, so $x = \dfrac{1}{4}y$.
Volume of frustum $= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(24) - \dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^2 y$
Volume of upper cone $=$ Volume of frustum $+$ Volume of hemisphere
$\dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^2 y = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(24) - \dfrac{1}{3}\pi x^2 y + \dfrac{2}{3}\pi(6)^3$
$\dfrac{2}{3}\pi x^2 y = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(24) + \dfrac{2}{3}\pi(6)^3$
$\dfrac{2}{3}x^2 y = \dfrac{1}{3}(6)^2(24) + \dfrac{2}{3}(6)^3$ (divide both sides by $\pi$)
$\dfrac{2}{3}x^2 y = 432$
Sub $x = \dfrac{1}{4}y$ into the equation,
$\dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}y\right)^2 y = 432$
$\dfrac{1}{24}y^3 = 432$
$y^3 = 10368$
$y = 21.8$ cm (3 s.f.)

before.question_text: It is given that the volume of a circular cone with base radius $r$ and vertical height $h$ is $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.

parts.text: A hopper consists of an open cylinder of height $h$ m joined to an open cone of radius $r$ m and height $h$ m (see Fig. 1). The slant edge of the cone has a fixed length of $2$ m. As $r$ and $h$ vary, use differentiation to find the exact maximum volume of the hopper.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
Slant edge $= 2$: $h^2 + r^2 = 2^2$, so $r^2 = 4 - h^2$.
Volume of hopper $= $ cylinder $+$ cone $= \pi r^2 h + \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^2 h$.
$V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi h(4 - h^2) = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi(4h - h^3)$
$\dfrac{dV}{dh} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi(4 - 3h^2)$
At stationary values, $4 - 3h^2 = 0 \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ (since $h > 0$).
$\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2} = -8\pi h < 0$, so $V$ is a maximum.
Maximum volume $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{64}{9\sqrt{3}}\pi$ m$^3$.

parts.text: A coffee manufacturer uses such a hopper that has a cone of radius $1.2$ m. For each batch, the coffee drink is initially filled to the brim of the hopper and mixed thoroughly before it is transferred to the packing chamber at a constant rate of $0.2$ m$^3$/s. At a particular point in time, the height of the coffee drink in the cylindrical section is $2.4$ m from the bottom of the cone (see Fig. 2, shaded region). Find the rate at which the height of the coffee drink is changing at this instant.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Coffee leaves at a constant rate, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = -0.2$ m$^3$/s. The surface is in the cylindrical section, radius constant at $1.2$ m.
For the cylinder, $V = \pi(1.2)^2 H$, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \pi(1.2)^2\dfrac{dH}{dt}$.
$\dfrac{dH}{dt} = \dfrac{-0.2}{\pi(1.2)^2} = -0.0442$ m/s.
The height is decreasing at $0.0442$ m/s.

parts.text: After some time has passed in the transfer process, there remains some coffee drink in the conical section with radius $p$ m and height $q$ m (see Fig. 3, shaded region). Find $p$ in terms of $q$ and hence calculate the rate of decrease of $q$ when $q = 0.5$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Height of the full cone $= \sqrt{4 - 1.2^2} = 1.6$ m.
By similar triangles, $\dfrac{p}{q} = \dfrac{1.2}{1.6}$, so $p = \dfrac{3q}{4}$.
Volume remaining in the cone: $V_2 = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi p^2 q = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{3q}{4}\right)^2 q = \dfrac{3}{16}\pi q^3$.
$\dfrac{dV_2}{dq} = \dfrac{9}{16}\pi q^2$
Using $\dfrac{dV_2}{dt} = \dfrac{dV_2}{dq}\cdot\dfrac{dq}{dt}$ with $\dfrac{dV_2}{dt} = -0.2$, $q = 0.5$:
$-0.2 = \dfrac{9}{16}\pi(0.5)^2\dfrac{dq}{dt}$
$\dfrac{dq}{dt} = -0.453$
$q$ is decreasing at $0.453$ m/s.

$\angle AOB = 120^\circ$, $\angle ABO = 30^\circ$

parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$\angle AOB = 120^\circ$, $\angle ABO = 30^\circ$
$\dfrac{OA}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{8}{\sin 120^\circ}$
$OA = \dfrac{8}{\sin 120^\circ}\times\sin 30^\circ \approx 4.6188$ cm
$= 4.619$ cm (3 d.p.)

parts.text: The triangle $ABC$ forms the base of a pyramid. The vertex $X$ is vertically above $O$ and $AX=18$ cm. Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Base area $\triangle ABC = \dfrac{1}{2}(8)(8)\sin 60^\circ \approx 27.7128$ cm$^2$
Slant height of $\triangle AXB$, $l = \sqrt{18^{2}-4^{2}} \approx 17.5499$ cm
Total surface area $= 3\times\dfrac{1}{2}(8)(17.5499)+27.7128$
$\approx 238.31$ cm$^2 = 238$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.)

before.question_text: A manufacturer designs a cylindrical water dispenser with a fixed volume, $V$ cm$^{3}$ where $V > 1$. The manufacturer decides to use stainless steel, with negligible thickness, for the cylindrical body of the water dispenser of height $y$ cm and the circular base of radius $r$ cm. Plastic, with negligible thickness, will be used instead for the circular lid of radius $r$ cm, as shown in Diagram 1. In order to insert a tap, an area of $1$ cm$^{2}$ of stainless steel will be removed from the cylindrical body of the water dispenser. The total area of stainless steel to be used for the cylindrical body and circular base of the water dispenser, as shown in Diagram 2, is denoted by $A$ cm$^{2}$. The manufacturer wants the value of $A$ to be as small as possible.

parts.text: Show that $A = \pi r^{2} + \frac{2V}{r} - 1$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$V = \pi r^2 y$
$y = \frac{V}{\pi r^2}$ ... (1)
$A = \pi r^2 + 2\pi r y - 1$ ... (2)
Substitute (1) into (2):
$A = \pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\frac{V}{\pi r^2}\right) - 1$
$A = \pi r^2 + \frac{2V}{r} - 1$ (Shown)

parts.text: Using differentiation, find in terms of $V$ and $\pi$, the minimum value of $A$, proving that it is a minimum. Simplify your answer.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$\frac{dA}{dr} = 2\pi r - \frac{2V}{r^2}$
When $\frac{dA}{dr} = 0$:
$2\pi r = \frac{2V}{r^2} \Rightarrow r^3 = \frac{V}{\pi} \Rightarrow r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$
$\frac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 2\pi + \frac{4V}{r^3}$
When $r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$: $\frac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 2\pi + \frac{4V}{\frac{V}{\pi}} = 2\pi + 4\pi = 6\pi > 0$
Therefore $A$ is minimum when $r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$.
Minimum value of $A$:
$= \pi\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}\right)^2 + \frac{2V}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}} - 1$
$= \frac{\pi\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}\right)^3 + 2V}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}} - 1$
$= \frac{V + 2V}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}} - 1$
$= \frac{3V}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}} - 1$
$= 3(V^2\pi)^{\frac{1}{3}} - 1$

parts.text: Sketch the graph of $A$ as $r$ varies, stating the coordinates of any turning point(s) in terms of $V$ and $\pi$ and the equations of any asymptotes.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The graph of $A$ against $r$ has a minimum turning point at $\left(\left(\frac{V}{\pi}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}},\ 3(V^2\pi)^{\frac{1}{3}} - 1\right)$ and a vertical asymptote $r = 0$.
See sketch.

parts.text: It is given that the water dispenser, with the minimum value of $A$ found in part (ii), is completely filled with water. When the tap is turned on, the rate of decrease of the volume of water, $W$ cm$^{3}$, in the water dispenser with respect to time $t$ seconds is $ye^{-\frac{t}{\pi r^{3}}}$ cm$^{3}$/s. Find the rate of change of the height of water, $h$ cm, in the water dispenser 1 minute after the tap is turned on, as shown in Diagram 3. Simplify your answer in terms of $V$ and $\pi$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
$W = \pi r^2 h$ is the volume of water and $h$ cm is the height of water.
Given $\frac{dW}{dt} = -y\,e^{-\frac{t}{\pi r^3}}$.
When $A$ is minimum, $r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$ and $y = \frac{V}{\pi r^2} = \frac{V}{\pi\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}\right)^2} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$.
Therefore $W = \pi\left(\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}\right)^2 h \Rightarrow W = (V^2\pi)^{\frac{1}{3}} h$
$\frac{dW}{dh} = (V^2\pi)^{\frac{1}{3}}$
$\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{dh}{dW} \times \frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{1}{(V^2\pi)^{\frac{1}{3}}} \times \left(-y\,e^{-\frac{t}{\pi r^3}}\right)$
When $t = 1$ min $= 60$ s, with $r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$ (so $\pi r^3 = V$) and $y = \sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}$:
$\frac{dh}{dt} = -\frac{\sqrt[3]{\frac{V}{\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{60}{V}}}{(V^2\pi)^{\frac{1}{3}}} = -\frac{e^{-\frac{60}{V}}}{(\pi^2 V)^{\frac{1}{3}}}$ cm/s
The rate of change of the height of water is decreasing.

before.question_text: The stem-and-leaf diagram shows the time, in seconds, taken by some students to complete a task.

parts.text: Find the range.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Range $=$ largest value $-$ smallest value
$= 114 - 40 = 74$ s

parts.text: Find the median.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
There are $23$ values, so the median is the $12^{\text{th}}$ value when they are in order.
Counting through the stem-and-leaf diagram gives
Median $= 73$ s

parts.text: Construct a box-and-whisker plot that represents the above data. Label the crucial data clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Box-and-whisker plot with minimum $= 40$, lower quartile $= 64$, median $= 73$, upper quartile $= 84$, maximum $= 114$.
parts.solution:
The five values needed are read from the ordered data:
minimum $= 40$, lower quartile $= 64$, median $= 73$, upper quartile $= 84$, maximum $= 114$.
Draw a box from $64$ to $84$ with a line at $73$, and whiskers out to $40$ and $114$, all against a numbered time axis.

parts.text: The students are expected to take at most $70$ seconds to complete the task. Find, as a fraction in its simplest form, the probability that
parts.label: d

subparts.text: a student, who is randomly selected, meets the expectation of the teacher,
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$10$ of the $23$ students meet the expectation.
$P = \dfrac{10}{23}$

subparts.text: one of the two students who are randomly selected, does not meet the expectation of the teacher.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$13$ of the $23$ do not meet the expectation.
Exactly one of the two selected does not meet it — the other one does — and this can happen in two orders:
$P = \dfrac{13}{23} \times \dfrac{10}{22} + \dfrac{10}{23} \times \dfrac{13}{22}$
$= 2 \times \dfrac{130}{506} = \dfrac{260}{506} = \dfrac{130}{253}$

before.question_text: Singapore aims to be a test-bed for micro-wind technology generating electricity with low wind speeds. A wind power station is proposed to be erected in a 250 m by 250 m horizontal field at Pulau Ubin and some wind towers will be built. Each wind tower has three rotor blades and the length of each blade is 40 m.

parts.text:
According to building regulations, the minimum distance between two wind towers, measured from the foot of one tower to another, has to be five times the length of a rotor blade.
An engineer made a suggestion on how to arrange five wind towers $W_{1},\ W_{2},\ W_{3},\ W_{4}$ and $W_{5}$ in a square field. The arrangement is shown in the diagram below, with $W_{1},\ W_{2},\ W_{4},\ W_{5}$ at the four corners and $W_{3}$ at the centre.
Explain why the engineer's suggestion does not meet the building regulations. Support your answer with working.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: The required minimum distance is $5 \times 40 = 200$ m, but a corner tower is only $176.8$ m from the centre tower $W_{3}$, which is less than 200 m. So the arrangement does not meet the regulations.
parts.solution:
Minimum distance required $= 5 \times \text{blade length} = 5 \times 40 = 200$ m.
The distance from a corner tower to the centre tower $W_{3}$ is half the diagonal of the square field. By Pythagoras' Theorem:
$$\text{diagonal} = \sqrt{250^{2} + 250^{2}} = \sqrt{125\,000} = 353.55\ldots \text{ m}$$
$$W_{1}W_{3} = \frac{353.55}{2} = 176.8 \text{ m (1 d.p.)}$$
Since $176.8 \text{ m} < 200 \text{ m}$, the distance from each corner tower to $W_{3}$ is less than the required minimum.
$\therefore$ the engineer's suggestion does not meet the building regulations.
(The side distances $W_{1}W_{2} = W_{1}W_{4} = 250$ m are acceptable; it is only the four distances to the centre that fail.)

parts.text:
Singapore wants to estimate the cost savings from generating electricity through this wind station. The formula $C = -10y^{2} + 90y - 130$ is used to estimate the cost savings in $C$ million dollars during the first $y$ years of operation.
This formula can be re-written as $C = a(y - n)^{2} + m$ where it will take $n$ years to achieve the maximum cost savings of $m$ million dollars. Find the maximum cost savings and the number of years it will take to achieve this.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: It takes 4.5 years to achieve a maximum cost savings of 72.5 million dollars.
parts.solution:
Complete the square:
$$C = -10y^{2} + 90y - 130$$
$$= -10(y^{2} - 9y) - 130$$
$$= -10\left[(y - 4.5)^{2} - 4.5^{2}\right] - 130$$
$$= -10(y - 4.5)^{2} + 10(20.25) - 130$$
$$= -10(y - 4.5)^{2} + 202.5 - 130$$
$$= -10(y - 4.5)^{2} + 72.5$$
So $a = -10$, $n = 4.5$ and $m = 72.5$.
Since $-10(y - 4.5)^{2} \leq 0$, the greatest value of $C$ is $72.5$, occurring when $y = 4.5$.
$\therefore$ it takes 4.5 years to achieve a maximum cost savings of 72.5 million dollars.

before.question_text: A hot water tank, shown in Diagram I, is made by joining a hemisphere of radius 30 cm to an open cylinder of radius 30 cm and height 70 cm. The tank is full of water.

parts.text: Calculate the volume of water, in litres, that the tank can contain.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
The tank is a cylinder topped by a hemisphere, both of radius 30 cm.
$$V_{\text{cylinder}}=\pi r^2h=\pi(30)^2(70)=63\,000\pi\text{ cm}^3$$
$$V_{\text{hemisphere}}=\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3=\frac{2}{3}\pi(30)^3=18\,000\pi\text{ cm}^3$$
$$V_{\text{total}}=63\,000\pi+18\,000\pi=81\,000\pi=254\,469.0\text{ cm}^3$$
Convert to litres using $1\text{ litre}=1000\text{ cm}^3$:
$$V=\frac{254\,469.0}{1000}=254.469\approx 254\text{ litres (3 s.f.)}$$

parts.text: Calculate the total surface area, including the base, of the outside of the tank.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The outside consists of the curved surface of the cylinder, the flat circular base, and the curved surface of the hemisphere. (The cylinder is open at the top, where the hemisphere joins it, so no extra circle is counted there.)
$$\text{Curved surface of cylinder}=2\pi rh=2\pi(30)(70)=4200\pi$$
$$\text{Base}=\pi r^2=\pi(30)^2=900\pi$$
$$\text{Curved surface of hemisphere}=2\pi r^2=2\pi(30)^2=1800\pi$$
$$\text{Total}=4200\pi+900\pi+1800\pi=6900\pi$$
$$=21\,676.99\ldots\approx 21\,700\text{ cm}^2\text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

parts.text: All of the water from the tank runs into a bath, shown in Diagram II, which it just completely fills. The bath is a prism whose cross-section is a trapezium. The lengths of the parallel sides of the trapezium are 0.4 m and 0.6 m. The depth of the bath is 0.3 m. Calculate the length of the bath, in metres.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Cross-sectional area of the trapezium:
$$A=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h=\frac{1}{2}(0.4+0.6)(0.3)=0.15\text{ m}^2$$
Convert the volume of water to cubic metres using $1\text{ m}^3=1\,000\,000\text{ cm}^3$:
$$V=254\,469.0\text{ cm}^3=0.2544690\text{ m}^3$$
For a prism, $V=A\times \ell$, so
$$\ell=\frac{V}{A}=\frac{0.2544690}{0.15}=1.6964\ldots$$
$$\ell\approx 1.70\text{ m (3 s.f.)}$$

$$\text{Curved surface of cylinder}=2\pi rh=2\pi(30)(70)=4200\pi$$
$$\text{Base}=\pi r^2=\pi(30)^2=900\pi$$
$$\text{Curved surface of hemisphere}=2\pi r^2=2\pi(30)^2=1800\pi$$
$$\text{Total}=4200\pi+900\pi+1800\pi=6900\pi$$

parts.text: All of the water from the tank runs into a bath, shown in Diagram II, which it just completely fills. The bath is a prism whose cross-section is a trapezium. The lengths of the parallel sides of the trapezium are 0.4 m and 0.6 m. The depth of the bath is 0.3 m. Calculate the length of the bath, in metres.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Cross-sectional area of the trapezium:
$$A=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h=\frac{1}{2}(0.4+0.6)(0.3)=0.15\text{ m}^2$$
Convert the volume of water to cubic metres using $1\text{ m}^3=1\,000\,000\text{ cm}^3$:
$$V=254\,469.0\text{ cm}^3=0.2544690\text{ m}^3$$
For a prism, $V=A\times \ell$, so
$$\ell=\frac{V}{A}=\frac{0.2544690}{0.15}=1.6964\ldots$$
$$\ell\approx 1.70\text{ m (3 s.f.)}$$

before.question_text: A flag pole with Flag A is attached to a pillar by a rope of length 21 cm, as shown in the diagram.

parts.text: Find $\angle PQR$, the angle between the pole of Flag A and the wall.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
In $\triangle PQR$, $\angle QRP = 90^\circ$, $QR = 20$ cm and $RP = 21$ cm.
$\tan \angle PQR = \frac{21}{20}$
$\angle PQR = \tan^{-1}\frac{21}{20} = 46.397^\circ$
$\angle PQR = 46.4^\circ$ (1 d.p.)

parts.text: A flag pole with Flag B, which is longer than that of Flag A, is fixed to the wall at the same angle. Given that $\angle SQT$ is equal to $\angle PQR$, without the use of a calculator, write down the value of $\tan \angle SQT$ and suggest a reason for your answer.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: $\tan \angle SQT = \frac{21}{20}$, because $\angle SQT = \angle PQR$ and equal angles have equal tangents.
parts.solution:
$\tan \angle SQT = \tan \angle PQR = \frac{21}{20}$
Reason: $\angle SQT$ is given to be equal to $\angle PQR$, and equal angles have equal tangent ratios. (Equivalently, $\triangle QST$ is an enlargement of $\triangle QRP$, so the ratio of opposite side to adjacent side is unchanged.)

parts.text: The vertical distance between the top of both ropes is 10 cm. Find $ST$, the length of rope attaching the pole of Flag B to the pillar.
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
In $\triangle PQR$ (right-angled at $R$):
$PQ = \sqrt{20^{2} + 21^{2}} = \sqrt{841} = 29$ cm
$T$ is 10 cm above $P$ on the pillar, so $QT = QP + PT = 29 + 10 = 39$ cm.
In $\triangle QST$, $\angle QST = 90^\circ$ and $\angle SQT = 46.397^\circ$.
$ST = QT \sin \angle SQT = 39 \sin 46.397^\circ = 28.24$
$ST = 28.2$ cm (3 s.f.)

before.question_text: Figure 4a shows a wire frame in the shape of a sector $OAB$ with centre $O$ and radius $x\text{ cm}$. Angle $AOB = 75^{\circ}$ and the area of the sector $OAB$ is $128\frac{1}{3}\text{ cm}^{2}$. [Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$]

parts.text: Find the value of $x$.
parts.label: i

parts.text: Find the perimeter of sector $OAB$, leaving your answer as a fraction.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$$\text{Arc } AB = \frac{75}{360} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = \frac{5}{24} \times 88 = \frac{55}{3}\text{ cm}$$
$$\text{Perimeter} = OA + OB + \text{arc } AB = 14 + 14 + \frac{55}{3} = \frac{84 + 55}{3} = \frac{139}{3} = 46\frac{1}{3}\text{ cm}$$

parts.text: The wire frame is then reshaped to form an isosceles trapezium, $PQRS$, as shown in Figure 4b. It is given that $PS = QR = 6\text{ cm}$, $PQ$ is parallel to $SR$ and the length of $PQ$ is equal to the radius of the sector in Figure 4a. Show that the shortest distance between $PQ$ and $SR$ is 5.096 cm, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The same wire is used, so the perimeter of $PQRS$ equals the perimeter of the sector, $\frac{139}{3}$ cm. Also $PQ = 14$ cm.
$$SR = \frac{139}{3} - 14 - 6 - 6 = \frac{139 - 78}{3} = \frac{61}{3}\text{ cm}$$
Drop perpendiculars from $P$ and $Q$ to $SR$. By symmetry the horizontal overhang at each end is
$$\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{61}{3} - 14\right) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{19}{3} = \frac{19}{6}\text{ cm}$$
By Pythagoras' Theorem, the perpendicular distance $h$ satisfies
$$h^{2} = 6^{2} - \left(\frac{19}{6}\right)^{2} = 36 - \frac{361}{36} = \frac{935}{36}$$
$$h = \frac{\sqrt{935}}{6} = 5.09629\ldots = 5.096\text{ cm (4 s.f.)}\quad\text{(shown)}$$

parts.text: Hence, find the area of trapezium $PQRS$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
$$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}(PQ + SR) \times h = \frac{1}{2}\left(14 + \frac{61}{3}\right) \times 5.09629\ldots$$
$$= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{103}{3} \times 5.09629\ldots = 87.486\ldots$$
$$= 87.5\text{ cm}^{2} \text{ (3 s.f.)}$$

before.question_text: The diagram shows a pentagon, $ABCDE$, with all sides of length $3$ cm. Two of the interior angles are each $90^\circ$.

parts.text: Show that angle $ADB$ is $41.41^\circ$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution: $AD = BD = \sqrt{3^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{18}$ cm. In $\triangle ADB$ with $AB = 3$: $3^2 = 18 + 18 - 2(18)\cos\angle ADB$; $\cos\angle ADB = \dfrac{18+18-9}{2(18)} = \dfrac{27}{36}$; $\angle ADB = 41.41^\circ$ (shown).

parts.text: The diagram also shows a container in the shape of an inverted pyramid. The open end of the container is the pentagon $ABCDE$. The container has a volume of $60\text{ cm}^3$. Calculate the vertical height, $OX$, of the pyramid.

parts.text:
A curve $C$ is defined by the equation $xy + y^{2} - x^{3} = 7$.

Find the coordinates of the point where the tangent line to the curve $C$ is parallel to the $y$-axis and state the equation of this tangent line.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Differentiating $xy + y^{2} - x^{3} = 7$ implicitly with respect to $x$:

$y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 3x^{2} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3x^{2} - y}{x + 2y}$

The tangent is parallel to the $y$-axis when $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ is undefined, i.e. $x + 2y = 0$, so $x = -2y$.

Substituting into the curve: $(-2y)y + y^{2} - (-2y)^{3} = 7$

$-2y^{2} + y^{2} + 8y^{3} = 7 \Rightarrow 8y^{3} - y^{2} - 7 = 0$

$y = 1$ is a root, so $(y-1)\left(8y^{2} + 7y + 7\right) = 0$. The quadratic has discriminant $49 - 224 < 0$, so $y = 1$ is the only real root.

Then $x = -2(1) = -2$, giving the point $(-2,\ 1)$ and tangent line $x = -2$.

parts.text:
A curve is defined parametrically by the equations $x = at$, $y = \dfrac{a}{t^{2}}$. The fixed point $P$ on the curve has parameter $p$.

Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point $P$, leaving your answer in terms of $a$ and $p$. $[3]$

Given that the normal at point $P$ does not meet the curve again, find exactly the range of values of $p$. $[4]$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\dfrac{2a}{t^{3}}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2}{t^{3}}$.

At $P$ (where $t = p$) the tangent gradient is $-\dfrac{2}{p^{3}}$, so the normal gradient is $\dfrac{p^{3}}{2}$.

$P$ has coordinates $\left(ap,\ \dfrac{a}{p^{2}}\right)$, so the normal is

$y = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}\left(x - ap\right) + \dfrac{a}{p^{2}}$.

For the normal to meet the curve again, substitute $x = at$, $y = \dfrac{a}{t^{2}}$:

$\dfrac{a}{t^{2}} - \dfrac{a}{p^{2}} = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}\left(at - ap\right)$

$\dfrac{1}{t^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{p^{2}} = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}(t - p)$

$\dfrac{p^{2} - t^{2}}{t^{2}p^{2}} = \dfrac{p^{3}}{2}(t-p) \Rightarrow \dfrac{(p-t)(p+t)}{t^{2}p^{2}} = -\dfrac{p^{3}}{2}(p-t)$

Since $t \neq p$ for another intersection, divide by $(p-t)$:

$\dfrac{p+t}{t^{2}p^{2}} = -\dfrac{p^{3}}{2} \Rightarrow 2(p+t) = -p^{5}t^{2} \Rightarrow p^{5}t^{2} + 2t + 2p = 0$

The normal does not meet the curve again when this quadratic in $t$ has no real root:

Discriminant $= 4 - 4\left(p^{5}\right)(2p) < 0 \Rightarrow 4 - 8p^{6} < 0 \Rightarrow p^{6} > \dfrac{1}{2}$

$|p| > \dfrac{1}{2^{1/6}}$, i.e. $p < -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[6]{2}}$ or $p > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt[6]{2}}$.

parts.text:
By using the method of difference, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = k - \mathrm{f}(n)$, where $k$ is a constant and $\mathrm{f}(n)$ is an expression in $n$ to be found. $[4]$

Explain why $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)}$ is a convergent series and state the value of the sum to infinity. $[2]$
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
By partial fractions, $\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = \dfrac{1}{r+2} - \dfrac{1}{r+3}$ (with $A = 1$, $B = -1$).
$\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = \sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{1}{r+2} - \dfrac{1}{r+3}\right)$
Telescoping gives $= \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{n+3}$ (Shown), so $k = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $\mathrm{f}(n) = \dfrac{1}{n+3}$.
As $n \to \infty$, $\dfrac{1}{n+3} \to 0$, so $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} \to \dfrac{1}{3}$. Hence the series is convergent.
$S_\infty = \dfrac{1}{3}$

parts.text: In the sketch of the curve $y = \sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$, $0 \le x \le 5$, the region under the curve is split into 5 vertical strips of equal width of 1 unit.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show by means of a sketch that $\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{4}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$ is less than the actual area under the graph.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution: The five rectangles using the left endpoint of each strip lie entirely below the increasing curve, so their total area $\displaystyle\sum_{x=0}^{4}\sqrt{\ln(3+x)}$ is an underestimate of the actual area under the graph. (See sketch.)

subparts.label: i
subparts.text: By using the method of difference, show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = k - \mathrm{f}(n)$, where $k$ is a constant and $\mathrm{f}(n)$ is an expression in $n$ to be found.

subparts.label: ii
subparts.text: Explain why $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)}$ is a convergent series and state the value of the sum to infinity.
subparts.solution:
By partial fractions, $\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = \dfrac{1}{r+2} - \dfrac{1}{r+3}$ (with $A = 1$, $B = -1$).
$\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} = \sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{1}{r+2} - \dfrac{1}{r+3}\right)$
Telescoping gives $= \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{n+3}$ (Shown), so $k = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $\mathrm{f}(n) = \dfrac{1}{n+3}$.
As $n \to \infty$, $\dfrac{1}{n+3} \to 0$, so $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{1}{(r+2)(r+3)} \to \dfrac{1}{3}$. Hence the series is convergent.
$S_\infty = \dfrac{1}{3}$

subparts.text:
The point $P$ on the Argand diagram represents the complex number $w$ given by $w = u + iv$, where $u$ and $v$ are real and positive.
Explain algebraically why $arg(kw) = arg(w)$ for any real constant $k > 1$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Since $w = u + iv$ with $u > 0$ and $v > 0$:
$kw = ku + ikv$ with $ku > 0$ and $kv > 0$.

$\arg(w) = \tan^{-1}\frac{v}{u}$

$\arg(kw) = \tan^{-1}\frac{kv}{ku} = \tan^{-1}\frac{v}{u} = \arg(w)$

subparts.text:
Points $Q$ and $R$ represent the complex numbers $kw$ and $ikw$, where $k$ is a real constant and $k > 1$.
On the same Argand diagram in the Printed Answer Booklet, plot the points $Q$ and $R$. Show clearly the geometrical relationship between the points $P,Q$ and $R$.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Graph sketch showing $Q$ on the ray $OP$ extended and $R$ obtained by rotating $Q$ by $90°$ anticlockwise about $O$.
subparts.solution:
[See solution diagram: Argand diagram]

$Q$ represents $kw$: on the same ray from $O$ through $P$, but further from $O$ (since $k > 1$).
$R$ represents $ikw$: obtained by rotating $OQ$ by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about $O$.

Geometrical relationship: $OR$ is perpendicular to $OQ$, and $OR = OQ$.

parts.text: In another Argand diagram, the points $A,B$ and $C$ represent the complex numbers $z,f(z)$ and $f(f(z))$ respectively, where $f(z) = z^{2} - 2z$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that $f(f(z)) - f(z) = z(z - 2)(z - 3)(z + 1)$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text:
It is given that $ABC$ is a right-angled triangle, described in an anticlockwise sense, with a right angle at $B$, and $BC = mBA$, where $m$ is a positive real constant.
By considering $\frac{f(f(z)) - f(z)}{f(z) - z}$, or otherwise, show that [2]
$$\left( z - 2 \right)\left( z + 1 \right) = mi$$
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
Rotate $\overrightarrow{BC}$ anticlockwise by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ about $B$ to obtain $m\overrightarrow{BA}$:
$i[f(f(z)) - f(z)] = m(z - f(z))$

$\frac{f(f(z)) - f(z)}{f(z) - z} = -\frac{m}{i} = mi$

Note $f(z) - z = z^2 - 3z = z(z-3)$.

$\frac{z(z-2)(z-3)(z+1)}{z(z-3)} = mi$

$(z-2)(z+1) = mi$ (shown)

subparts.text: In the case where $z = x + 2i$, where $x$ is a positive real number, find $x$ and $m$. Hence obtain the complex number represented by the point $B$.
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
$z = x + 2i$ where $x > 0$.

$(z-2)(z+1) = mi$
$z^2 - z - 2 = mi$
$(x+2i)^2 - (x+2i) - 2 = mi$
$x^2 + 4ix - 4 - x - 2i - 2 = mi$
$(x^2 - x - 6) + i(4x - 2) = mi$

Compare real parts: $x^2 - x - 6 = 0$
$(x-3)(x+2) = 0$
$x = 3$ (reject $x = -2$ since $x > 0$)

Compare imaginary parts: $m = 4x - 2 = 4(3) - 2 = 10$

$f(z) = z^2 - 2z = (3+2i)^2 - 2(3+2i)$
$= 9 + 12i - 4 - 6 - 4i$
$= -1 + 8i$

$B$ represents the complex number $-1 + 8i$.

parts.text: Consider the equation $az^{3} - 9z^{2} + bz - 5 = 0$, where $a$ and $b$ are real constants.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: One root of the equation $az^{3} - 9z^{2} + bz - 5 = 0$ is $z = 2 - i$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
Since $a$ and $b$ are real, the non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs, so $z = 2 + i$ is also a root.
$\left( z - (2 - i) \right)\left( z - (2 + i) \right) = z^{2} - 4z + 5$ is therefore a factor.
The constant term of the cubic is $-5$, so the remaining linear factor must be $az - 1$:
$az^{3} - 9z^{2} + bz - 5 = \left( z^{2} - 4z + 5 \right)(az - 1)$
Expanding: $az^{3} - z^{2} - 4az^{2} + 4z + 5az - 5 = az^{3} - (1 + 4a)z^{2} + (4 + 5a)z - 5$
Comparing $z^{2}$: $-(1 + 4a) = -9 \Rightarrow a = 2$.
Comparing $z$: $b = 4 + 5(2) = 14$.

subparts.text: Hence find all the roots of the equation in part (a)(i) in exact form.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
With $a = 2$ and $b = 14$ the equation is $2z^{3} - 9z^{2} + 14z - 5 = 0$.
As $a$ and $b$ are real and $2 - i$ is a root, its conjugate $2 + i$ is also a root.
A cubic with real coefficients has three roots, so the third root must be real.
From the factorisation $\left( z^{2} - 4z + 5 \right)(2z - 1) = 0$, the third root is $2z - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow z = \frac{1}{2}$.
The roots are $2 - i$, $2 + i$ and $\frac{1}{2}$.
(Check: product of roots $= \frac{5}{2}$, and $(2 - i)(2 + i)\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = 5 \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2}$.)

parts.text:
Solve the equation $w^{5} = 32$, giving the roots in the form $re^{i\alpha}$, where $r > 0$ and $-\pi < \alpha \leq \pi$. [3]
When shown in an Argand diagram, these roots form the vertices of a polygon. Deduce the area of this polygon in the form $k\sin\theta$, where $k$ and $\theta$ are values to be determined. [2]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
$w^{5} = 32 = 32e^{i(2k\pi)}$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$
$w = 32^{\frac{1}{5}}e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{5}} = 2e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{5}}$
Taking $k = -2,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 2$ to keep $-\pi < \alpha \leq \pi$:
$w = 2e^{-i\frac{4\pi}{5}},\ 2e^{-i\frac{2\pi}{5}},\ 2,\ 2e^{i\frac{2\pi}{5}},\ 2e^{i\frac{4\pi}{5}}$
The five roots all have modulus 2 and are equally spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{5}$, so they are the vertices of a regular pentagon inscribed in the circle $|w| = 2$.
The pentagon splits into 5 congruent triangles, each with two sides of length 2 and included angle $\frac{2\pi}{5}$:
Area $= 5 \times \frac{1}{2}(2)(2)\sin\frac{2\pi}{5} = 10\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}$
So $k = 10$ and $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}$ (area $\approx 9.51$).

parts.text:
Joanne begins a monthly savings plan. In the first month, she puts $\$1000$ into her savings, and for each subsequent month she puts 5% more than in the previous month. How many months would it take for Joanne's total savings to first exceed $\$20000$? [3]

Jim starts a monthly savings plan two months later than Joanne with an initial savings of $\$2000$, and for each subsequent month he puts $\$100$ more than in the previous month. The table below shows the person whose total savings exceeds the other person's total savings in the $N$th month since Joanne started saving.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline N & \text{Person with more total savings in the } N\text{th month} \\ \hline 1 & \text{Joanne} \\ 2 & \text{Joanne} \\ 3 & \text{Joanne} \\ 4 & \text{Joanne} \\ 5 & \text{Jim} \\ 6 & \text{Jim} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ n-1 & \text{Jim} \\ n & \text{Joanne} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ \hline \end{array}$

Find the value of $n$. [4]
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Joanne's monthly amounts form a geometric progression with first term $1000$ and common ratio $1.05$.
Total after $n$ months $= \frac{1000\left(1.05^{n}-1\right)}{1.05-1} = 20000\left(1.05^{n}-1\right)$.
$20000\left(1.05^{n}-1\right) > 20000 \Rightarrow 1.05^{n} > 2 \Rightarrow n > \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.05} = 14.20669908$
Since $n$ is a whole number of months, it takes 15 months.

In the $N$th month since Joanne started, Jim has been saving for $N-2$ months, and his amounts form an arithmetic progression with first term $2000$ and common difference $100$.
Jim's total $= \frac{N-2}{2}\left[2(2000) + (N-3)(100)\right] = \frac{N-2}{2}\left[4000 + 100(N-3)\right]$.
Joanne's total $= 20000\left(1.05^{N}-1\right)$.
When $N = 49$: Jim $= \frac{47}{2}(8600) = 202100$ and Joanne $= 20000\left(1.05^{49}-1\right) = 198427$, so Jim has more.
When $N = 50$: Jim $= \frac{48}{2}(8700) = 208800$ and Joanne $= 20000\left(1.05^{50}-1\right) = 209349$, so Joanne has more.
Hence the first month after month 5 in which Joanne again has more is $n = 50$.

parts.text: Suppose instead that Joanne puts a fixed amount of $\$1000$ into her bank account on the first day of every month. The interest rate is $r\%$ per month, so that on the last day of each month the amount in the account on that day is increased by $r\%$. At the end of 2 years, the total amount in her account will be at least $\$30000$. Find the smallest value of $r$, correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: $r \geq 1.74302$, so the least value of $r$ is $1.8$
parts.solution:
Let $k = 1 + \frac{r}{100}$. The deposit made at the start of month 1 earns interest for 24 months, the deposit at the start of month 2 for 23 months, and so on.
Total at the end of 24 months $= 1000k + 1000k^{2} + \cdots + 1000k^{24} = \frac{1000k\left(k^{24}-1\right)}{k-1}$.
$\frac{1000k\left(k^{24}-1\right)}{k-1} \geq 30000 \Rightarrow \frac{k\left(k^{24}-1\right)}{k-1} \geq 30$
Solving with the GC gives $k \geq 1.0174302$, that is $r \geq 1.74302$.
Checking to 1 decimal place: $r = 1.7$ gives a total of $\$29831.6 < \$30000$, while $r = 1.8$ gives $\$30079.6 \geq \$30000$.
Hence the smallest value of $r$ is $1.8$.

Hence, find the area of the region bounded by the curve, the $x$- and $y$-axes and the line $x = 5$. [1]
parts.label: a

parts.text: Evaluate, in terms of $k$, the integral $\int_{2}^{k}\left( \frac{1}{x^{2}} - \frac{2}{1 - x} \right)dx$ where $k > 2$.
parts.label: b

subparts.label: i

parts.text: Find a vector equation of $l$, the line of intersection between $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
A direction vector of $l$ is perpendicular to both normals:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} (1)(-2) - (-1)(-1) \\ (-1)(2) - (1)(-2) \\ (1)(-1) - (1)(2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix} = -3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$
A point on both planes: $(2, -2, 0)$ satisfies $2 - 2 - 0 = 0$ and $4 + 2 - 0 = 6$.
Hence $l: \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix},\ \lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.

parts.text:
Another line, $l_{1}$, has equation $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$, where $\mu$ is a real parameter. Use the result in part (i) to show that $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $l_{1}$ have exactly one common point of intersection. (You are not allowed to use any calculator for this part of the question.) [3]

A third plane, $p_{3}$, has equation $\mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = d$. If $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ have a common line of intersection, show that $b = -1$. [1]
parts.label: ii
parts.answer: Shown. The unique common point is $(0, -2, -2)$.
parts.solution:
Every point common to $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ lies on $l$, so a common point of $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $l_{1}$ is a point of intersection of $l$ and $l_{1}$.
Equating: $2 + \lambda = 2 + \mu$, $-2 = \mu$, $\lambda = 8 + 5\mu$.
From the second equation $\mu = -2$; the first then gives $\lambda = -2$; the third gives $8 + 5(-2) = -2 = \lambda$, which is consistent.
So there is exactly one solution, $\lambda = \mu = -2$, giving the single common point $(0, -2, -2)$ (shown).

If $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ have a common line of intersection, that line must be $l$, so $l$ lies in $p_{3}$ and the direction of $l$ is perpendicular to the normal of $p_{3}$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 @@ 0 @@ 1 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 @@ a @@ b \end{pmatrix} = 1 + b = 0 \Rightarrow b = -1$ (shown).

parts.text: If it is further given that $p_{2}$ bisects the acute angle between $p_{1}$ and $p_{3}$, find the equation for $p_{3}$ completely, in scalar-product form.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
From part (ii), $\mathbf{n}_{3} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ a \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\mathbf{n}_{1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{n}_{2} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$.
If $p_{2}$ bisects the acute angle between $p_{1}$ and $p_{3}$, then $p_{2}$ makes equal angles with $p_{1}$ and $p_{3}$:
$\frac{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{1}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\right|\left|\mathbf{n}_{1}\right|} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{3}\right|}{\left|\mathbf{n}_{2}\right|\left|\mathbf{n}_{3}\right|}$
$\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\left|4-a\right|}{\sqrt{2+a^{2}}} \Rightarrow \sqrt{3}\sqrt{2+a^{2}} = \left|4-a\right|$
$3\left(2+a^{2}\right) = (4-a)^{2} = 16 - 8a + a^{2} \Rightarrow 2a^{2} + 8a - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow a^{2} + 4a - 5 = 0$
$(a+5)(a-1) = 0 \Rightarrow a = -5$ or $a = 1$.
$a = 1$ gives $\mathbf{n}_{3} = \mathbf{n}_{1}$, so $p_{3}$ would be parallel to $p_{1}$ and could not form an angle with it; reject $a = 1$.
Hence $\mathbf{n}_{3} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, and since $(2, -2, 0)$ lies on $l \subset p_{3}$,
$d = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 2 + 10 + 0 = 12$
$p_{3}: \mathbf{r}\cdot\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 12$

parts.text:
Sketch the graph with equation $x^2 + (y - r)^2 = r^2$, where $r > 0$ and $y \leq r$. [2]

A hemispherical bowl of fixed radius $r$ cm is filled with water. Water drains out from a hole at the bottom of the bowl at a constant rate.

Use your graph to show that when the depth of water is $h$ cm (where $h \leq r$), the volume of water in the bowl is given by
$$V = \frac{\pi h^2}{3}(3r - h)$$ [3]
parts.label: i
parts.answer: The graph is the lower half of the circle of centre $(0,\ r)$ and radius $r$, passing through $(-r,\ r)$, $(0,\ 0)$ and $(r,\ r)$. The volume result follows by rotating this arc about the $y$-axis.
parts.solution:
**Sketch.** $x^2 + (y-r)^2 = r^2$ is a circle of centre $(0,\ r)$ and radius $r$. The restriction $y \leq r$ keeps the lower semicircle, which runs from $(-r,\ r)$ down through the origin $(0,\ 0)$ and back up to $(r,\ r)$. This is the cross-section of the bowl, with its lowest point at the origin.

**Volume.** Rotating the arc about the $y$-axis gives the bowl. Water to depth $h$ occupies $0 \leq y \leq h$, and from the equation $x^2 = r^2 - (y - r)^2 = 2ry - y^2$. Hence
$$V = \pi\int_0^h x^2\,dy = \pi\int_0^h \left(2ry - y^2\right)dy = \pi\left[ry^2 - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^h = \pi\left(rh^2 - \frac{h^3}{3}\right)$$
$$V = \frac{\pi h^2}{3}\left(3r - h\right)$$ as required.

parts.text: Given that a full bowl of water would become empty in 24 s, find the rate of decrease, in terms of $r$ and $h$, of the depth of water in the bowl at the instant when the depth of water is $h$ cm.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
When the bowl is full, $h = r$, so
$$V_{\text{full}} = \frac{\pi r^2}{3}(3r - r) = \frac{2\pi r^3}{3}$$

The water drains at a constant rate and the bowl empties in 24 s, so
$$\frac{dV}{dt} = -\frac{1}{24}\cdot\frac{2\pi r^3}{3} = -\frac{\pi r^3}{36}$$

From $V = \pi\left(rh^2 - \frac{h^3}{3}\right)$,
$$\frac{dV}{dh} = \pi\left(2rh - h^2\right)$$

By the chain rule,
$$\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{dV}{dt} \div \frac{dV}{dh} = \frac{-\frac{\pi r^3}{36}}{\pi\left(2rh - h^2\right)} = -\frac{r^3}{36\left(2hr - h^2\right)}$$

The depth is therefore decreasing at a rate of $\dfrac{r^3}{36\left(2hr - h^2\right)}$ cm s$^{-1}$.

parts.text: Without any differentiation, determine, in terms of $r$, the slowest rate at which the depth of water is decreasing.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
The rate of decrease $\dfrac{r^3}{36\left(2hr - h^2\right)}$ is slowest when the denominator, and hence $2hr - h^2$, is greatest.

Completing the square, $2hr - h^2 = r^2 - (h - r)^2$, which is greatest when $h = r$ — the largest depth allowed — giving the value $r^2$. (No differentiation is needed.)

The slowest rate of decrease is therefore
$$\frac{r^3}{36r^2} = \frac{r}{36}\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$$

parts.text: With reference to the Venn diagram below, $S$ is the universal set and $A$ and $B$ are non-empty proper subsets of $S$. Explain whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, and write down the value of $P(A \mid B)$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$.
Since $B \subset A$, $P(A \cap B) = P(B)$ and since $A \subset S$, $P(A) \neq 1$.
So $P(A \cap B) = P(B) \neq P(A)P(B)$. Hence $A$ and $B$ are not independent.
$P(A \mid B) = 1$

parts.text: A fair die has three sides numbered 2, two sides numbered 1 and one side numbered 0 . A game is played by throwing this fair die three times and the score, $X$, is the sum of the numbers obtained.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that $P(X = 2) = \frac{7}{72}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$P(X = 2) = P($'2' appears once and '0' appears twice or '1' appears twice and '0' appears once$)$
$= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3!}{2!} + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3!}{2!} = \frac{7}{72}$

subparts.text:
The table shows an incomplete probability distribution of $X$. Find the missing probabilities, showing your workings clearly. [3]
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \frac{1}{216} & \frac{1}{36} & \frac{7}{72} & {} & \frac{7}{24} & {} & {} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$P(X = 6) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}$
$P(X = 5) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3!}{2!} = \frac{1}{4}$
$P(X = 3) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{6} \times 3! + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{11}{54}$

subparts.text:
The game is played 5 time
Find the probability that exactly one of the games obtained a score of 0 and exactly 2 games obtained a score of more than 2 .
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Required Probability $= P(X = 0) \times [P(X > 2)]^2 \times [P(X = 1 \text{ or } 2)]^2 \times \frac{5!}{2!2!}$
$= \frac{1}{216} \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{216} - \frac{1}{36} - \frac{7}{72}\right)^2 \times \left(\frac{1}{36} + \frac{7}{72}\right)^2 \times \frac{5!}{2!2!}$
$= 0.00164$ (3 s.f.)

subparts.text: Show that $P(X = 2) = \frac{7}{72}$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$P(X = 2) = P($'2' appears once and '0' appears twice or '1' appears twice and '0' appears once$)$
$= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3!}{2!} + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3!}{2!} = \frac{7}{72}$

subparts.text:
The table shows an incomplete probability distribution of $X$. Find the missing probabilities, showing your workings clearly.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \frac{1}{216} & \frac{1}{36} & \frac{7}{72} & {} & \frac{7}{24} & {} & {} \\ \hline \end{array}$$
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
$P(X = 6) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}$
$P(X = 5) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{3!}{2!} = \frac{1}{4}$
$P(X = 3) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{6} \times 3! + \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{11}{54}$

subparts.text:
The game is played 5 time
Find the probability that exactly one of the games obtained a score of 0 and exactly 2 games obtained a score of more than 2 .
subparts.label: iii
subparts.solution:
Required Probability $= P(X = 0) \times [P(X > 2)]^2 \times [P(X = 1 \text{ or } 2)]^2 \times \frac{5!}{2!2!}$
$= \frac{1}{216} \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{216} - \frac{1}{36} - \frac{7}{72}\right)^2 \times \left(\frac{1}{36} + \frac{7}{72}\right)^2 \times \frac{5!}{2!2!}$
$= 0.00164$ (3 s.f.)

before.question_text: In the diagram, $AC = 10$ cm, $BC = 5$ cm and $AB = x$ cm. It is also given that $\sin\angle ACB = \frac{3}{5}$.

parts.text:
Find
(a) the value of $\cos\angle ACB$, leaving your answer in fraction, [1]
(b) the exact value of $x^{2}$. [2]
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
(a) From the diagram $\angle ACB$ is acute, so $\cos\angle ACB$ is positive.
$\cos\angle ACB = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} = \frac{4}{5}$
(b) By the cosine rule,
$x^{2} = AC^{2} + BC^{2} - 2(AC)(BC)\cos\angle ACB$
$x^{2} = 10^{2} + 5^{2} - 2(10)(5)\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)$
$x^{2} = 100 + 25 - 80$
$x^{2} = 45$

parts.text: Hence find the exact value of $\sin\angle BAC$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$AB = x = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}$
By the sine rule,
$\frac{\sin\angle BAC}{BC} = \frac{\sin\angle ACB}{AB}$
$\sin\angle BAC = \frac{5 \times \frac{3}{5}}{3\sqrt{5}}$
$= \frac{3}{3\sqrt{5}}$
$= \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$

parts.text: An air defence technology company develops an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) for surveillance purposes. The wing of the UAV is in the shape of a triangle $ABC$ with dimensions $AB = 10$ m, $AC = 8$ m and angle $BAC = \frac{\pi}{6}$ radians (see Figure 2). The wing of the UAV is to be mounted into a slot of length 5.05 m in the main body. During the manufacturing of the wing, the magnitude of the error for the angle $BAC$ allowed is denoted by $\theta$ radians. Assume that $\theta$ is a sufficiently small angle, show that $$BC^2 \approx \left(a\sqrt{3}\right)\theta^2 + b\theta + \left(c - b\sqrt{3}\right)$$ for constants $a$, $b$ and $c$ to be determined. [4] Hence find the largest value of $\theta$ (in radians) so that the wing can be fitted into the slot, leaving your answer correct to 6 decimal places. [3] Comment on the validity of the method used to calculate $\theta$. [1]
parts.label: a
parts.answer: $a = 40$, $b = 80$, $c = 164$. Largest $\theta = 0.000831$. Since the value obtained for $\theta$ is sufficiently small, using the small-angle approximation result to calculate the maximum value of $\theta$ is valid.

parts.text: The company has decided to build a new manufacturing facility. The facility will have a horizontal rectangular base $OPQR$ where $OP = 20$ m and $PQ = 10$ m. The trapezoidal wall $ORVS$ has fixed heights $OS = 8$ m and $RV = 13$ m. The trapezoidal wall $PQUT$ has heights $PT = x$ m and $QU = y$ m such that the roof $STUV$ is always a plane. All walls are perpendicular to the base $OPQR$. The unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{k}$ are taken along $OP$, $OR$ and $OS$ respectively.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: If the two trapezoidal walls $ORVS$ and $PQUT$ are identical, determine the angle between the roof $STUV$ and the line passing through $O$ and $Q$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: The company decides to cover the entire roof $STUV$ with solar panels. The roof $STUV$ is to be constructed such that the sun ray perpendicular to the roof is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$. Find the equation of the roof $STUV$. Is it feasible to construct such a roof? Justify your answer.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Equation of plane $STUV$: $\mathbf{r} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = 16$. By observation, $(16, 0, 0)$ lies on the plane $STUV$. Since $OP = 20$ m, it is not feasible to build such a roof. Alternatively, $\overrightarrow{OT} = \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \\ x \end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \\ x \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = 16$, so $x = -2$; it is impossible to build the roof as one edge would have to be underground.

before.question_text:
The position vector of the point $A$ is $2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{k}$, and the equation of the line $l$ is $\mathbf{r} = -7\mathbf{i} + 15\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k} + \lambda\left(3\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}\right)$.
Find the position vectors of the points $B$ and $C$, both lying on $l$, such that $AB = AC = 10$. [3]
Given that the point $P$ is the midpoint of $BC$, show that the equation of the plane $\Pi_{1}$, which contains $l$ and is perpendicular to $AP$, is $\mathbf{r} \cdot \left(-3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}\right) = \alpha$, where $\alpha$ is an integer to be determined. [2]
The planes $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$ have equations $\mathbf{r} \cdot \left(\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}\right) = 5$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \left(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}\right) = 1$ respectively, and $A$ lies in both $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$.

parts.text: Determine the position vector of $D$, the point of intersection between $\Pi_{1}$, $\Pi_{2}$ and $\Pi_{3}$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
First the two results demanded in the stem.
A general point of $l$ is $\begin{pmatrix} -7 + 3\lambda \\ 15 - 7\lambda \\ -5 + 4\lambda \end{pmatrix}$, so $\overrightarrow{AX} = \begin{pmatrix} -9 + 3\lambda \\ 15 - 7\lambda \\ -4 + 4\lambda \end{pmatrix}$ and
$\left|\overrightarrow{AX}\right|^{2} = 74\lambda^{2} - 296\lambda + 322 = 100 \Rightarrow \lambda^{2} - 4\lambda + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 1 \text{ or } 3$.
$\lambda = 1$: $\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 8 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$; $\lambda = 3$: $\overrightarrow{OC} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -6 \\ 7 \end{pmatrix}$.
$P$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $\overrightarrow{OP} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$.
$\overrightarrow{AP} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -7 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = -9 - 7 + 16 = 0$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}$ is perpendicular to $l$ and is a normal of $\Pi_{1}$; using the point $(-7,\ 15,\ -5)$ of $l$,
$\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} -7 \\ 15 \\ -5 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = 21 + 15 - 20 = 16$.
Now solve the three plane equations simultaneously:
$-3x + y + 4z = 16$, $x + 2y - 3z = 5$, $x - 2y + z = 1$.
Solving (e.g. with the GC) gives $x = 15$, $y = 13$, $z = 12$, so $\overrightarrow{OD} = \begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 13 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$.

parts.text: Hence find the volume of the tetrahedron $ABCD$. $\left[\text{Volume of tetrahedron} = \frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height}\right]$
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Take triangle $ABC$ as the base. With $A(2,\ 0,\ -1)$,
$\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 8 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -6 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 64 \\ 48 \\ 36 \end{pmatrix}$.
Base area $= \frac{1}{2}\left|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}\right| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{7696} = 43.863$ units$^2$.
A unit normal to plane $ABC$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{481}}\begin{pmatrix} 16 \\ 12 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$, so the height is
$\left|\overrightarrow{AD} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{481}}\left|\begin{pmatrix} 13 \\ 13 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 16 \\ 12 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}\right| = \frac{481}{\sqrt{481}} = \sqrt{481} = 21.932$ units.
Volume $= \frac{1}{3} \times 43.863 \times 21.932 = 320.67 \approx 321$ units$^3$.
(Equivalently $\frac{1}{6}\left|\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \left(\overrightarrow{AC} \times \overrightarrow{AD}\right)\right| = \frac{1924}{6} = 320.67$.)

before.question_text:
Given that $y=\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]$, show that
$$\cos y\,\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{x+1} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \cos y\,\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\sin y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$$
[2]

parts.text: By further differentiation, find the Maclaurin series for $y$, up to and including the term in $x^{3}$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
From $y=\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]$ we have $\sin y=\ln(x+1)$; differentiating gives $\cos y\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$, and differentiating again gives
$$\cos y\,\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\sin y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}.$$
Differentiating once more:
$$\cos y\,\frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}-3\sin y\,\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-\cos y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3}=\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}}.$$
At $x=0$: $\sin y=\ln 1=0$, so $y=0$ and $\cos y=1$.
From the first equation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$.
From the second: $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-0=-1$, so $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-1$.
From the third: $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}-0-1=2$, so $\dfrac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}=3$.
Hence
$$y=0+x+\frac{-1}{2!}x^{2}+\frac{3}{3!}x^{3}+\cdots=x-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{3}+\cdots$$

parts.text: Find the set of values of $x$ for which the value of $y$ is within $\pm 0.1$ of the value found by its Maclaurin series.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Require
$$\left|\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]-\left(x-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{3}\right)\right|<0.1.$$
The function $y$ is defined only where $-1 \leq \ln(x+1) \leq 1$, i.e. $e^{-1}-1 \leq x \leq e-1$.
Using a graphic calculator to sketch $\left|y-\left(x-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{3}\right)\right|$ and $y=0.1$, the curves meet at $x=-0.521$ and $x=0.783$ (3 s.f.).
Hence the required set is $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -0.521<x<0.783\right\}$.

parts.text: Deduce the series expansion for $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}}}$ up to and including the term in $x^{2}$.
parts.label: iii
parts.solution:
Since $\sin y=\ln(x+1)$ and $y=\sin^{-1}\left[\ln(x+1)\right]$ lies in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, we have $\cos y=\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}} \geq 0$.
From $\cos y\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x+1}$,
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}}}.$$
Differentiating the series in part (i) term by term:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=1-x+\frac{3}{2}x^{2}+\cdots$$
Hence $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-\left(\ln(x+1)\right)^{2}}}=1-x+\dfrac{3}{2}x^{2}+\cdots$

before.question_text: Evaluate the following integrals.

parts.text: By using the substitution $x = \frac{1}{t}$, find $\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}\,dx$ leaving your answer in exact form.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $x = \frac{1}{t}$, so $dx = -\frac{1}{t^{2}}\,dt$.
When $x = \sqrt{2}$, $t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$; when $x = 2$, $t = \frac{1}{2}$.
For $t > 0$, $\sqrt{x^{2} - 1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{t^{2}} - 1} = \frac{\sqrt{1 - t^{2}}}{t}$.
$\int_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}dx = \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{1}{\frac{1}{t}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}{t}}\left(-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)dt$
$= \int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{t^{2}}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}\left(-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)dt$
$= -\int_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}dt$
$= -\left[\sin^{-1}t\right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}^{\frac{1}{2}}$
$= -\left(\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$
$= \frac{\pi}{12}$

parts.text:
Show that $\int\frac{x + 1}{x^{2} + 4x + 7}dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^{2} + 4x + 7\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{x + 2}{\sqrt{3}} + c$. [4]

Hence find $\int_{-2}^{1}\frac{\left| x + 1 \right|}{x^{2} + 4x + 7}dx$ exactly. [3]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Write $x + 1 = \frac{1}{2}(2x + 4) - 1$, and note $x^{2} + 4x + 7 = (x + 2)^{2} + 3$.
$\int\frac{x+1}{x^{2}+4x+7}dx = \frac{1}{2}\int\frac{2x+4}{x^{2}+4x+7}dx - \int\frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}+3}dx$
$= \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^{2}+4x+7\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{3}} + c$ (shown)

For the definite integral, $\left|x+1\right| = -(x+1)$ on $[-2,\ -1]$ and $x+1$ on $[-1,\ 1]$.
Let $F(x) = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(x^{2}+4x+7\right) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{3}}$.
$F(-2) = \frac{1}{2}\ln 3 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}0 = \frac{1}{2}\ln 3$
$F(-1) = \frac{1}{2}\ln 4 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \ln 2 - \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}}$
$F(1) = \frac{1}{2}\ln 12 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \frac{1}{2}\ln 12 - \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}$
$\int_{-2}^{1}\frac{|x+1|}{x^{2}+4x+7}dx = -\left[F(-1) - F(-2)\right] + \left[F(1) - F(-1)\right]$
$= \left(\frac{1}{2}\ln 3 - \ln 2 + \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{2}\ln 12 - \ln 2 - \frac{\pi}{6\sqrt{3}}\right)$
The $\tan^{-1}$ terms cancel:
$= \frac{1}{2}\ln 36 - 2\ln 2 = \ln 6 - \ln 4 = \ln\frac{3}{2}$

parts.text:
The masses, in grams, of $200$ apples of each of variety A and variety B are recorded.
The cumulative frequency curves show the distributions of their masses.
parts.label: a

subparts.text:
Use the curve to estimate

(a) the median mass for variety A, **[1]**

(b) the $60$th percentile for variety B, **[1]**

(c) the interquartile range for variety B. **[2]**
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) The median is the $100$th value. Read across from a cumulative frequency of $100$ to the variety A curve, then down to the mass axis.

Median mass for variety A $= 94$ g

(b) $60\%$ of $200 = 120$. Read across from a cumulative frequency of $120$ to the variety B curve.

$60$th percentile for variety B $= 106$ g

(c) Lower quartile: read at a cumulative frequency of $\dfrac{1}{4} \times 200 = 50$, giving $Q_1 = 87$ g.

Upper quartile: read at a cumulative frequency of $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 200 = 150$, giving $Q_3 = 114$ g.

Interquartile range $= 114 - 87 = 27$ g

subparts.text:
George sells apples in packs of $6$.
He uses apples with a mass between $80$ g and $120$ g and rejects the rest.

Which variety of apples would be better for George to use?
Justify your answer using appropriate figures.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Variety A, since $180 - 24 = 156$ of the variety A apples have a mass between $80$ g and $120$ g, compared with $164 - 32 = 132$ of the variety B apples.
subparts.solution:
Variety A: at $120$ g the cumulative frequency is $180$; at $80$ g it is $24$.

Number George can use $= 180 - 24 = 156$

Variety B: at $120$ g the cumulative frequency is $164$; at $80$ g it is $32$.

Number George can use $= 164 - 32 = 132$

Since $156 > 132$, variety A gives more usable apples, so George should use variety A.

parts.text: A box contains $9$ apples of variety A and $7$ apples of variety B.
parts.label: b

subparts.text:
Two apples are taken from the box at random, without replacement.

Find, as a fraction in its simplest form, the probability that the two apples are the same variety.
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
$P(\text{same variety}) = P(AA) + P(BB)$

$= \dfrac{9}{16} \times \dfrac{8}{15} + \dfrac{7}{16} \times \dfrac{6}{15}$

$= \dfrac{72}{240} + \dfrac{42}{240}$

$= \dfrac{114}{240} = \dfrac{19}{40}$

subparts.text:
These two apples are returned to the box and $4$ apples of variety C are also added to the box.
Three apples are taken from the box, at random, without replacement.

Find, as a fraction in its simplest form, the probability that two out of the three apples are of variety C.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
The box now holds $9 + 7 + 4 = 20$ apples, of which $4$ are variety C.

$P(\text{exactly two of variety C}) = \dfrac{\binom{4}{2} \times \binom{16}{1}}{\binom{20}{3}}$

$= \dfrac{6 \times 16}{1140} = \dfrac{96}{1140} = \dfrac{8}{95}$

parts.text: Given that the complex number $z$ satisfies the equation $z = \dfrac{4}{z^{*}}$, show that $|z| = 2$.
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$$z = \frac{4}{z^{*}} \;\Longrightarrow\; z z^{*} = 4 .$$
For any complex number, $z z^{*} = |z|^2$, so
$$|z|^2 = 4 \;\Longrightarrow\; |z| = 2 \quad (|z| \ge 0). \qquad \text{(shown)}$$

parts.text: Express $1 - i\sqrt{3}$ in the form $r e^{i\theta}$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
$$r = \left|1 - i\sqrt3\right| = \sqrt{1^2 + \left(\sqrt3\right)^2} = \sqrt4 = 2 .$$
The point $(1,\,-\sqrt3)$ lies in the fourth quadrant, so
$$\theta = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{1}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{3} .$$
$$\boxed{1 - i\sqrt3 = 2e^{-i\pi/3}}$$

parts.text:
On a single Argand diagram, sketch the loci

(a) $z = \dfrac{4}{z^{*}}$,\ \ [3]

(b) $|z+2| = \left|z - 1 + i\sqrt3\right|$.\ \ [3]
parts.label: iii
parts.answer: (a) the circle centre $O$, radius $2$; (b) the straight line $y = \sqrt3\,x$ (the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $(-2,\,0)$ and $(1,\,-\sqrt3)$).
parts.solution:
**(a)** From part (i) the equation is equivalent to $|z| = 2$: a **circle with centre the origin and radius $2$**.

**(b)** Write the equation as
$$\left|z - (-2)\right| = \left|z - \left(1 - i\sqrt3\right)\right| ,$$
so the locus is the **perpendicular bisector** of the segment joining $A(-2,\,0)$ and $B\left(1,\,-\sqrt3\right)$.

Midpoint of $AB$: $\left(-\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Gradient of $AB$: $\dfrac{-\sqrt3 - 0}{1 - (-2)} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so the perpendicular bisector has gradient $\sqrt3$:
$$y + \frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \sqrt3\left(x + \frac12\right) \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \sqrt3\,x .$$

The two loci are sketched on one Argand diagram: the circle $|z|=2$ and the line $y = \sqrt3 x$ through the origin, which cuts the circle at two points.

parts.text: The complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2$ satisfy the equations $z = \dfrac{4}{z^{*}}$ and $|z+2| = \left|z - 1 + i\sqrt3\right|$, where $\arg(z_1) > \arg(z_2)$. Find the exact values of $z_1$ and $z_2$, giving your answers in the form $x + iy$.
parts.label: iv
parts.solution:
$z_1$ and $z_2$ are the intersections of the two loci, i.e. of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ with the line $y = \sqrt3\,x$:
$$x^2 + 3x^2 = 4 \;\Longrightarrow\; 4x^2 = 4 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = \pm 1 .$$
So the points are $\left(1,\ \sqrt3\right)$ and $\left(-1,\ -\sqrt3\right)$, i.e. $1 + \sqrt3\,i$ and $-1 - \sqrt3\,i$.

Their arguments are
$$\arg\!\left(1 + \sqrt3\,i\right) = \frac{\pi}{3}, \qquad \arg\!\left(-1 - \sqrt3\,i\right) = -\frac{2\pi}{3} ,$$
and $\dfrac{\pi}{3} > -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so
$$\boxed{z_1 = 1 + \sqrt3\,i, \qquad z_2 = -1 - \sqrt3\,i}$$

parts.text: Another complex number $w$ satisfies $w = \dfrac{4}{w^{*}}$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}\pi < \arg(w) < \pi$. Explain why $\arg(z_1 - w) - \arg(z_2 - w) = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$.
parts.label: v
parts.answer: Since $z_2 = -z_1$, the chord $z_1z_2$ is a diameter of the circle $|z| = 2$, on which $w$ also lies; the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so the angle between $z_1 - w$ and $z_2 - w$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
parts.solution:
$w$ also satisfies $w = \dfrac{4}{w^{*}}$, so by part (i) $|w| = 2$: $w$ lies on the same circle as $z_1$ and $z_2$ (and $\tfrac12\pi < \arg w < \pi$ puts $w$ in the second quadrant, so $w \ne z_1,\,z_2$).

Since $z_2 = -z_1$, the points $z_1$ and $z_2$ are diametrically opposite, so the chord $z_1z_2$ is a **diameter** of the circle. The vectors $z_1 - w$ and $z_2 - w$ are the two chords from $w$ to the ends of that diameter, and the **angle in a semicircle is a right angle**, so the angle between them is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Taking directions into account (with $w$ in the second quadrant, $z_1$ in the first and $z_2$ in the third),
$$\arg(z_1 - w) - \arg(z_2 - w) = \frac{\pi}{2} .$$
*Check with $w = 2e^{i2\pi/3} = -1 + \sqrt3 i$:* $z_1 - w = 2$ (argument $0$) and $z_2 - w = -2\sqrt3\,i$ (argument $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$), giving a difference of $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. $\checkmark$

before.question_text:
On an Argand diagram, sketch the locus of the points representing the complex number $z$ such that $\left|z - 2 + i\right| = \sqrt{5}$. [2]

Hence find exactly the range of

parts.text: $\left|1 - z\right|$,
parts.label: i
parts.solution:
$\left|z - (2 - i)\right| = \sqrt{5}$ is the circle with centre $C(2,\ -1)$ and radius $\sqrt{5}$.

$\left|1 - z\right| = \left|z - 1\right|$ is the distance from the fixed point $A(1,\ 0)$ to $z$.

$$CA = \sqrt{(2-1)^{2} + (-1-0)^{2}} = \sqrt{2}$$

Since $\sqrt{2} < \sqrt{5}$, the point $A$ lies inside the circle, so the distance from $A$ to a point on the circle ranges between $\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{2}$.

$$\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{2} \leq \left|1 - z\right| \leq \sqrt{5} + \sqrt{2}$$

parts.text: $\arg\left(iz - 1 + 3i\right)$.
parts.label: ii
parts.solution:
Factor out $i$:
$$iz - 1 + 3i = i\left(z + 3 + i\right)$$
(check: $i(z+3+i) = iz + 3i + i^{2} = iz + 3i - 1$).

$$\therefore\ \arg\left(iz-1+3i\right) = \arg i + \arg\left(z - (-3 - i)\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} + \arg\left(z - (-3-i)\right)$$

Let $B(-3,\ -1)$. Distance from $B$ to the centre $C(2,\ -1)$ is $CB = 5 > \sqrt{5}$, so $B$ lies outside the circle and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is parallel to the positive real axis, i.e. $\arg\overrightarrow{BC} = 0$.

The tangents from $B$ make an angle $\alpha$ with $BC$, where
$$\sin\alpha = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow \alpha = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)$$

$$\therefore\ -\sin^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right) \leq \arg\left(z+3+i\right) \leq \sin^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)$$

$$\frac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right) \leq \arg\left(iz - 1 + 3i\right) \leq \frac{\pi}{2} + \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)$$

parts.text: Find $\int\frac{1}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$$\int\frac{1}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int\frac{1}{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2} + x^{2}}\,dx$$
$$= \frac{1}{9}\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{2}{3}}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{\frac{2}{3}}\right) + C = \frac{1}{6}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right) + C$$

parts.text: Find the exact value of $\int_{0}^{2}\frac{x}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator ($\frac{d}{dx}\left(4+9x^{2}\right) = 18x$):
$$\int_{0}^{2}\frac{x}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{18}\int_{0}^{2}\frac{18x}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{18}\Big[\ln\left(4+9x^{2}\right)\Big]_{0}^{2}$$
$$= \frac{1}{18}\left(\ln 40 - \ln 4\right) = \frac{1}{18}\ln 10$$

Sketch the graph of $y = e^{\sqrt{x}}$ where $x \geq 0$. [1]

The region bounded by the curve $y = e^{\sqrt{x}}$, the line $x = 4$ and the $x$- and $y$-axes is rotated completely about the $x$-axis. Use the substitution $t = \sqrt{x}$ to show that the volume of the solid obtained is given by $2\pi\int_{0}^{2}te^{2t}\,dt$, and evaluate this integral exactly. [6]
parts.label: c
parts.solution:
Sketch: $y = e^{\sqrt{x}}$ starts at $(0,\ 1)$, is increasing for all $x \geq 0$, and rises steeply (at $x = 4$, $y = e^{2} \approx 7.39$). The gradient is infinite at the origin.

$$V = \pi\int_{0}^{4}y^{2}\,dx = \pi\int_{0}^{4}e^{2\sqrt{x}}\,dx$$

Let $t = \sqrt{x}$, so $x = t^{2}$ and $\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t$.
When $x = 0$, $t = 0$; when $x = 4$, $t = 2$.

$$V = \pi\int_{0}^{2}e^{2t}\left(2t\right)dt = 2\pi\int_{0}^{2}te^{2t}\,dt\quad\blacksquare$$

By parts, with $u = t$ and $\frac{dv}{dt} = e^{2t}$:
$$\int_{0}^{2}te^{2t}\,dt = \left[\frac{t e^{2t}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} - \int_{0}^{2}\frac{e^{2t}}{2}\,dt = e^{4} - \left[\frac{e^{2t}}{4}\right]_{0}^{2}$$
$$= e^{4} - \left(\frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{3e^{4}}{4} + \frac{1}{4}$$

$$V = 2\pi\left(\frac{3e^{4}+1}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\pi\left(3e^{4}+1\right)\ \text{units}^{3}$$

parts.text: Find $\int\frac{1}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
$$\int\frac{1}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{9}\int\frac{1}{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2} + x^{2}}\,dx$$
$$= \frac{1}{9}\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{2}{3}}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{\frac{2}{3}}\right) + C = \frac{1}{6}\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3x}{2}\right) + C$$

parts.text: Find the exact value of $\int_{0}^{2}\frac{x}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx$.
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
The numerator is a multiple of the derivative of the denominator ($\frac{d}{dx}\left(4+9x^{2}\right) = 18x$):
$$\int_{0}^{2}\frac{x}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{18}\int_{0}^{2}\frac{18x}{4+9x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{18}\Big[\ln\left(4+9x^{2}\right)\Big]_{0}^{2}$$
$$= \frac{1}{18}\left(\ln 40 - \ln 4\right) = \frac{1}{18}\ln 10$$

parts.text:
The random variable $X$ has a binomial distribution with mean 4 and variance $\frac{4}{3}$.

Show that the largest value which $X$ can take is 6. [2]

A sample of $N\ (> 50)$ independent observations of $X$ is taken. Find the least value of $N$ such that there is a probability of more than 0.9 for the sample mean to be at least 3.8. [3]
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Let $X \sim B(n,\ p)$.
$$np = 4,\qquad np(1-p) = \frac{4}{3}$$

Dividing: $1 - p = \frac{4/3}{4} = \frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow p = \frac{2}{3}$, hence $n = \frac{4}{p} = 6$.

$X$ takes the values $0,\ 1,\ \ldots,\ n$, so the largest value $X$ can take is $6$. $\blacksquare$

For a sample of size $N$, by the Central Limit Theorem (since $N > 50$ is large)
$$\overline{X} \sim N\!\left(4,\ \frac{4/3}{N}\right)\ \text{approximately}$$

$$P\!\left(\overline{X} \geq 3.8\right) > 0.9 \Rightarrow P\!\left(Z \geq \frac{3.8-4}{\sqrt{\frac{4}{3N}}}\right) > 0.9$$

$$\frac{-0.2}{\sqrt{\frac{4}{3N}}} < -1.281552 \Rightarrow \frac{0.2\sqrt{3N}}{2} > 1.281552$$

$$\sqrt{3N} > 12.81552 \Rightarrow 3N > 164.237 \Rightarrow N > 54.7$$

$$\therefore\ \text{least } N = 55$$

parts.text:
In a study of a certain species of tigers, a sample of 120 cubs is observed. The number of cubs which will reach its matured age is denoted by $Y$. State, in context, two assumptions needed for $Y$ to be well modelled by a binomial distribution. [2]

Assume now that $Y$ has a binomial distribution and that the probability for a cub to reach its matured age is $\frac{3}{4}$. Using a suitable approximation, find the probability that at least 90 of these cubs will reach their matured age. [3]
parts.label: b
parts.solution:
Assumptions:
1. Each of the 120 cubs has the same probability of reaching its matured age.
2. Whether one cub reaches its matured age is independent of whether any other cub does.

$Y \sim B\!\left(120,\ \frac{3}{4}\right)$.
$$np = 120\times\frac{3}{4} = 90 > 5,\qquad nq = 120\times\frac{1}{4} = 30 > 5$$

Since $n$ is large and both $np$ and $nq$ exceed 5,
$$Y \sim N(90,\ 22.5)\ \text{approximately}$$

Applying a continuity correction:
$$P(Y \geq 90) \approx P(Y_{c} > 89.5) = P\!\left(Z > \frac{89.5 - 90}{\sqrt{22.5}}\right) = P(Z > -0.10541)$$

$$= 0.5420\ (4\ \text{s.f.}) \approx 0.542$$

subparts.text: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 2p \\ 5p \end{pmatrix}$ and $|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \frac{5\sqrt{29}}{2}$. Find the two possible values of $p$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: A line joins the two points $X(-6, 2)$ and $Z(6, -2)$. Use vectors to show whether or not the point $Y(3, 1)$ lies on this line.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: $Y$ does not lie on the line (vectors $\overrightarrow{XY}$ and $\overrightarrow{XZ}$ are not parallel).
subparts.solution:
$\overrightarrow{XZ} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$

$\overrightarrow{XY} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$

Since $\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix} \neq k\begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ for any scalar $k$, $\overrightarrow{XZ}$ and $\overrightarrow{XY}$ are not parallel. Therefore $Y(3, 1)$ does not lie on the line $XZ$.

parts.text: In the diagram, $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $B$ is the midpoint of $OD$. $OA = \frac{2}{3}OC$, $CN = \frac{3}{7}CD$, $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Express each of the following vectors in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. (a) $\overrightarrow{CD}$ [1] (b) $\overrightarrow{ON}$ [2]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) $\overrightarrow{CD} = \overrightarrow{OD} - \overrightarrow{OC} = 2\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}$

(b) $\overrightarrow{ON} = \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CN} = \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a} + \dfrac{3}{7}\left(2\mathbf{b} - \dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{a}\right) = \dfrac{6}{7}(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b})$

subparts.text: Write down the ratio of (a) area of $\triangle OAB$ : area of $\triangle OCB$ [1] (b) area of $\triangle OAB$ : area of $\triangle OCD$ [2]
subparts.label: ii
subparts.solution:
(a) Triangles $OAB$ and $OCB$ share the same height from $B$ to line $OC$, so area ratio equals base ratio $OA : OC = 2 : 3$.

(b) $\dfrac{[\triangle OAB]}{[\triangle OCD]} = \dfrac{[\triangle OAB]}{[\triangle OCB]} \times \dfrac{[\triangle OCB]}{[\triangle OCD]} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Ratio $= 1 : 3$

parts.text:
The table shows the scores of 10 students in a Mathematics test.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline \text{Test score} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 21 & 2 \\ \hline 49 & 3 \\ \hline 55 & 1 \\ \hline 65 & 1 \\ \hline 80 & 1 \\ \hline 95 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
The test scores are also represented in the box-and-whisker plot below. Write down the values of $w$, $x$, $y$ and $z$.
parts.label: a
parts.solution:
Ordered scores (10 values): 21, 21, 49, 49, 49, 55, 65, 80, 95, 95.
Minimum $= 21$, maximum $z = 95$.
Lower quartile $w = $ 3rd value $= 49$.
Median $x = \frac{49 + 55}{2} = 52$.
Upper quartile $y = $ 8th value $= 80$.
$w = 49$, $x = 52$, $y = 80$, $z = 95$

parts.text: The temperature at Ang Mo Kio was recorded every day for 60 days. The cumulative frequency graph shows the distribution of the temperatures.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Use the graph to estimate (a) the number of days that had temperatures above $29^\circ$C, [1] (b) the interquartile range of the temperatures. [1]
subparts.label: i
subparts.solution:
(a) Number of days with temperature above $29^\circ$C $= 60 - 48 = 12$ days
(b) From the graph, $Q_3 = 28.9$ and $Q_1 = 28.2$.
Interquartile range $= 28.9 - 28.2 = 0.7^\circ$C

subparts.text: The temperature at Jurong was recorded every day for the same period. The interquartile range of the temperatures at Jurong is $1.5^\circ$C. Explain what this tells us about the temperature at Jurong compared with the temperature at Ang Mo Kio.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: The temperatures at Jurong have a larger spread than the temperatures at Ang Mo Kio.
subparts.solution: The interquartile range at Jurong ($1.5^\circ$C) is larger than that at Ang Mo Kio ($0.7^\circ$C), so the temperatures at Jurong have a larger spread (are more varied) than those at Ang Mo Kio.
